body: **MAIN CASE**: a principal case in the assigned reading. **NOTE CASE**: a principal case from the same chapter, included for context.

**Cites:** R2d § 13 means Restatement (Second) of Torts § 13; R3d is the Restatement (Third) of Torts (Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm unless noted). R3d Misc. Prov. is the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024); its boxes say "approved" for sections the ALI membership adopted (2022–2023) and "T.D. 3, draft" for sections still in draft. The Restatement supplement has the text of each, with the Comments for the T.D. 3 sections. [[Gray italic text]] comes from outside the class materials, such as Delaware law and later cases. Verify it before relying on it.

blocks.title: Every tort question runs the same five steps (all required)

body.text: Professor Johnson frames tort law as a conflict-resolution device: when should the injured person be able to sue and win? Work every fact pattern the same way.

items: **Who sues whom?** List every plaintiff and every defendant, including employers, owners, hosts, and the government. Vicarious and direct claims are separate.
**Which basis of liability?** Intent (Parts II–III), negligence (Parts IV–IX), or strict liability (Parts XIII–XIV). Many facts support more than one.
**Prima facie case.** Run the elements one at a time, using the labels in the rule boxes. Name the element that is weakest on the facts.
**Defenses and privileges.** Consent, self-defense, necessity, comparative fault, assumption of risk, limitations, and immunity.
**Remedy and allocation.** Compensatory and punitive damages, joint and several liability, contribution, and indemnity.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 8/25, 15th ed. pp. 1–16 · 13th ed. Ch. 1 (Development of Liability Based upon Fault).

items: **A tort** is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law gives the injured person a remedy, usually damages. Tort law is mostly state common law made by judges.

**Goals (weighed together):** (1) compensating injured people; (2) deterring unsafe conduct and giving the actor the cost of the harm; (3) corrective justice, so the wrongdoer repairs the wrong; (4) spreading losses across insurers and enterprises; and (5) giving people a peaceful way to resolve conflict instead of self-help.

**Systemic bias (Goal B).** Ask whose experience defines "reasonable," "outrageous," or "normal" use of land, and how damages rules value different people's lives and earnings. §§ 12, 27 and 33 flag where this matters.

blocks.title: History: the writs of trespass and case

items: **Trespass** covered direct, forcible injuries and was effectively strict liability (Case of Thorns). **Trespass on the case** covered indirect injuries and came to require fault. The 19th century moved most accidental-injury law to a fault (negligence) basis (Brown v. Kendall).
**Burden of proof.** Under fault-based liability, the plaintiff must prove the defendant was at fault. The defendant does not have to prove that it was blameless.

blocks.name: Hulle v. Orynge (The Case of Thorns)
blocks.facts: The defendant cut thorns from his hedge, and they fell onto the plaintiff's land. He went onto the land to retrieve them, and the plaintiff sued in trespass. The casebook excerpt prints only the arguments.
blocks.held: Brian, arguing as counsel in a view later adopted from the bench: every unwarranted invasion of another's land that causes damage is actionable, without regard to fault. A person who acts must act so as not to damage others. If A's timber falls on B's house, A is liable; if A, defending himself against C, strikes B with a stick, A is liable to B.
blocks.why: This is the starting point: early trespass liability was strict. Compare Brown v. Kendall.

blocks.name: Weaver v. Ward
blocks.facts: Weaver and Ward were soldiers in a training skirmish. Ward's musket went off accidentally and wounded Weaver. Ward pleaded that the injury was accidental and against his will. Weaver demurred to the plea.
blocks.held: An actor is liable for a direct injury unless he shows it was "utterly without his fault," as where it was inevitable (for example, if someone had jerked his arm). A plea of accident alone is not enough. Judgment for Weaver on the demurrer.
blocks.why: Fault enters as an excuse the defendant must prove. The burden is still on the defendant.

blocks.name: Brown v. Kendall
blocks.facts: Two dogs, one Brown's and one Kendall's, were fighting. Kendall beat at them with a four-foot stick to separate them. As he backed away and raised the stick over his shoulder, he struck Brown, who was standing behind him, in the eye. The trial judge told the jury that unless separating the dogs was a necessary act, Kendall was liable unless he used extraordinary care, and that he bore the burden on those points.
blocks.held: Shaw, C.J.: there is no liability for an unintended injury caused while doing a lawful act with ordinary care (the care prudent and cautious people use to guard against probable danger). The plaintiff bears the burden of proving the defendant's lack of ordinary care. Under the contributory negligence rule of the time, the plaintiff also lost if he failed to use ordinary care himself. The instructions placed the burden on the wrong party. A new trial was ordered.
blocks.why: This is the American shift to negligence as the basis of accident liability, with the burden on the plaintiff.

blocks.name: Cohen v. Petty
blocks.facts: Petty was driving with Cohen as a guest passenger. He suddenly fainted, lost control, and the car crashed, injuring Cohen. The evidence was that Petty had never fainted before and had no warning. The trial court directed a verdict for Petty.
blocks.held: There is no negligence when a driver loses control because of a sudden illness he could not foresee. A reasonable person could not have guarded against it, so there was no duty to do so. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Foreseeability is the core of fault. Compare Breunig (§ 12), where the driver had warning.

blocks.name: Spano v. Perini Corp.
blocks.facts: Perini's dynamite blasting for a tunnel nearby sent shock waves that wrecked Spano's garage and damaged Davis's car parked inside. There was no physical intrusion of debris and no proof of negligence. The trial court found for the plaintiffs; the Appellate Division reversed under an old rule requiring a physical trespass.
blocks.held: Fuld, C.J.: one who uses explosives is strictly liable for the resulting damage. It makes no difference whether debris entered the land (trespass) or concussion caused the damage (case), and no fault is needed. The blaster, who chose to engage in the activity, should bear its costs rather than the innocent neighbor. Reversed for the plaintiffs.
blocks.why: Fault did not take over everything: abnormally dangerous activities remain strict liability (§ 32).

body.text: Name the basis of liability in your first sentence. If the defendant meant to cause the contact or invasion, start with intentional torts. If not, go to negligence, then consider strict liability. On the essay, plead the alternatives when the facts allow.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 8/27, 15th ed. pp. 27–38; Module on Intent (due 9/1), pp. 38–45 · 13th ed. Ch. 2.A.

body.text: An actor intends a consequence when (any one suffices): (1) the actor acts with the purpose (desire) of causing it; or (2) the actor knows that the consequence is substantially certain to result.

items: **Intent is about consequences, not acts.** Raising an arm is voluntary. The question is whether the actor intended the contact, the apprehension, the confinement, or the entry.
**Substantial certainty** is actual subjective knowledge, not what a reasonable person would have known. That would be negligence. A high probability or a known risk is not enough.
**Motive is irrelevant.** A practical joke, a mistaken belief, or a good-faith purpose does not negate intent.
**Recklessness** (conscious disregard of a known, high risk) is not intent for most intentional torts. IIED is the exception, and recklessness can also support punitive damages.
**Single intent (Wagner):** the actor must intend the contact. Whether the contact is harmful or offensive is judged by the law.
**Dual intent:** the actor must intend the contact and also intend that it harm or offend. [[White v. Muniz (Colo. 2000) took this view for an elderly woman with dementia.]]
Most courts and R3d use single intent. The difference matters most for very young children and people with mental illness.

blocks.name: Garratt v. Dailey
blocks.facts: Brian Dailey, five years nine months old, was in Ruth Garratt's backyard. Garratt said Brian pulled a lawn chair out from under her as she sat down. Brian said he had moved the chair, sat in it himself, and then saw her about to sit where it had been and could not move it back in time. She fell and broke her hip. The trial court first found for Brian.
blocks.held: Hill, J.: a battery is intended if the actor acts for the purpose of causing the contact or knows with substantial certainty that it will result. No desire to harm is needed. The case was remanded to decide whether Brian knew with substantial certainty that Garratt would try to sit where the chair had been. On remand the trial court found that he did, and the judgment for Garratt ($11,000) was affirmed on a second appeal.
blocks.why: This is the leading substantial-certainty case. Children can form intent, and no hostility is needed.

blocks.name: Wagner v. State
blocks.facts: Tracy Wagner was standing in line at a K-Mart when Sam Giese, a mentally disabled patient of the Utah State Developmental Center on a supervised outing, attacked her without provocation. Giese had a history of violence. The Wagners sued the state for negligent supervision. The state moved to dismiss, because the Governmental Immunity Act retained immunity for injuries "arising out of" a battery. The Wagners argued Giese could not commit a battery because he could not appreciate that his contact was harmful.
blocks.held: Battery requires only an intent to make the contact. The contact must be harmful or offensive as a matter of law, but the actor need not intend or understand that it is harmful or offensive. Giese committed a battery, so the claim arose out of a battery and the state was immune. Dismissal affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the single-intent rule. Note the irony: the injured plaintiff argued against finding a battery, because battery triggered immunity.

blocks.name: Ranson v. Kitner
blocks.facts: The defendants were hunting wolves and shot and killed the plaintiff's dog, which looked like a wolf. They acted in good faith. The trial court awarded the plaintiff $50.
blocks.held: A mistake about identity or ownership is no defense to an intentional tort. The hunters intended to kill the animal and are liable for its value. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Intent is the intent to bring about the physical result. An honest mistake does not undo it, though a mistake can matter to privileges.

blocks.name: McGuire v. Almy
blocks.facts: McGuire, a registered nurse, was hired to care for Almy, who was mentally ill, around the clock. During a violent episode Almy broke furniture, threatened to kill anyone who entered, and stood holding the leg of a piece of furniture over her head. When McGuire entered and reached for her hand, Almy struck her. The jury found for McGuire.
blocks.held: Qua, J.: an insane person who forms the intent to strike is liable for battery, even if the decision was irrational. The intent required is to do the act, not to harm. Policy supports the rule: of two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it, and liability encourages guardians to restrain dangerous wards. Judgment for McGuire.
blocks.why: Mental illness does not prevent intent. It can bear on punitive damages, and it is handled separately in negligence (Breunig, § 12).

blocks.name: Talmage v. Smith
blocks.facts: Several boys were on the roofs of sheds on Smith's property. Smith ordered them down and, before they had all left, threw a stick intending to hit one boy, Byron Smith. It hit another, Talmage, in the eye, and he lost the sight of that eye.
blocks.held: When an actor intends an unjustified injury to one person, it does not matter that another person was injured instead. Smith is liable to Talmage. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Transferred intent works between people and, by the traditional rule, between the "trespass" torts.

body.text: Intent transfers when the actor (any one suffices): (1) intends a tort against one person but commits it against another; (2) intends one of the five trespass-based torts but commits a different one; or (3) both.
**The five torts:** battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass to land, and trespass to chattels. Intent generally does **not** transfer into IIED (see § 5, R2d § 46(2)) or into conversion.

A child or a mentally ill person is liable for an intentional tort if he formed the intent. Parents are not vicariously liable at common law, though statutes may make them liable up to a cap. A parent can be liable for the parent's own negligence in supervising the child.

blocks.title: Restatement (Third): no immunity for minors or people with disabilities

body.text: R3d Misc. Prov. Immunities §§ 6–7 (approved 2022): minors and adults with a mental or emotional disability are not immune from tort liability. Age and disability matter only to whether the person committed the tort, for example whether the person formed the intent for battery (as in McGuire and Wagner) or acted negligently (§ 12).

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/1, 15th ed. pp. 45–66 (with § 4) · 13th ed. Ch. 2.B–C.

body.text: The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to cause a harmful or offensive contact with the person of another or a third person, or an imminent apprehension of one; and (2) a harmful or offensive contact with the plaintiff's person directly or indirectly results.

items: **Harmful** means bodily harm: physical impairment, pain, or illness.
**Offensive** means it offends a reasonable sense of personal dignity (R2d § 19), judged by social norms. A particular plaintiff's unusual sensitivity counts only if the defendant knew of it.
**Contact** can be indirect: a thrown object, poison, a trap. It can also be with something closely identified with the body (Fisher).
**Awareness not required.** A plaintiff who was asleep or anesthetized can recover for a battery discovered later.
**No damages needed.** Nominal damages are available, and so are damages for the full harm, foreseeable or not. Punitive damages are available on proof of malice.

blocks.name: Cole v. Turner
blocks.facts: The report records no facts. Chief Justice Holt stated the rules in the abstract.
blocks.held: (1) The least touching of another in anger is a battery. (2) Gently touching someone to get past them in a narrow way, without violence, is not a battery. (3) Violently and rudely forcing one's way past in a struggle is.
blocks.why: The line between offensive contact and the ordinary contacts of social life has been drawn since the earliest cases.

blocks.name: Wallace v. Rosen
blocks.facts: Mable Wallace, recovering from foot surgery, came to her daughter's high school with homework and stopped at the top of a stairway to talk with her daughter and two friends. A fire drill began, and students poured down the stairs. Teacher Harriet Rosen told the group to "move it"; Wallace did not hear, so Rosen touched her on the back to get her attention. Wallace fell down the stairs. The trial court refused Wallace's instruction defining battery as "the knowing or intentional touching of one person by another in a rude, insolent, or angry manner," and the jury found for Rosen.
blocks.held: Kirsch, J.: the instruction was properly refused because the evidence did not support it, but the rule it stated is correct. Battery requires an intentional touching that is rude, insolent, or angry: one that would offend an ordinary person not unduly sensitive about her dignity. Tortious intent means an intent to violate another's legally protected interest, not hostility. A light touch to move someone along during a fire drill is not a battery. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Contacts customary in social life (tapping a shoulder, jostling in a crowd) are not offensive. They are covered by implied consent.

blocks.name: Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel, Inc.
blocks.topic: contact with an object identified with the body
blocks.facts: Fisher, a Black NASA mathematician, was attending a business conference at the hotel. While he stood in the buffet line holding his plate, the manager of the hotel's club snatched the plate from his hand and shouted that a Negro could not be served there. Fisher was not touched and suffered no physical injury, but he was highly embarrassed. The jury found for Fisher, but the trial court entered judgment for the defendants notwithstanding the verdict, and the court of civil appeals affirmed.
blocks.held: Greenhill, J.: snatching an object from a person's hand in an offensive manner is a battery. Battery protects personal dignity, so contact with anything closely identified with the body counts. Damages for humiliation are recoverable without physical injury. The hotel was liable for punitive damages because the club manager acted in a managerial capacity within the scope of his employment. Reversed; judgment for Fisher on the verdict.
blocks.why: This is the "extended personality" rule. It is also a bias case: battery redressed a racial insult when no IIED claim was available. For punitive damages against employers, see § 28.

body.text: The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to cause a harmful or offensive contact, or an imminent apprehension of one; and (2) the plaintiff is thereby put in imminent apprehension of such a contact.

items: **Apprehension** means expectation, not fear. A boxer can apprehend a punch without being afraid of it. The plaintiff must be aware of the threat at the time.
**Imminent:** a threat of future harm ("I'll get you tomorrow") is not an assault (R2d § 29).
**Apparent present ability** is enough, so an unloaded gun counts if the plaintiff does not know it is unloaded. A threat that is plainly impossible to carry out is not (Western Union).
**Words alone** are not an assault unless acts or circumstances make the threat imminent (R2d § 31). Words can also negate an assault ("If you weren't my friend, I'd hit you").
**Conditional threats** ("your money or your life") are an assault when the defendant has no right to impose the condition.

blocks.name: I de S et ux. v. W de S
blocks.facts: At night, W came to I's tavern, which was closed, and beat on the door with a hatchet, wanting wine. When I's wife put her head out of a window and told him to stop, he struck at her with the hatchet and missed.
blocks.held: Thorpe, C.J.: there was harm, and so a trespass, even though no blow landed. Putting a person in fear of a blow is actionable, and damages are recoverable.
blocks.why: This is the origin of assault as a separate tort, which protects the mental interest in freedom from apprehension.

blocks.name: Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Hill
blocks.facts: Mrs. Hill went to the Western Union office to have Sapp, the manager, fix her electric clock. Sapp, who had been drinking, said he would fix it if she would let him "love and pet" her, and reached across the counter toward her shoulder. She stepped back. The counter was 4 feet 2 inches high and so wide that Sapp, stretching, could barely reach its far edge. The jury found for Mrs. Hill against Western Union.
blocks.held: Samford, J.: an assault requires a well-founded apprehension of an imminent battery, which needs an apparent present ability to carry it out. The evidence on whether Sapp could reach her conflicted, so that issue was for the jury. But the judgment was reversed because Sapp's advance was a personal one, outside the scope of his employment, so Western Union was not liable for it.
blocks.why: Reasonable apprehension and apparent ability are what count. It is also an early respondeat superior case (§ 31): the conduct must serve the employer's business.

rows: Freedom from apprehension of a contact
To contact, or to cause apprehension; transfers

body.text: A swing that misses is an assault (if the plaintiff saw it). A swing that connects is a battery, and also an assault if the plaintiff saw it coming. For an unseen blow from behind, there is a battery but no assault.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/1, 15th ed. pp. 45–66 (with § 3) · 13th ed. Ch. 2.D.

body.text: The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to confine the plaintiff (or a third person) within boundaries fixed by the actor; (2) the act directly or indirectly results in such a confinement; and (3) the plaintiff is conscious of the confinement or is harmed by it.

blocks.text: **Means of confinement (any one suffices):** (1) physical barriers; (2) physical force; (3) threats of immediate force against the plaintiff, the plaintiff's family, or the plaintiff's property; (4) asserted legal authority (false arrest); (5) duress, such as keeping the plaintiff's valuable property or purse; or (6) refusing to release the plaintiff when under a duty to provide a means of release (Whittaker).

items: **No reasonable means of escape.** If an exit is reasonable, safe, and known, there is no confinement. A person need not take a dangerous or humiliating exit, such as leaving without clothes.
**Moral pressure or a wish to clear one's name** is not confinement. Neither are future threats, or a demand to stay without any threat of force (Hardy).
**Duration is irrelevant** to liability, though it matters to damages.
**Being shut out** of a place is not confinement. The boundaries must be complete.

blocks.name: Big Town Nursing Home, Inc. v. Newman
blocks.facts: Newman, a retiree, was taken to the nursing home by his nephew on September 19, 1968. The admission papers said he would not be kept against his will. Three days later he tried to leave and to call a taxi. Staff stopped him, took away his phone privileges, locked up his clothes and bag, and caught and brought him back each time he tried to leave. He was put in a wing for senile patients, alcoholics, and the mentally ill, and repeatedly tied into a "restraint chair." He escaped on November 11, having lost 30 pounds. There was no court order of commitment.
blocks.held: False imprisonment is the direct restraint of a person's physical liberty without adequate legal justification. Big Town's whole course of conduct was meant to keep Newman in, in violation of his admission papers. Because it acted intentionally in disregard of his rights, exemplary damages were proper. Affirmed after Newman accepted a remittitur.
blocks.why: Institutional confinement without consent or legal process is false imprisonment, and willful disregard of the plaintiff's rights supports punitive damages (§ 28).

blocks.name: Parvi v. City of Kingston
blocks.facts: Two Kingston police officers found Parvi, who was drunk, in a downtown alley. He told them he had nowhere to go, so they drove him to an abandoned golf course outside the city to "dry out" and left him. He wandered onto the New York State Thruway and was hit by a car. At trial he said he could not remember whether he had been aware of being confined. The trial court dismissed his false imprisonment claim.
blocks.held: Fuchsberg, J.: in New York, false imprisonment, a dignitary tort, requires that the plaintiff be conscious of the confinement. But a present memory of that awareness is not required. Alcohol or his injuries may have erased the memory, and other evidence could show he was aware at the time. Reversed.
blocks.why: Under the dignitary-tort view, the plaintiff must know of the confinement or be harmed by it (R2d § 42).

body.text: **Dissent (Breitel, C.J.):** Parvi remembered nothing and knew of the incident only from later conversations, so he did not make out a prima facie case.

blocks.name: Hardy v. LaBelle's Distributing Co.
blocks.facts: Hardy, a temporary employee, was asked to "tour" the store and was taken into the manager's office, where other employees and a uniformed police officer were present. She was told she had been accused of stealing a watch. She denied it, agreed to take a lie detector test, passed, and received an apology. She testified that she felt she could not leave but that she stayed voluntarily to clear her name. The jury found for LaBelle's.
blocks.held: False imprisonment is the unlawful restraint of a person against her will. Hardy admitted she wanted to stay to exonerate herself, and no threats or force kept her there. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Restraint against the plaintiff's will is required. Staying to protect one's reputation is not confinement.

blocks.name: Enright v. Groves
blocks.facts: Officer Groves saw a dog running loose in violation of the Fort Collins leash ordinance. Mrs. Enright's 11-year-old son said it was his dog and that his mother was in a car at the curb. Groves demanded Mrs. Enright's driver's license. She gave her name and address but refused to produce the license. He told her to produce it or go to jail; she said "Isn't this ridiculous?" and he arrested her. She was later convicted of the leash violation, and a jury awarded her $1,500 for false imprisonment.
blocks.held: Probable cause, or a conviction for the offense for which the person was arrested, defeats a false arrest claim. But Groves arrested Enright for failing to produce her license, not for the leash violation, and no law required a person who was not driving to produce a license on demand. Groves had no authority to make the arrest. Affirmed.
blocks.why: False arrest is false imprisonment under asserted legal authority. Justification depends on the offense for which the person was actually arrested.

blocks.name: Whittaker v. Sandford
blocks.facts: Whittaker had been a member of a religious sect abroad led by Sandford. She decided to leave and accepted his offer of passage home to America on his yacht, on his promise that she would not be detained on board, especially not to reconvert her. When the yacht reached port, Sandford refused to provide a boat to take her ashore, and she was kept on the yacht for about a month, though she was otherwise free to move about it.
blocks.held: Savage, J.: false imprisonment does not require laying hands on the plaintiff; it is enough that her freedom of movement is restrained. When the defendant has a duty to provide a means of release, as Sandford did here by his promise and control of the boats, refusing to do so is an imprisonment. The verdict was upheld on liability.
blocks.why: An omission counts when there is a duty to release (R2d § 45). Compare the general no-duty-to-act rule in negligence (§ 21).

body.text: **Shopkeeper's privilege** and other justifications are in § 9 (Bonkowski) and § 10 (Sindle). Treat them as defenses after you have set out the prima facie case.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/3, 15th ed. pp. 66–79; Module on IIED (due 9/8), pp. 79–95 · 13th ed. Ch. 2.E.

body.text: The defendant is liable when (all required): (1) the conduct is intentional or reckless; (2) the conduct is extreme and outrageous; (3) the conduct causes the emotional distress; and (4) the distress is severe.

items: **Outrageous** means "so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency," so that "atrocious" is the community's reaction (R2d § 46 cmt. d). Mere insults, indignities, threats, annoyances, and petty oppressions are not enough.

**Factors pointing to outrageousness (weighed together):** (1) abuse of a position of power or authority, such as an employer, police officer, landlord, or collection agency; (2) knowledge of the plaintiff's special susceptibility; (3) repeated conduct or a campaign of harassment; (4) threats of violence; and (5) public humiliation or racial or other identity-based abuse.
**Recklessness:** the defendant acts in deliberate disregard of a high probability that distress will follow.
**Severe:** distress no reasonable person could be expected to endure. Physical symptoms are not required but help prove it. The intensity and duration of the distress count.
**Common carriers and innkeepers** are traditionally liable for gross insults to passengers and guests even without outrageousness (Slocum discusses this exception).

blocks.name: State Rubbish Collectors Ass'n v. Siliznoff
blocks.facts: Siliznoff took over collecting rubbish from a brewery that an association member claimed. Association officers told him he had to join and pay, or they would beat him up, destroy his truck, and put him out of business. He signed notes to pay the association, then refused to pay. The association sued on the notes, and he cross-claimed for the distress the threats caused; he testified he was so frightened he became ill, vomited, and missed work. The jury found for Siliznoff.
blocks.held: Traynor, J.: one who, without privilege, intentionally causes severe emotional distress by outrageous conduct is liable, even without physical injury and even though the threats of future harm were not an assault. Mental suffering is already compensated as part of assault, battery, and false imprisonment, so it is anomalous to deny it standing alone. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This case established IIED as a stand-alone tort. Physical injury is not required.

blocks.name: Slocum v. Food Fair Stores of Florida
blocks.facts: Slocum asked a Food Fair employee the price of an item. He replied, "If you want to know the price, you'll have to find out the best way you can... you stink to me." She said the shock brought on a heart attack. The trial court dismissed her complaint.
blocks.held: There is no liability for mere insults, indignities, or threats, whatever their consequences. An ordinary person would suffer only slight distress from this remark, and the special liability of common carriers and innkeepers for insulting patrons does not extend to a grocery store. Making trivial insults actionable would also chill speech. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This sets the floor: rudeness is not outrageous, and the plaintiff's unknown susceptibility does not make it so.

blocks.name: Harris v. Jones
blocks.facts: Harris, a General Motors employee, had stuttered all his life and was nervous about it. His supervisor, Jones, knowing this, mimicked and ridiculed his stutter about 30 times over five months. Harris said this made him more nervous and worsened his stutter. The jury found for Harris against Jones and GM, but the trial court granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
blocks.held: Murphy, C.J.: Maryland recognizes IIED with four elements: (1) intentional or reckless conduct; (2) extreme and outrageous conduct; (3) causation; and (4) severe distress. Jones's conduct, knowing Harris's susceptibility, satisfied the first three, but Harris failed on severity. His stutter and nervousness predated the abuse, and he offered no evidence of how much worse they became. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the elements case. Severity is a real hurdle, and a supervisor's power and knowledge of a susceptibility go to outrageousness, not severity.

blocks.title: IIED aimed at a third person: R2d § 46(2)

body.text: When outrageous conduct is directed at a third person, the actor is liable if he intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress (any one suffices): (a) to a member of that person's immediate family who is present at the time, whether or not the distress results in bodily harm; or (b) to any other person who is present at the time, if the distress results in bodily harm.
Most courts also require that **the defendant know the plaintiff is present** (Taylor).

blocks.name: Taylor v. Vallelunga
blocks.facts: Vallelunga beat Taylor's father. Taylor watched the beating and suffered severe emotional distress. Her complaint did not allege that Vallelunga knew she was present or intended to distress her. The trial court sustained a demurrer.
blocks.held: A plaintiff who witnesses an attack on a family member recovers for her own distress only if the defendant knew she was present, so that he intended, or was substantially certain, to cause her distress. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Intent does not transfer into IIED. Knowledge of the bystander's presence takes its place.

items: [[Racial slurs by an employer or supervisor can be outrageous because of the power imbalance and the history the words carry (Alcorn v. Anbro Engineering, Cal. 1970).]] Compare Fisher (§ 3), which used battery.

[[The First Amendment limits IIED for speech on public matters: public figures must prove actual malice (Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, 1988), and speech on public issues in a public place is protected (Snyder v. Phelps, 2011).]]

body.text: IIED often comes up as a backup claim. Ask first whether a traditional tort (assault, battery, false imprisonment) fits. Then argue outrageousness with the factors and confront severity directly. Graders look for both elements.

blocks.title: Trespass to Land, Trespass to Chattels, and Conversion

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/8, 15th ed. pp. 97–114, and Bradley v. American Smelting (Canvas) · 13th ed. Ch. 2.F–H.

body.text: One who intentionally does any of the following is liable, whether or not harm results (any one suffices): (a) enters land in the possession of another, or causes a thing or a third person to do so; (b) remains on the land; or (c) fails to remove from the land a thing which he is under a duty to remove.

items: **Intent** means intent to enter the land, not intent to trespass. Believing in good faith that the land is your own is no defense (compare Ranson). An involuntary entry, such as being thrown onto the land, is not a trespass.
**No damage needed** (Dougherty). Nominal damages are available, and the actor is liable for any harm the intrusion causes, even if it was unforeseeable and caused without negligence.

**Airspace and subsurface.** The possessor owns the space above the land within the zone of reasonable use, and the area beneath it (Herrin). [[Aircraft overflights in navigable airspace are privileged (United States v. Causby, 1946).]]
**Continuing trespass:** staying, or leaving a thing on the land, after permission ends is a trespass (Rogers; R2d § 160).
**Unintended intrusions** that are negligent or reckless are governed by negligence and require actual harm (R2d § 165).
**Plaintiff:** the person in possession, such as a tenant, not necessarily the owner.

blocks.name: Dougherty v. Stepp
blocks.facts: Stepp entered Dougherty's land without permission and surveyed part of it with a surveyor's chain, claiming it as his own. He marked no trees and cut no brush. The jury found for Stepp, apparently because there was no damage.
blocks.held: Ruffin, C.J.: every unauthorized entry on another's land is a trespass, whether or not it causes actual damage. The law infers damage, "if nothing more, the treading down the grass or herbage." Reversed; new trial ordered.
blocks.why: Trespass protects the right to exclude. Nominal damages vindicate the right and can establish title.

blocks.name: Herrin v. Sutherland
blocks.facts: While hunting, Sutherland repeatedly fired his shotgun at ducks and other birds flying over Herrin's land, over his house and cattle. The shot did not land on the property, but the firing disturbed Herrin's quiet enjoyment.
blocks.held: Callaway, C.J.: firing through the airspace close to the surface is a trespass, though nothing touched the ground. A possessor's rights extend to the airspace he may reasonably use, and missiles crossing it endanger people and property. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Intrusions into the airspace near the ground are trespasses.

blocks.name: Rogers v. Board of Road Comm'rs for Kent County
blocks.facts: The Board had a license to put up a snow fence on the Rogers farm each winter, on the condition that it remove the fence, posts included, at the end of each season. It left an anchor post in the ground. The next summer, Rogers's husband was mowing the field when his mower hit the post; he was thrown off and killed. The trial court dismissed the complaint.
blocks.held: Reid, J.: once the license expired, leaving the post on the land was a trespass, and the Board is liable for the resulting harm whether or not it was negligent. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: R2d § 158(c): a lawful entry becomes a trespass when the duty to remove arises, and liability extends to the consequences.

blocks.title: Trespass by airborne particles: Bradley; Borland v. Sanders Lead (Ala. 1979)

body.text: An invasion by microscopic airborne particles is a trespass only if (all required): (1) it is an invasion affecting an interest in the exclusive possession of property; (2) the defendant intentionally did the act that resulted in the invasion; (3) it was reasonably foreseeable that the act could result in an invasion of the plaintiff's possessory interest; and (4) the property (the res) suffered substantial damage.
If the particles cause no damage to the land itself, the claim is in nuisance (§ 33), which requires a substantial interference with use and enjoyment.

blocks.name: Bradley v. American Smelting & Refining Co.
blocks.topic: particle trespass needs damage to the land
blocks.source: Canvas reading (9/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.
blocks.facts: The Bradleys owned land on the southern end of Vashon Island, about four miles north of ASARCO's copper smelter at Ruston, Washington. For years the smelter emitted particles of arsenic and cadmium that the wind carried onto their land; the particles were imperceptible to human senses. The Bradleys sued in trespass and nuisance. The federal court certified questions to the Washington Supreme Court, which held (104 Wash. 2d 677 (1985)) that intentionally emitting imperceptible pollutants that settle on another's land may be a trespass as well as a nuisance; that such a trespass requires proof of actual and substantial damages; and that the three-year trespass limitations period applies. Back in federal court, soil from the Bradleys' garden showed 53 ppm arsenic and 1.7 ppm cadmium, above normal background levels. ASARCO's experts said these levels posed no danger. The Bradleys offered no evidence of actual harm or of lost property value, only their worry about health risks.
blocks.held: Rothstein, J.: summary judgment for ASARCO. Trespass: under the test the Washington Supreme Court adopted from Borland, the plaintiff must show substantial damage to the land. Without that rule, "every landowner within a hundred miles of a manufacturing plant" could sue. The evidence showed the particles had not harmed the land, and claimed loss of value was unsupported. Nuisance: the plaintiff must show substantial interference with use and enjoyment. Worry about a health risk the evidence shows does not exist is not enough, because distress counts in nuisance only if it causes physical symptoms or accompanies an actual or threatened invasion of the plaintiff's person or security. Action dismissed.
blocks.why: The modern rule for pollution trespass. Trespass protects exclusive possession and does not ask whether the defendant acted reasonably, so courts require real damage to the land before treating invisible particles as a trespass. Otherwise the claim belongs in nuisance, which balances reasonableness.

body.text: **Conduct (any one suffices):** the actor intentionally (a) dispossesses another of the chattel; or (b) uses or intermeddles with a chattel in the possession of another.

**Liability, beyond nominal damages, only if (any one suffices):** (a) the possessor is dispossessed; (b) the chattel is impaired as to its condition, quality, or value; (c) the possessor is deprived of the use of the chattel for a substantial time; or (d) bodily harm is caused to the possessor, or harm is caused to some person or thing in which the possessor has a legally protected interest.

blocks.name: Glidden v. Szybiak
blocks.facts: Four-year-old Elaine Glidden climbed on the Szybiaks' dog, Toby, on the porch of a store and pulled its ears. The dog bit her. A New Hampshire statute made dog owners liable for bites unless the victim was committing "a trespass or other tort." The owner argued Elaine had committed a trespass to the dog.
blocks.held: Branch, C.J.: harmless intermeddling with a chattel is not actionable. A trespass to chattels requires actual damage to the chattel or deprivation of its use, and there was no evidence the dog was harmed. Because Elaine committed no tort, the statutory defense failed and she could recover.
blocks.why: R2d § 218: harmless meddling with a chattel is not actionable, unlike trespass to land.

blocks.name: CompuServe Inc. v. Cyber Promotions, Inc.
blocks.facts: Cyber Promotions sent unsolicited email advertisements to CompuServe's subscribers by the millions. CompuServe told it to stop and installed filters; Cyber increased its volume and falsified the return information to get past the filters. CompuServe sought a preliminary injunction on a trespass to chattels theory.
blocks.held: Graham, J.: electronic signals sent to a computer system can be a use of or intermeddling with a chattel (R2d § 217(b)). Harm was shown: (1) the volume burdened CompuServe's processing power and disk space, diminishing the equipment's value (§ 218(b)); and (2) subscribers complained and canceled, harming CompuServe's goodwill and business interests (§ 218(d)). Cyber's First Amendment defense failed because CompuServe is a private actor. Preliminary injunction granted.
blocks.why: The old tort applied to new technology, though actual harm is still required. [[Intel Corp. v. Hamidi (Cal. 2003) found no harm from a few emails.]]

blocks.title: Conversion (the casebook's next section; not on the syllabus pages)

body.text: Conversion is an intentional exercise of dominion or control over a chattel that so seriously interferes with another's right to control it that the actor may justly be required to pay its full value.

**Seriousness factors (weighed together):** (a) the extent and duration of the actor's exercise of dominion or control; (b) the actor's intent to assert a right in fact inconsistent with the other's right of control; (c) the actor's good faith; (d) the extent and duration of the resulting interference with the other's right of control; (e) the harm done to the chattel; and (f) the inconvenience and expense caused to the other.

blocks.name: Pearson v. Dodd
blocks.facts: Two former members of Senator Dodd's staff, aided by two current members, entered his office at night without authority, removed documents from his files, photocopied them, and put the originals back. They gave the copies to columnists Drew Pearson and Jack Anderson, who knew how they had been obtained and published articles based on them. The district court granted Dodd partial summary judgment on conversion.
blocks.held: J. Skelly Wright, J.: there was no conversion. The originals were returned before they were missed, so Dodd was not deprived of them. The information itself was not literary property, a scientific invention, or a secret business plan, the kinds of information the law protects as property. Reversed.
blocks.why: Conversion protects tangible things and a few forms of intellectual property. The remedy for publishing information is privacy or defamation law.

rows: Serious: destroying, keeping, selling, major alteration
Actual harm or loss of use (no nominal damages without harm)
Full value at the time of conversion, a forced sale
Irrelevant to liability, but a factor in seriousness
Moving a car to another space
Stealing it, or wrecking it while joyriding

blocks.title: Privileges and Defenses to Intentional Torts

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/10, Module on Consent (due 9/15), 15th ed. pp. 137–140, 145–156 · 13th ed. Ch. 3.A.

body.text: Consent bars an intentional tort claim when (all required): (1) the plaintiff had the capacity to consent; (2) the plaintiff consented, actually or apparently, to the defendant's conduct or to substantially the same conduct; (3) the consent was not procured by fraud about an essential matter or by duress; and (4) the defendant stayed within the scope of the consent.

items: (1) **Express**, in words or writing;
(2) **Implied in fact, or apparent:** the plaintiff's conduct reasonably appears to show consent, judged objectively (O'Brien). Silence counts where a reasonable person would object if unwilling.
(3) **Implied by custom:** the ordinary contacts of social life and the rules of a game (Wallace, Hackbart).
(4) **Implied by law:** in an emergency, when the person cannot consent, a reasonable person would consent, and the actor has no reason to think this person would refuse (R2d § 892D).
**Capacity.** Children, intoxicated people, and people with significant cognitive impairments may lack capacity. A parent or guardian can consent for them.
**Fraud** about the essential character of the act, not just a collateral matter, vitiates consent (De May; R2d § 892B(2)). A lie about collateral matters, such as payment, does not.

**Consent to a crime.** The majority view is that consent to a criminal act, such as an illegal boxing match or a mutual fight, is ineffective, so each participant can sue. R2d § 892C makes consent effective unless the statute was meant to protect a class from its own poor judgment, as with statutory rape and child-labor laws.
**Burden:** consent is usually an affirmative defense, but for offensive battery its absence is often treated as part of the plaintiff's case.

blocks.name: O'Brien v. Cunard S.S. Co.
blocks.facts: To spare passengers quarantine on arrival in Boston, Cunard vaccinated immigrants on board against smallpox and posted notices in several languages. O'Brien stood in line with about 200 women. The surgeon examined her arm, said there was no vaccination mark, and she held up her arm and was vaccinated without objecting. She later claimed she had been vaccinated before, did not want it, and suffered ulceration from the vaccine.
blocks.held: Knowlton, J.: consent is judged by the plaintiff's outward conduct. A surgeon may act on what a person's behavior shows, and her standing in line and holding up her arm, without objecting, showed consent. Verdict for Cunard affirmed.
blocks.why: Consent is judged objectively: the defendant may rely on outward manifestations. Note the power imbalance, though. Immigrants needed vaccination to land.

blocks.name: Hackbart v. Cincinnati Bengals, Inc.
blocks.facts: During a regular season game, Bengals fullback Charles "Booby" Clark, frustrated after a play had ended, struck Broncos safety Dale Hackbart on the back of the head with his forearm while Hackbart was kneeling. Hackbart suffered a serious neck fracture. The trial court ruled that professional football is so violent that tort law does not reach blows between players.
blocks.held: Doyle, J.: players consent to contact within the rules and customs of the game, not to an intentional blow the rules prohibit, struck in anger after the play. The NFL rules forbid striking an opponent on the head with a forearm. Liability can rest on intentional or reckless conduct. Reversed for a new trial.
blocks.why: Consent is limited to the risks inherent in the activity, as defined by its rules and customs. Violations outside the game support liability for intentional or reckless conduct.

blocks.name: Mohr v. Williams
blocks.facts: Mohr consented to an operation on her right ear. Once she was anesthetized, Dr. Williams found the right ear less serious than he had thought and, on examining the left ear, found it diseased and more in need of surgery. Without waking her, he operated on the left ear, successfully. She sued for battery. The jury awarded $14,322.50, but the trial judge granted a new trial as excessive. Both sides appealed.
blocks.held: Brown, J.: operating on a different part of the body than the one consented to is a battery, however skillful or beneficial. A surgeon may go beyond the consent only if he finds, during the authorized operation, a condition that endangers life or health and requires immediate action. The left ear was not discovered during the authorized operation, and its condition was not an emergency. The order for a new trial (on damages) was affirmed.
blocks.why: Medical consent covers only the procedure authorized. [[Many courts now allow reasonable extensions of an operation when a condition is found under anesthesia and immediate action is in the patient's interest (Kennedy v. Parrott, N.C. 1956).]]

blocks.name: De May v. Roberts
blocks.facts: Dr. De May attended Mrs. Roberts in childbirth at her home. He brought with him Scattergood, a young unmarried man with no medical training, whom the Robertses took to be the doctor's assistant. Scattergood stayed throughout the delivery and held Mrs. Roberts's hand during a contraction.
blocks.held: Marston, C.J.: consent obtained by deceit about a material fact is no consent. Mrs. Roberts allowed Scattergood's presence and touch only because she believed he was a medical assistant. Both De May and Scattergood are liable. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Fraud about the essential nature of the act or the actor vitiates consent. The case is also an ancestor of the privacy tort.

rows: No consent at all, or a substantially different procedure (Mohr)
An unconsented touching; no expert testimony needed
Consent to the procedure, but material risks were not disclosed (Scott v. Bradford, § 13)
A breach of the duty to disclose; causation must be shown
Consent obtained by lying about who will operate ("ghost surgery")

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Privileges (due 9/15), 15th ed. pp. 140–145, 162–166 · 13th ed. Ch. 3.B–C.

body.text: The actor is privileged to use force when (all required): (1) the actor reasonably believes that another is about to inflict a harmful or offensive contact or confinement on him; (2) the threat is imminent, not past or future; and (3) the force used is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the threat.
**Deadly force** (force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm) is privileged only if the actor reasonably believes he faces death or serious bodily harm.

items: **Reasonable mistake** preserves the privilege. The test is whether a reasonable person would have believed force was needed. [[In Courvoisier v. Raymond (Colo. 1896), a store owner who shot a deputy sheriff, mistaking him for one of a rioting crowd, was entitled to an instruction on reasonable appearances.]]

**Retreat.** Under R2d § 65, before using deadly force, the actor must retreat if he can do so in complete safety, except in his own dwelling. Many states impose no duty to retreat, and stand-your-ground statutes eliminate it outside the home. No one must retreat before using non-deadly force.
**Words alone** never justify force. Neither does revenge for a completed attack.
**Excessive force:** the defender is liable for the excess, and the original aggressor may then defend himself against it.

**Injury to a bystander:** a defender who injures a third person while acting in privileged self-defense is liable only if he was negligent toward that person (R2d § 75). Transferred intent does not apply.

body.text: The actor may use the same force to defend a third person that he could use to defend himself when (all required): (1) the actor reasonably believes that the third person would be privileged to defend himself; and (2) the actor reasonably believes that his intervention is necessary to protect the third person.

**Mistake:** the modern majority (and R2d) protects a reasonable mistake. The older rule put the intervenor "in the shoes" of the person defended, so he was liable if that person was actually the aggressor.

For any privilege, separate the elements: (1) the belief; (2) whether it was reasonable; (3) imminence; and (4) proportionality. Most exam answers turn on proportionality, such as deadly force against a non-deadly threat, or on the timing of force used after the threat ended.

blocks.title: Defense and Recovery of Property; the Shopkeeper's Privilege

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/15, 15th ed. pp. 167–187 · 13th ed. Ch. 3.D–E.

body.text: A possessor may use force to prevent or end an intrusion onto land or chattels when (all required): (1) the intrusion is not privileged; (2) the possessor reasonably believes force is necessary to prevent or end it; (3) the possessor first asks the intruder to desist, unless asking would be futile or dangerous; and (4) the force is reasonable. Force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily harm is never privileged to protect property alone.

items: **Mechanical devices** (spring guns, traps) are privileged only to the extent the possessor could have used the same force in person, and only if a warning is given where needed (R2d § 85). A device cannot tell a burglar from a child or a firefighter.
**Mistake:** unlike self-defense, a mistaken belief that the intruder is not privileged generally does not protect the defender, unless the intruder caused the mistake.
**Defense of the dwelling** against someone threatening the occupants is governed by self-defense, so deadly force may be justified by a threat to people, not by the intrusion itself.

blocks.name: Katko v. Briney
blocks.facts: The Brineys owned an unoccupied, boarded-up farmhouse that had been broken into repeatedly. They rigged a 20-gauge shotgun in a bedroom to fire at the legs of anyone who opened the door, and posted no warning. Katko broke in to steal old bottles and fruit jars. When he opened the bedroom door, the blast tore away much of his leg. He had pleaded guilty to larceny. The jury awarded $20,000 in actual and $10,000 in punitive damages.
blocks.held: Moore, C.J.: a possessor may not use, to protect property alone, force or a device intended to kill or seriously injure an intruder. Such force is justified only when the intruder is committing a violent felony or endangering human life. The law values human life and limb above property, even a trespasser's who is committing a crime. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Human life and limb outweigh property interests. The force allowed through a device is no more than the possessor could use in person.

body.text: **Dissent (Larson, J.):** the jury should have been told it could find the gun was set only to frighten, the rule had never been applied to a burglar, and punitive damages should not be awarded to a plaintiff engaged in crime.

An owner may use reasonable force to recover a chattel when (all required): (1) the owner was wrongfully dispossessed, by force, fraud, or theft (not merely a debtor's failure to return it); (2) the owner acts in fresh pursuit, promptly after discovering the taking; (3) the owner first demands its return, unless a demand would be futile or dangerous; and (4) the force used is reasonable and not likely to cause serious bodily harm.

blocks.name: Hodgeden v. Hubbard
blocks.facts: Hodgeden bought a stove from the Hubbards on credit, misrepresenting his finances. Discovering the fraud almost at once, they rode after him and overtook him a few miles away. When he refused to return the stove and drew a knife, one of them held him while the other took the stove. Hodgeden sued for assault and battery and won below.
blocks.held: Williams, C.J.: an owner who has been defrauded of goods may retake them by force if he acts without unreasonable delay and uses no unnecessary violence. The wrongdoer has no privilege to resist, and if he does, the owner may use the force needed to protect himself. Reversed.
blocks.why: Self-help recapture is allowed only in fresh pursuit and with reasonable force. Later, the owner must go to court.

body.text: A merchant may detain a person when (all required): (1) the merchant reasonably believes the person has taken, or is taking, goods without paying; (2) the detention is on the premises or in their immediate vicinity; (3) the detention is for a reasonable time and only to investigate; and (4) the detention is carried out in a reasonable manner, with no more force than is reasonably necessary.
[[Most states codify the privilege. In Delaware, see 11 Del. C. § 840 (detention of suspected shoplifters).]]

blocks.name: Bonkowski v. Arlan's Department Store
blocks.facts: As Mrs. Bonkowski walked to her car after leaving the store, a store security guard stopped her outside, said someone had told him she had taken costume jewelry, and told her to empty her purse. She did so on a ledge outside the store and showed receipts for her items; he let her go. She claimed psychological harm. The jury awarded her $43,750.
blocks.held: Fitzgerald, J.: a merchant who reasonably believes a person has taken goods without paying may detain her for a reasonable investigation, in a reasonable manner, on or in the immediate vicinity of the premises. The jury should have been told about this privilege. Reversed and remanded for a new trial.
blocks.why: The privilege resolves the merchant's dilemma of letting a suspected thief go or risking false imprisonment liability.

body.text: [[The shopkeeper's privilege turns on "reasonable" suspicion. Studies and litigation show that store detentions fall disproportionately on Black shoppers ("shopping while Black"). Ask on the essay whether the grounds for suspicion were particular to the plaintiff, and whether the manner of detention was reasonable.]]

rows: The actor reasonably believes it necessary to avert an imminent public disaster, such as fire, flood, or epidemic
The actor reasonably believes it necessary to protect his own or a third person's person or property from serious harm
Complete: no liability for the harm
Incomplete: privileged to enter and use, but liable for actual damage
The owner may not resist or expel. An owner who does is liable [[(Ploof v. Putnam, Vt. 1908: unmooring a boat in a storm)]]
None from the actor. [[A taking claim against the government may lie.]]
The actor pays for the damage caused

blocks.name: Surocco v. Geary
blocks.facts: During the great San Francisco fire of 1849, Geary, the alcalde, ordered Surocco's house blown up with gunpowder to stop the fire from spreading. Surocco was removing goods at the time and said he could have saved more of them if not for the blast. The trial court found for Surocco.
blocks.held: Murray, C.J.: destroying private property to stop a conflagration is privileged by public necessity, if done in good faith under apparent necessity. No action lies against the person who did it, even if the property would have been saved, because otherwise no one would act to save the community. Reversed.
blocks.why: The community's safety outweighs one owner's property. The privilege is complete. Whether the destruction was actually necessary is judged by the circumstances at the time.

blocks.name: Vincent v. Lake Erie Transp. Co.
blocks.topic: private necessity: pay for the damage
blocks.facts: The steamship Reynolds was unloading at Vincent's dock in Duluth when a violent storm arose. The crew kept the ship moored to the dock overnight, replacing lines as they broke. The waves threw the ship against the dock, causing $500 of damage. The jury found for Vincent.
blocks.held: O'Brien, J.: the ship was privileged by private necessity to stay at the dock, and keeping it there was prudent seamanship, not negligence. But a party who deliberately uses another's property to save his own must pay for the damage caused. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the incomplete privilege: an act can be both justified and compensable. The dissent would have treated the damage as a risk of the dock owner's business.

body.text: **Dissent (Lewis, J.):** the ship was lawfully at the dock and could not safely leave; the damage was an inevitable accident, and the dock owner, who invited the ship for profit, should bear the risk.

**Discipline:** a parent, a person in loco parentis, or a teacher may use reasonable force, or confinement, reasonably believed necessary to control, train, or educate a child (R2d §§ 147–155). Reasonableness considers (weighed together): (1) the child's age, sex, and condition; (2) the nature of the offense and the child's motive; (3) the influence of the child's example on others; (4) whether the force is necessary and appropriate to compel obedience; and (5) whether it is disproportionate or likely to cause serious harm.
**Restraint to protect people or property:** reasonable detention, in time and manner, to prevent another from injuring people or damaging property in one's lawful custody is not unlawful (Sindle).

blocks.name: Sindle v. New York City Transit Authority
blocks.facts: Students on a school bus run by the Transit Authority became unruly and vandalized it. The driver, Mooney, warned them, then locked the doors, skipped the remaining stops, and drove toward the police station. Sindle, 14, jumped out of a window to escape and was run over by the rear wheels. At trial he waived his negligence claim, and the judge refused to let the defendants plead justification and excluded evidence of it. The jury awarded damages for false imprisonment.
blocks.held: Jasen, J.: refusing leave to plead justification was an abuse of discretion; the defendants had the burden of proving it, and Sindle could not have been prejudiced. A restraint reasonable in time and manner, imposed to prevent injury to persons or damage to property in one's lawful custody, is not unlawful. The driver, entrusted with both the students and the bus, stood in a position like a teacher in loco parentis. Whether his detention was reasonable was for the jury. Reversed; new trial.
blocks.why: Justification is a defense to false imprisonment, but its reasonableness is a fact question. Detaining every passenger, including the innocent, presses the limits.

items: [[A police officer may arrest without a warrant for a felony if he reasonably believes one was committed and that the arrestee committed it. A private citizen is privileged only if a felony was in fact committed and he reasonably believes the arrestee committed it.]]

[[For a misdemeanor, an arrest without a warrant generally requires a breach of the peace committed in the arrester's presence.]] See Enright (§ 4): the justification must fit the offense for which the person was actually arrested.

blocks.title: Intentional torts and privileges: the week 5 MC checklist

items: **Tort.** Name each act and match it to a tort: contact (battery), apprehension (assault), confinement (false imprisonment), outrageous conduct (IIED), land (trespass), chattel (trespass to chattels or conversion).
**Intent.** Purpose or substantial certainty? Transferred between people or torts? Child, mental illness, or mistake does not defeat it.
**Element traps.** Awareness (needed for assault and, usually, false imprisonment; not for battery), imminence, reasonable means of escape, severity of distress, actual harm for chattels.

**Privilege.** Consent (scope, fraud, capacity), self-defense, defense of others, defense of property (never deadly force), recapture (fresh pursuit), shopkeeper, necessity (public is complete, private pays), discipline.
**Damages.** Nominal for battery, assault, and trespass to land; punitive damages for malice (Big Town, Katko, Fisher).

blocks.title: The Negligence Case and Unreasonable Risk
The prima facie case for negligence

body.text: The plaintiff must prove (all required): (1) **duty**, an obligation to conform to a standard of conduct for the protection of others against unreasonable risks; (2) **breach**, conduct that falls below that standard; (3) **cause in fact**, the conduct was a but-for or substantial-factor cause of the harm; (4) **proximate cause**, the harm is within the scope of the risk that made the conduct negligent; and (5) **damages**, actual harm to person or property (nominal damages are not available).

items: **Negligence is conduct, not a state of mind.** It is the creation of an unreasonable risk of harm to others (R2d § 282). The plaintiff need not show the defendant knew of the risk, only that a reasonable person would have.
**Duty and breach.** The general duty is reasonable care toward foreseeable plaintiffs (§ 21 covers limits). The standard is the reasonable person under the same or similar circumstances (§ 12).

**Unreasonable risk** has two parts: (1) the risk must be foreseeable; and (2) a reasonable person would have taken a precaution against it, given its likelihood and severity and the burden of avoiding it.

blocks.name: Lubitz v. Wells
blocks.facts: Mr. Wells left a golf club in his backyard. His son, J. Wells Jr., picked it up and swung it at a stone without warning Judith Lubitz, who was playing nearby, and hit her in the jaw. She sued the son for negligent swinging and the father for leaving the club where it could cause harm.
blocks.held: Troland, J.: leaving a golf club in a yard is not negligent. It is not an inherently dangerous instrument, and the chance that a child would injure someone with it was not reasonably foreseeable. Demurrer as to the father sustained.
blocks.why: Without a foreseeable risk there is no negligence. Contrast a loaded gun or a dangerous chemical left where children play.

blocks.name: Blyth v. Birmingham Waterworks Co.
blocks.facts: The waterworks company installed water mains and fire plugs that had worked properly for 25 years. During the severe frost of 1855, ice forced out a plug's stopper, and water flooded Blyth's house. The jury found for Blyth.
blocks.held: Alderson, B.: negligence is "the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do." A reasonable company guards against ordinary frosts, not one of extraordinary severity. Reversed; judgment for the company.
blocks.why: This is the standard definition of negligence. Foreseeability is measured by ordinary experience at the time.

blocks.name: Pipher v. Parsell
blocks.facts: Parsell, 16, was driving two other 16-year-olds in a pickup truck at 55 mph, all three in the front seat. Passenger Biesel suddenly grabbed the wheel, and the truck veered toward the shoulder; Parsell regained control and did nothing. About 30 seconds later Biesel grabbed the wheel again; the truck left the road and hit a tree, injuring Pipher, the middle passenger. Parsell admitted at trial he could have told Biesel not to do it again, moved her, or made her get out. The trial judge ruled as a matter of law that Parsell had no duty to act after the first grab.
blocks.held: Holland, J.: a driver owes passengers and the public a duty of reasonable care. When it is foreseeable that a passenger's conduct may interfere with safe driving, failing to prevent it may breach that duty. After the first grab, a reasonable jury could find the second foreseeable and Parsell's inaction a breach. Breach and proximate cause were jury questions. Reversed.
blocks.why: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Foreseeability can arise during the events, and whether the response was reasonable is usually for the jury.

body.text: An act is negligent if its risk outweighs its utility. **Factors (weighed together):** (1) the foreseeable likelihood that the conduct will cause harm; (2) the foreseeable severity of any harm; and (3) the burden of precautions that would eliminate or reduce the risk, including the social value of the conduct.

blocks.name: Chicago, B. & Q. R. Co. v. Krayenbuhl
blocks.facts: Children often played on the railroad's turntable, which was near a public path. Company rules required it to be padlocked when not in use, but the rule was often ignored. Four-year-old Krayenbuhl went there with other children, who found the turntable unlocked (or unlocked it), and his foot was caught and severed above the ankle. The jury found for him.
blocks.held: A possessor who knows or has reason to know that young children will be attracted to a dangerous machine on its land must use reasonable care to protect them. Whether a precaution is required depends on balancing the machine's usefulness and the cost of the precaution against the danger. A lock costs little and would not impair the turntable's use. The judgment was reversed on other grounds (an error in the instructions).
blocks.why: This is risk-utility balancing before the Hand formula. It is also an ancestor of the attractive nuisance doctrine (§ 26).

blocks.name: Davison v. Snohomish County
blocks.facts: Coming off a county bridge onto a curved, elevated approach, Davison's car skidded, broke through the wooden guardrail, and fell. He claimed the rail was too weak to stop a car, the curve was improperly banked, and dirt on the road caused the skid. The jury found for Davison.
blocks.held: Beals, J.: a county is not required to build guardrails strong enough to stop cars on all elevated roads. The cost would be prohibitive and would discourage building roads. The banking deviation was small in relation to the whole slope, and the county is not liable for an ordinary accumulation of dirt. Reversed.
blocks.why: The burden of the precaution, measured across all similar roads, can make a risk reasonable.

blocks.name: United States v. Carroll Towing Co.
blocks.facts: In January 1944, in crowded New York Harbor, the barge Anna C was moored with others at a pier. A tug crew employed by Carroll Towing negligently readjusted the mooring lines, and the barges broke loose. The Anna C drifted against a tanker, whose propeller holed her, and she sank with her cargo of government flour. Its bargee had been ashore for 21 hours, though barges were constantly being moved in the harbor. The trial court divided damages.
blocks.held: Hand, J.: an owner's duty to guard against a barge breaking loose depends on three variables: (1) the probability that it will break away (P); (2) the gravity of the resulting injury (L); and (3) the burden of adequate precautions (B). Liability follows if B < P × L. Keeping a bargee aboard during the working hours of daylight, in a crowded wartime harbor, was a small burden compared with the risk. The owner's own negligence reduced its recovery. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the canonical risk-utility test. On an essay, put rough values on B, P, and L and compare them.

blocks.title: Using and criticizing the Hand formula

items: The formula compares the marginal (additional) precaution with the marginal reduction in risk.
Values are often unquantifiable, and juries rarely do the arithmetic. Courts use it as a way to organize the argument.
Critics say it values harm by market measures, such as lost earnings, which can undervalue harm to lower-income people, and that it treats safety as just another cost.

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Standard of Care (due 9/24), 15th ed. pp. 218–227; 9/24, pp. 227–235, 240–245 · 13th ed. Ch. 4.B–C.

body.text: The standard of conduct is that of a reasonable person of ordinary prudence under the same or similar circumstances. It is objective: the actor's own good faith or best judgment does not count (Vaughan v. Menlove).

rows: No allowance; the objective standard applies
Charged with what a reasonable person knows, including common facts and knowledge from reasonable inspection; superior knowledge counts
Evidence of due care, not conclusive
A reasonable person in that emergency, if not of the actor's making
A reasonable person with that disability
A child of like age, intelligence, and experience, except in adult activities
No allowance, except sudden mental incapacity without warning
Held to the standard of a sober person

blocks.name: Vaughan v. Menlove
blocks.facts: Menlove built a hayrick near the edge of his land, beside Vaughan's cottages. He was warned several times that it was likely to catch fire. He said his stock was insured and he "would chance it," though he cut a chimney through it as a precaution. The hay ignited spontaneously, and the fire destroyed Vaughan's cottages. Menlove argued he should be liable only if he failed to act honestly and to the best of his own judgment.
blocks.held: Tindal, C.J.: the standard is objective: whether the defendant used the caution a man of ordinary prudence would use. A standard based on each individual's judgment would be "as variable as the length of the foot of each individual." The verdict for Vaughan stood.
blocks.why: This is the origin of the objective standard. Low intelligence is no excuse.

blocks.name: Delair v. McAdoo
blocks.facts: McAdoo tried to pass Delair's car when his left rear tire blew out, and his car crashed into Delair's. Witnesses said the tire was worn through to the fabric. McAdoo said he did not know the tires were worn. The jury found for Delair.
blocks.held: Kephart, C.J.: every adult is charged with knowledge of facts common to the community, such as gravity, fire, and the danger of worn tires. The owner or operator of a car is charged with knowledge of its condition that a reasonable inspection would reveal, and the wear here was visible. Affirmed.
blocks.why: A defendant cannot plead ignorance of what everyone knows. Inspection duties arise from the activity.

blocks.name: Trimarco v. Klein
blocks.facts: Trimarco, a tenant in Klein's building, was badly cut when he fell through the glass door of his bathtub enclosure. The door was ordinary thin glass, though it looked like tempered glass. His expert testified that by the 1950s it had become the common practice of landlords to use shatterproof glass in such enclosures. The jury found for Trimarco, but the Appellate Division reversed, holding the landlord had no duty to replace the glass without notice of the danger.
blocks.held: Fuchsberg, J.: evidence of custom and usage by others in the same business is admissible to show what is reasonable, but it is not conclusive. Quoting Holmes: "What usually is done may be evidence of what ought to be done, but what ought to be done is fixed by a standard of reasonable prudence, whether it usually is complied with or not." The custom evidence was properly admitted. A new trial was ordered because of other erroneously admitted evidence.
blocks.why: Custom is a sword (deviation is evidence of negligence) and a shield (compliance is evidence of care), but never conclusive. The T.J. Hooper (2d Cir. 1932, Hand, J.) holds that a whole industry can lag behind reasonable care.

blocks.name: Cordas v. Peerless Transportation Co.
blocks.facts: A man who had just committed a robbery, chased by a crowd shouting "Stop thief," jumped into a Peerless cab, pointed a gun at the driver, and ordered him to drive. The driver started off, then threw the car out of gear, braked, and jumped out. The cab, still moving, mounted the sidewalk and hit Mrs. Cordas and her two children.
blocks.held: Carlin, J.: a person faced with a sudden emergency not of his own making is not held to the judgment he would use with time to reflect. He is judged by what a reasonable person would do in that emergency. The driver was not negligent; the law does not require heroism. Complaint dismissed.
blocks.why: The emergency is a circumstance, not a separate standard. It does not help someone whose own negligence created the emergency.

blocks.name: Roberts v. State of Louisiana
blocks.facts: Burson, a blind man, ran a snack bar in a state office building. He left the counter to go to the restroom without his cane, relying on his familiarity with the area and his "facial sense" of nearby obstacles, and bumped into Roberts, who fell and hurt his hip. Roberts sued the state as Burson's employer and for negligent supervision. His only evidence of Burson's negligence was an expert who had never examined Burson. The trial court dismissed.
blocks.held: Laborde, J.: a person with a physical disability must take the precautions that a reasonable person with the same disability would take. Burson's evidence showed his method of moving through familiar areas was reasonable, and Roberts did not prove otherwise. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The disability is part of the circumstances, so the standard is a reasonable blind person, not a reasonable sighted one.

blocks.name: Robinson v. Lindsay
blocks.facts: Billy Anderson, 13, was driving a snowmobile when an accident injured Kelly Robinson, 11, who lost full use of her thumb. The jury was instructed to judge Billy by the standard of a reasonable child of his age and found for him. The trial judge then granted a new trial, ruling that an adult standard should have applied.
blocks.held: Utter, C.J.: children are generally held to the standard of a reasonable child of like age, intelligence, and experience. But a child engaged in an inherently dangerous activity normally pursued only by adults, such as operating a powerful motorized vehicle, is held to the adult standard. Snowmobiles qualify. The new trial was properly ordered. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the adult-activity exception. [[Some states hold that children under a set age, often 5 or 7, are incapable of negligence (tender-years rule).]]

blocks.name: Breunig v. American Family Ins. Co.
blocks.facts: Erma Veith, insured by American Family, was driving when she believed God was taking control of her car. Seeing a truck ahead, she stepped on the gas so the car would become airborne, believing she could fly like Batman. Her car crossed the center line and hit Breunig's truck. A psychiatrist testified she had a sudden delusion; there was also evidence she had had similar visions before. The jury found her negligent.
blocks.held: Hallows, C.J.: insanity is generally no defense to negligence, for policy reasons (weighed together): (1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it; (2) liability gives those interested in an insane person's estate a reason to restrain him; and (3) it prevents false claims of insanity. But a sudden mental incapacity that strikes without warning, like a heart attack or epileptic seizure, is an exception. Because the jury could find Veith had forewarning of her delusions, the verdict for Breunig was affirmed.
blocks.why: The general rule rests on policies (weighed together): (1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it; (2) it encourages those responsible for the mentally ill to control them; and (3) it prevents false claims of insanity. Compare Cohen v. Petty (§ 1).

items: The "reasonable man" became the "reasonable person." Critics argue the standard can still build in the perspective of the people who historically served as jurors and judges.
Roberts takes disability into account, but mental illness gets no allowance (Breunig). Consider whether that distinction is principled.
[[Some scholars argue for a "reasonable woman" standard in harassment contexts, or for considering the plaintiff's community when judging what is offensive or reasonable.]]

blocks.text: **Reading:** 9/29, 15th ed. pp. 245–275 · 13th ed. Ch. 4.C.

body.text: A professional must use (all required): (1) the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by members of the profession in good standing (in the same specialty and, under older rules, the same or a similar locality); (2) reasonable care and diligence in applying that knowledge and skill; and (3) his best judgment.
