**Proof:** the standard and its breach must be shown by expert testimony unless the negligence is obvious to a layperson, such as leaving a sponge in the patient or operating on the wrong limb (Boyce).

R3d Medical Malpractice §§ 2–3 (approved 2022): a patient-care relationship arises when a provider manifests an intent to care for a patient and (any one suffices) (1) begins care without the patient's objection; (2) the patient reasonably believes the provider has undertaken care; or (3) the patient reasonably relies on the provider.

**Duties within the relationship (all owed):** (1) to exercise reasonable care; (2) to comply with the requirements of informed consent; (3) to use reasonable care to protect confidential patient information; and (4) not to end the relationship without giving the patient a reasonable opportunity to find other care.

items: **Professional custom sets the standard.** Unlike ordinary custom (Trimarco), what the profession does is the measure of care, not just evidence of it.
**Schools of thought:** a doctor who follows a method accepted by a respectable minority of the profession is not negligent.
**Error in judgment:** a professional is not liable for an honest error in an area where reasonable professionals disagree or the law is unsettled (Hodges).
**Specialists** are held to the standard of a reasonable specialist in that field, usually national (Morrison).

blocks.name: Heath v. Swift Wings, Inc.
blocks.facts: A small plane crashed shortly after takeoff, killing the pilot and his passengers. In the passengers' estates' suit against the pilot's estate, the jury was instructed that negligence meant failing to use the care that "an ordinarily prudent pilot having the same training and experience as" this pilot would use. The jury found the pilot not negligent.
blocks.held: Morris, C.J.: the instruction was wrong. A professional's standard is objective: the care of a reasonably prudent pilot with the knowledge and skill the profession requires. Tying the standard to the defendant's own training and experience would create a different standard for every defendant. New trial ordered.
blocks.why: Even professionals are judged objectively. "Best judgment" is required, but it is not enough by itself.

blocks.name: Hodges v. Carter
blocks.facts: Hodges's drugstore and its contents burned, and his four fire insurers refused to pay. His lawyers, Topping and Carter, sued and served process on the foreign insurers by mail through the state Commissioner of Insurance, the method in standard use for more than 20 years. The North Carolina Supreme Court then held that method invalid, and the limitations period had run. Hodges sued the lawyers for negligence, including their failure to obtain new summonses in time. The trial court entered a nonsuit.
blocks.held: Barnhill, C.J.: a lawyer is liable if the client's loss results from (1) a lack of the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by lawyers similarly situated, (2) a failure to use reasonable care and diligence, or (3) a failure to use his best judgment. A lawyer who acts in good faith and follows the settled practice of the bar is not liable for a mistake on a point of law later decided against him. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Lawyers are not guarantors of results. They are liable for lacking ordinary skill, for failing to use reasonable care, or for not using their best judgment.

blocks.name: Boyce v. Brown
blocks.facts: In 1927, Dr. Brown set Mrs. Boyce's fractured ankle by surgically inserting a metal screw. In 1934 she returned with a swollen, painful ankle; he taped it and filed down her arch support but took no X-ray. In 1936, Dr. Kent X-rayed the ankle, found the bone around the screw had deteriorated, and removed the screw; she recovered. At trial, Dr. Kent testified about what he did in 1936 but not about the standard of care in 1934. The trial court directed a verdict for Dr. Brown.
blocks.held: Lockwood, J.: medical negligence must be proved by expert testimony that the doctor departed from the accepted standard of practice, unless the negligence is so grossly apparent that a layperson would have no difficulty recognizing it. A different method is not negligence, and failing to take an X-ray is not obvious negligence. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The plaintiff's expert must address the standard and the breach, not just what he would have done.

blocks.name: Morrison v. MacNamara
blocks.facts: MacNamara, a nationally accredited medical laboratory in Washington, D.C., performed a urethral smear test for trichomonas on Morrison while he stood. He fainted and was seriously injured in the fall. The court excluded his expert's testimony that the national standard was to perform the test with the patient sitting or lying down, but admitted local doctors' testimony that in D.C. it was done standing. The jury found for the laboratory.
blocks.held: Newman, C.J.: the standard of care for board-certified physicians, hospitals, medical laboratories, and other health care providers is national. The locality rule was premised on disparities between urban and rural medicine that national certification has removed, and it can shield substandard local practice. The expert's testimony should have been admitted. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: The locality rule is giving way to a national standard, at least for specialists and accredited facilities. Some states use a "same or similar locality" rule.

body.text: The plaintiff must prove (all required): (1) the physician failed to disclose a material risk of, or alternative to, the treatment; (2) had the risk been disclosed, the plaintiff would have declined the treatment (causation); and (3) the undisclosed risk materialized and injured the plaintiff.

**Exceptions (any one suffices):** (1) emergency; (2) the risk was known to the patient or is common knowledge; (3) disclosure would seriously harm the patient (therapeutic privilege); or (4) the patient waived disclosure.

rows: What a reasonable patient would find material to the decision
What a reasonable physician would disclose (professional custom)
Not needed on what to disclose
Scott: subjective (would this patient have refused?). Canterbury and most courts: objective (would a reasonable patient have refused?)

blocks.name: Scott v. Bradford
blocks.facts: Dr. Bradford performed a hysterectomy on Mrs. Scott to remove fibroid tumors. He did not tell her of the risks or of alternatives to surgery. After the operation she suffered incontinence and needed several corrective operations. She testified she would have refused the surgery had she been told. The jury found for the doctor.
blocks.held: Doolin, J.: a doctor must disclose the material risks of, and alternatives to, a proposed treatment. To recover, the patient must prove (1) the doctor failed to inform her of a material risk; (2) had she been informed, she would not have consented (judged subjectively, by her own testimony); and (3) the undisclosed risk occurred and injured her. The jury was properly instructed and simply did not believe she would have refused. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Informed consent protects patient autonomy, and it is a negligence claim, not battery. Oklahoma's subjective causation test is the minority view.

blocks.name: Moore v. Regents of the University of California
blocks.facts: Moore was treated for hairy-cell leukemia at UCLA Medical Center by Dr. Golde. Golde learned that Moore's cells had unusual commercial value. Without telling him, Golde removed his spleen and, over seven years, took blood and other samples, developing a patented cell line with potential value in the billions. Moore sued for conversion, breach of fiduciary duty, and lack of informed consent. The trial court dismissed.
blocks.held: Panelli, J.: a physician must disclose personal interests unrelated to the patient's health, whether research or economic, that may affect his medical judgment. Failing to disclose states a claim for breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent. But the court refused to recognize a conversion claim for the cells, because extending conversion would chill medical research. Remanded.
blocks.why: The disclosure duty extends to conflicts of interest. Note the bias and consent issues: compare the Henrietta Lacks cell line.

blocks.title: Judge and Jury; Negligence Per Se

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Alternative Standards of Care (due 10/1), 15th ed. pp. 278–293; 10/1 (hour 1), pp. 293–303 · 13th ed. Ch. 4.D–E.

items: The **judge** decides duty and whether the evidence is sufficient. The **jury** applies the standard of care to the facts, unless reasonable people could not disagree, in which case the judge decides as a matter of law.

Judges sometimes try to fix specific standards of conduct as rules of law, as in Holmes's "stop, look, and get out" rule for railroad crossings (Goodman, 1927). Cardozo limited that approach in Pokora.

blocks.name: Pokora v. Wabash Ry. Co.
blocks.facts: Pokora drove his truck to a four-track railroad crossing. Boxcars on the first track blocked his view to the north. He stopped, looked, and listened, heard nothing, and drove slowly forward without getting out to look. On the main track he was hit by a train from the north. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad on contributory negligence, citing Holmes's rule in Baltimore & Ohio R.R. v. Goodman (1927) that a driver who cannot see must get out and look.
blocks.held: Cardozo, J.: failing to get out of the vehicle to reconnoiter was not contributory negligence as a matter of law. Getting out may be futile, or more dangerous than not, since the train may arrive while the driver walks back. Standards of prudent conduct are ordinarily for the jury, and Goodman's rule must be confined. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: Cardozo limited Goodman. Judges should rarely fix standards of conduct, which vary with the circumstances.

body.text: An unexcused violation of a statute is negligence when (all required): (1) the statute prescribes specific conduct for the safety of others; (2) the defendant violated it without excuse; (3) the plaintiff is within the class of persons the statute was designed to protect; (4) the harm is of the type the statute was designed to prevent; and (5) the violation caused the harm (cause in fact and proximate cause).

rows: Negligence as a matter of law (per se); the jury decides only causation and damages
A rebuttable presumption of negligence; the defendant may prove an excuse
Many states, and R2d § 288A in practice
Evidence of negligence that the jury may weigh
Minority (e.g., ordinances, traffic rules in some states)
Ney v. Yellow Cab (prima facie evidence)

blocks.text: **Excuses, R2d § 288A(2) (any one suffices):** (a) the violation is reasonable because of the actor's incapacity; (b) he neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance; (c) he is unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply; (d) he is confronted by an emergency not due to his own misconduct; or (e) compliance would involve a greater risk of harm to the actor or to others.

blocks.title: The plaintiff's own violations: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment §§ 4 A–4 B (approved 2022)

body.text: **§ 4 A (wrongful acts doctrine):** a person injured by tortious conduct is not barred from recovery merely because she was engaged in an illegal, tortious, or otherwise wrongful act at the time.

**§ 4 B(a):** an injured victim is negligent if, without excuse, she violates a criminal statute or other safety regulation designed to protect against the type of accident her conduct caused, and she is within the class the statute protects. **§ 4 B(b):** if that negligence is a factual cause of her harm, it reduces her recovery under comparative responsibility; otherwise it has no effect. This is negligence per se applied to the plaintiff, as in Martin v. Herzog and Zeni v. Anderson.

blocks.name: Osborne v. McMasters
blocks.facts: A clerk in McMasters's drugstore, acting in the course of his employment, sold a deadly poison to Osborne's decedent without labeling it "poison," as a criminal statute required. The decedent took it by mistake and died.
blocks.held: Mitchell, J.: where a statute imposes a specific duty for the protection of others, one who neglects that duty is liable to those it was meant to protect, for the kind of injury it was meant to prevent and that the violation proximately caused. Negligence is the breach of a legal duty, whether the duty comes from common law or statute. The employer is liable for the clerk's breach. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This is the classic statement of negligence per se and its class-of-persons and type-of-harm limits.

blocks.name: Stachniewicz v. Mar-Cam Corp.
blocks.topic: class of persons and type of harm
blocks.facts: A fight broke out in Mar-Cam's bar between a group in a booth, some visibly intoxicated, and Stachniewicz's party at a nearby table, after one of the group had been refused a dance. The bartender had received complaints about the group. Stachniewicz was later found unconscious outside the door with retrograde amnesia. He relied on Oregon Liquor Control Commission regulations barring service to visibly intoxicated persons and barring licensees from permitting loud, noisy, disorderly, or boisterous conduct on the premises. The trial court refused to treat the violations as negligence per se, and the jury found for the bar.
blocks.held: Holman, J.: violation of a statute or regulation is negligence as a matter of law when the injured person is in the class protected and the harm is the kind the rule was meant to prevent. The regulation against permitting disorderly conduct bears directly on the start of fights, so it was meant to protect patrons from this kind of injury, and the jury could infer his injuries came from the fight. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: Courts often infer the legislature's purpose from the statute's text when legislative history is thin, which gives them latitude.

blocks.name: Ney v. Yellow Cab Co.
blocks.facts: A Yellow Cab driver left his cab unattended and unlocked with the key in the ignition, in violation of an Illinois Uniform Traffic Act section. A thief stole it and, while driving it, collided with Ney's car. The jury found for Ney, and the appellate court affirmed. Yellow Cab argued the statute was only a traffic regulation, not a safety measure.
blocks.held: Maxwell, J.: the statute was meant to protect public safety, including against the dangers of stolen cars driven carelessly, so its violation is prima facie evidence of negligence. Whether the thief's intervening crime cut off proximate cause was a fact question for the jury, which resolved it for Ney. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Purpose decides class and harm. Courts split on key-in-ignition cases, and many find the thief's act superseding (§ 20).

body.text: **Dissent (Hershey, J.):** leaving a key in the ignition is a minor cause of theft, the statute was not aimed at this harm, and the thief's act should be the proximate cause.

blocks.name: Perry v. S.N.
blocks.topic: when courts decline negligence per se
blocks.facts: Two children attended a day-care center run by the Kellers, where Daniel Keller allegedly abused them physically and sexually. The parents sued the Kellers and three of their friends, Perry, White, and Quintero, who allegedly saw the abuse and did not report it, as the Texas Family Code required of anyone who believes a child is being abused. The trial court granted summary judgment for the friends; the court of appeals reversed on negligence per se.
blocks.held: Phillips, C.J.: the children were in the protected class and suffered the type of harm the statute addressed, but that is not enough. Weighing factors against adopting the statute as a tort standard (weighed together): (1) there is no common-law duty to report, so the statute would be the only source of the duty; (2) the statute does not clearly define when its duty arises; (3) liability would be imposed without regard to fault; (4) the injury results only indirectly from the violation, through the abuser's crime; and (5) the liability would be ruinous and out of proportion to the conduct, and would fall on a broad class of people. Violation of the reporting statute is not negligence per se. Reversed.
blocks.why: Adopting a statute as the standard of care is a judicial choice. It is not automatic.

blocks.name: Martin v. Herzog
blocks.facts: Martin was driving a buggy at night without lights, in violation of a statute, when it collided with Herzog's car, which was coming around a curve without keeping to the right. Martin was killed. The trial judge instructed that driving without lights was not negligence in itself but only evidence of negligence. The jury found for Martin's estate; the Appellate Division reversed.
blocks.held: Cardozo, J.: the unexcused omission of a statutory safeguard is negligence in itself, not just evidence of it. Jurors have no power to relax a duty the statute imposes for the protection of other travelers. But the violation must also be a cause of the accident. Evidence that a car hit an unlighted buggy at night supports an inference that the lack of lights contributed. Affirmed (new trial).
blocks.why: Negligence per se determines breach, but causation is still required. A violation that did not contribute to the harm does not matter.

blocks.name: Zeni v. Anderson
blocks.facts: On a snowy winter morning, Zeni was walking to work. Rather than use the snow-covered sidewalk, she walked on a well-used path in the street, with her back to traffic, in violation of a statute requiring pedestrians to use sidewalks or face traffic. Anderson's car, possibly too close to the curb, hit her. The jury found for Zeni; the court of appeals reversed on the ground that her violation was negligence per se.
blocks.held: Williams, J.: violation of a statute creates a rebuttable presumption of negligence, which the violator may overcome by showing an adequate excuse. Rigid per se treatment would ignore reasonable justifications, like an impassable sidewalk. The issue was properly left to the jury. Reversed; verdict for Zeni reinstated.
blocks.why: This is the modern middle position, and it reflects R2d § 288A excuses.

items: **Compliance** with a statute is evidence of care, but not conclusive. The reasonable person may have to do more (R2d § 288C).
**Licensing statutes** usually do not support negligence per se. Practicing without a license does not prove the treatment was negligent [[(Brown v. Shyne, N.Y. 1926)]].
**Check the purpose.** A statute aimed at a different harm (e.g., a Sunday-closing law) does not make a violator liable for an unrelated accident.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 10/6, 15th ed. pp. 303–321, and McDougald v. Perry (Canvas) · 13th ed. Ch. 4.F.

items: **Burden:** the plaintiff must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence. Circumstantial evidence is enough if it permits a reasonable inference that the defendant was negligent, and not just a guess.

**Premises conditions:** the plaintiff must show (any one suffices) (1) the defendant created the dangerous condition; (2) the defendant had actual notice of it; or (3) the defendant had constructive notice, because the condition existed long enough that reasonable inspection would have discovered and remedied it.

blocks.name: Goddard v. Boston & Maine R.R. Co.
blocks.facts: Goddard got off a train and walked the length of a car along the platform, where many other passengers had just alighted. He slipped on a banana skin and fell. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.
blocks.held: Holmes, C.J.: the banana skin could have been dropped by one of the departing passengers within a minute before the fall. Without evidence it had been there long enough for the railroad to discover it, there was no negligence. Exceptions overruled.
blocks.why: This is the first of the banana-peel cases: no evidence of time means no constructive notice.

blocks.name: Anjou v. Boston Elevated Railway Co.
blocks.facts: Anjou got off a train at the Dudley Street terminal, waited for the crowd to clear, and followed a uniformed railway employee along a narrow platform toward a stairway he pointed out. She slipped on a banana peel and was hurt. Witnesses described the peel as dry, gritty, black, flattened, and trampled over. The trial court directed a verdict for the railway.
blocks.held: Rugg, J.: the railway had a duty to keep its platform reasonably safe, including by watching for and removing debris. From the peel's condition, the jury could infer it had been on the platform long enough to be discovered and removed. Exceptions sustained; judgment for Anjou under the terms of the report.
blocks.why: The condition of the object can supply the evidence of time that Goddard lacked.

blocks.name: Joye v. Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Co.
blocks.facts: Joye slipped on a banana in an A&P supermarket aisle. The banana was dark brown, sticky at the edges, and had dirt and sand on it, and the floor was dirty. The aisle may not have been swept for 35 minutes. No one knew how long the banana had been there or how it got there. The jury awarded Joye $10,000.
blocks.held: Craven, J.: without evidence of how long the hazard existed, there is no constructive notice. On this record a "jury could not tell whether the banana had been on A&P's floor for thirty seconds or three days." Reversed.
blocks.why: A banana that browns on its own does not show how long it has been on the floor. Compare Anjou.

blocks.name: Ortega v. Kmart Corp.
blocks.facts: Ortega slipped on a puddle of milk in a Kmart and seriously injured his knee. He could not prove how long the milk had been there, but he showed Kmart had not inspected the area for 15 to 30 minutes, and perhaps as long as two hours. The jury awarded $47,000.
blocks.held: Chin, J.: a store owner must make reasonable inspections of areas customers use. The plaintiff may prove constructive notice by circumstantial evidence that the condition existed long enough for a reasonably prudent owner to discover and correct it, including evidence that the owner failed to inspect within a reasonable time. He need not prove exactly how long the hazard was there. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The focus shifts from how long the hazard was there to how reasonable the inspection program was.

blocks.name: Jasko v. F.W. Woolworth Co.
blocks.facts: Jasko slipped on a slice of pizza on the terrazzo floor near Woolworth's "Pizza Hoagie Counter." Woolworth sold pizza by the slice on waxed paper to customers who often ate standing up, and it had employees clean the floor constantly. Jasko offered no evidence of how long the slice had been there. The trial court ruled for Woolworth.
blocks.held: Groves, J.: when a proprietor's method of operation makes dangerous conditions continuous or easily foreseeable, the plaintiff need not prove notice of the particular condition. The notice rule assumes dangers are unusual, and that assumption fails when the danger comes from the way the store chooses to operate. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: The mode-of-operation rule reaches self-service and food-on-the-floor settings, where the danger comes from how the store chooses to operate.

blocks.name: H.E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Resendez
blocks.facts: H-E-B displayed grapes in a bowl for customers to sample. The bowl sat on ice about five inches below the tabletop, and a three-inch rail ran around the table's edge. The floor was non-skid, mats surrounded the display, and warning cones stood nearby. Resendez slipped near the display. The jury found for her, and the court of appeals affirmed.
blocks.held: Per curiam: merely displaying produce for customer sampling, without more, does not create an unreasonable risk of harm. Resendez had to prove (all required) (1) actual or constructive knowledge of a condition; (2) that the condition posed an unreasonable risk; (3) the store's failure to use reasonable care to reduce it; and (4) causation. She failed on (2). Unlike the slanted display without mats in Corbin v. Safeway (Tex. 1983), H-E-B's display had safeguards. Reversed; judgment for H-E-B.
blocks.why: Texas rejects mode-of-operation liability. Distinguish Jasko by the store's precautions and the jurisdiction's rule.

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Res Ipsa / Factual Causation (due 10/8), 15th ed. pp. 325–326, 330–335, 337–340, and Ybarra v. Spangard (Canvas) · 13th ed. Ch. 4.G.

body.text: The jury may infer negligence when (all required): (a) the event is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur in the absence of negligence; (b) other responsible causes, including the conduct of the plaintiff and third persons, are sufficiently eliminated by the evidence; and (c) the indicated negligence is within the scope of the defendant's duty to the plaintiff.

**Traditional form (all required):** (1) the accident is the kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence; (2) the instrumentality was within the defendant's exclusive control; and (3) the plaintiff did not voluntarily act or contribute to it.

items: **Ordinarily does not occur without negligence** is shown by common experience or, in technical cases such as medical malpractice, by expert testimony.
**Exclusive control** is flexible today: the question is whether the defendant was probably responsible, as by control at the time of the negligent act, even if not at the time of injury.
**Specific evidence** of negligence does not necessarily forfeit res ipsa, unless it fully explains how the accident happened.

blocks.name: Byrne v. Boadle
blocks.facts: Byrne was walking on a public street past Boadle's flour shop when a barrel of flour fell from an upper window and hit him. He had no evidence of why it fell. The trial judge nonsuited him for lack of evidence of negligence.
blocks.held: Pollock, C.B.: "A barrel could not roll out of a warehouse without some negligence." The fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of negligence, and the plaintiff is not bound to show it could not have happened without negligence. If there are facts consistent with due care, the defendant, who controls the barrel and knows what happened, must prove them. Rule absolute to enter the verdict for Byrne.
blocks.why: This is the origin of res ipsa: an inference from the event itself, when the defendant has better access to the evidence.

blocks.name: McDougald v. Perry
blocks.topic: res ipsa from common experience: the flying spare tire
blocks.source: Canvas reading (10/6), from the opinion text in the course folder.
blocks.facts: On July 26, 1990, McDougald was driving his Jeep Wagoneer behind a tractor-trailer that Perry was driving for his employer, C & S Chemicals, on U.S. Highway 60 in Bartow, Florida. As the truck crossed railroad tracks, its 130-pound spare tire came out of its cradle under the trailer and fell to the road. The trailer's rear wheels ran over it, and it bounced up and smashed McDougald's windshield. The spare sat in an angled cradle, held by its own weight and by a four-to-six-foot chain that Perry believed was the original chain from 1969. The chain had originally been fastened with a latch but was now held by a nut and bolt. Perry had done a pre-trip inspection but did not check every link. Afterward the chain was dragging, and he thought a link had stretched and slipped off the bolt. The chain was not preserved. The jury, instructed on res ipsa loquitur, found for McDougald. The district court of appeal reversed, holding that McDougald had not proved the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence.
blocks.held: Wells, J.: res ipsa is a rule of evidence that permits, but does not compel, an inference of negligence. The plaintiff must show (1) the instrumentality was in the defendant's exclusive control and (2) the accident would not, in the ordinary course of events, have occurred without negligence by the one in control. Common experience shows that a spare tire carried on a truck, like a wheel on its axle, stays with the truck unless someone fails to use reasonable care: "no one expects the air to be filled with flying hubcaps." The plaintiff need not eliminate every other possible cause; it is enough that negligence is more likely than not. And direct proof was unavailable, because the chain and fastener were in the defendants' possession and were not preserved. The doctrine still applies only in "rare instances." Decision quashed; the jury's verdict on liability reinstated.
blocks.why: Common knowledge can supply the first element without expert testimony (R2d § 328D cmts. c–d). Contrast events that often happen without negligence, like a tire blowout or a fall down stairs. The defendant's control of the evidence strengthens the inference.

body.text: **Concurrence (Anstead, J.):** the result follows directly from Byrne v. Boadle (§ 16): "The common law tradition is alive and well."

blocks.name: Larson v. St. Francis Hotel
blocks.facts: On August 14, 1945, V-J Day, crowds were celebrating in San Francisco. Just after Larson stepped out from under the St. Francis Hotel's marquee onto the sidewalk, a heavy overstuffed armchair fell from an upper window and knocked her unconscious. No one saw where it came from. The trial court granted a nonsuit.
blocks.held: Bray, J.: res ipsa loquitur applies only if the instrumentality was under the defendant's exclusive control and management. Hotel guests, who rent rooms and use the furniture, have partial control. The likeliest explanation was that a celebrating guest threw the chair, which the hotel could not prevent with reasonable care. Affirmed.
blocks.why: If an equally likely cause lies outside the defendant's control, the inference fails.

blocks.name: Cruz v. DaimlerChrysler Motors Corp.
blocks.topic: negligence must point to this defendant
blocks.facts: Cruz was cleaning out his minivan when its front airbags suddenly deployed and injured him. He sued the maker, DaimlerChrysler, and Ricky Smith Pontiac, the dealer that had sold him the van three years earlier. After DaimlerChrysler went bankrupt, he dropped it and pressed negligence claims against the dealer, relying on res ipsa loquitur. The trial court granted summary judgment for the dealer.
blocks.held: Indeglia, J.: under R2d § 328D, element (a) was met, since airbags do not ordinarily deploy during cleaning without negligence. But element (b) failed: after three years in Cruz's hands, the evidence did not eliminate other causes or point the negligence to the dealer. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Element (b) of § 328D is the hurdle: other responsible causes must be sufficiently eliminated.

blocks.name: James v. Wormuth
blocks.facts: During a procedure to biopsy a lung nodule, a guide wire Dr. Wormuth had placed became dislodged. He searched for it by hand for about 20 minutes, could not find it, and decided to end the operation rather than keep James under anesthesia longer and enlarge the incision. He told her afterward. Weeks later, when she complained of pain, he removed it in a second operation. She sued for malpractice but offered no expert testimony that leaving the wire departed from accepted practice, relying on res ipsa. The trial court granted judgment for the doctor.
blocks.held: Rivera, J.: res ipsa applies to foreign objects left in the body unintentionally. It does not apply when the doctor deliberately left the object based on his judgment that doing so was in the patient's best interest. That judgment must be challenged with expert testimony on the standard of care. Exclusive control was also lacking, since other staff had handled the wire. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Res ipsa applies to forgotten sponges, not to deliberate choices. Those require expert proof.

blocks.name: Sullivan v. Crabtree
blocks.facts: Sullivan, the plaintiffs' son, was a guest passenger in a truck Crabtree was driving down a mountain highway. The truck suddenly swerved from the right lane to the left, ran off the road, and overturned down a steep embankment, killing Sullivan. Crabtree testified that gravel or broken pavement might have made him lose control but could not say for sure. The jury found for Crabtree.
blocks.held: Felts, J.: the facts made a case for res ipsa, which is evidence from which the jury may infer negligence. But res ipsa does not compel the jury to find negligence, even when the defendant cannot fully explain the accident; the jury may draw the inference it finds more probable. The verdict for Crabtree was affirmed.
blocks.why: Res ipsa usually creates a permissible inference, not a presumption, so the plaintiff can still lose.

rows: The case goes to the jury, which may or may not infer negligence
Shifts the burden of producing evidence; a directed verdict for the plaintiff if the defendant offers no rebuttal
Shift of the burden of proof
The defendant must prove it was not negligent
A few states, often for carriers

blocks.name: Ybarra v. Spangard
blocks.topic: res ipsa against a surgical team
blocks.source: Canvas reading (Res Ipsa module, due 10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.
blocks.facts: In October 1939, Dr. Tilley diagnosed Ybarra with appendicitis and arranged for Dr. Spangard to operate at a hospital owned and run by Dr. Swift. Dr. Reser, the anesthetist and Swift's employee, positioned Ybarra on the operating table, pulling him up so that the tops of his shoulders rested against two hard objects, and then anesthetized him. When Ybarra awoke the next morning, he had a sharp pain between his neck and right shoulder. It spread down his arm and led to paralysis and atrophy of the shoulder muscles. Two doctors testified the injury was traumatic, caused by pressure or strain, not by disease. Ybarra sued the doctors and nurses who had charge of him (Tilley, Spangard, Swift, Reser, and nurses Gisler and Thompson), but he could not say which one, or which instrumentality, injured him. The trial court granted nonsuits for all defendants.
blocks.held: Gibson, C.J.: res ipsa applies. (1) The injury was to a healthy part of the body away from the operation, which ordinarily does not happen without negligence, and (2) Ybarra contributed nothing to it. As for control, the test is right of control, not actual exclusive control. Every defendant in whose custody Ybarra was placed owed him ordinary care, employers answer for their employees, and the surgeon in charge answers for those who become his temporary servants during the operation. "Where a plaintiff receives unusual injuries while unconscious and in the course of medical treatment, all those defendants who had any control over his body or the instrumentalities which might have caused the injuries may properly be called upon to meet the inference of negligence by giving an explanation of their conduct." Reversed.
blocks.why: Ybarra stretches exclusive control to a team of defendants because the unconscious patient cannot identify the wrongdoer and the evidence is in their hands. Otherwise, the court said, there would rarely be any compensation for patients injured while unconscious. Compare Larson (control shared with strangers defeats res ipsa) and Summers v. Tice (burden-shifting on causation, § 18). [[On retrial the defendants were found liable, and the judgment was affirmed (Ybarra v. Spangard, 93 Cal. App. 2d 43 (1949)).]]

body.text: On the exam, walk through each element of § 328D with the facts. The usual weak spot is (b): who else could have caused it? Then state the procedural effect: the jury may infer negligence but need not.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 10/8 (hour 1), 15th ed. pp. 340–344, and Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch (Canvas); Module on Concurrent Causes (due 10/15), pp. 345–349, 356–366 · 13th ed. Ch. 5.A.

body.text: The defendant's negligence is a cause in fact of the harm if the harm would not have occurred without it. The plaintiff must show this by a preponderance of the evidence: more likely than not.

items: **The counterfactual:** imagine the defendant acting with due care (the train at the speed limit, the stairs lit), and ask whether the harm would still have happened.
**Possibility is not enough** (Kramer). Speculation, or an equally likely innocent explanation, fails.

**Expert proof** is often needed for medical and toxic causation. The expert must reach "more likely than not." [[Under Daubert (9th Cir. 1995, on remand), in pages the syllabus skips, an epidemiological study must generally show that the agent more than doubles the risk (relative risk above 2.0).]]

blocks.name: Perkins v. Texas and New Orleans R. Co.
blocks.facts: A train going 37 mph, over the 25 mph limit through the town of Vinton, hit a car at a blind crossing, killing Perkins's decedent, a passenger in the car. The car's speed could not be determined. The evidence showed that even at 25 mph the train could not have stopped in time once the car came into view. The jury found for Perkins, and the court of appeal affirmed.
blocks.held: Sanders, J.: negligence is not a cause in fact if the harm would have happened anyway. The engineer was negligent, but the plaintiff did not show that a slower train would have avoided the collision. Reversed; judgment for the railroad.
blocks.why: Negligence must be causally linked to the harm. A defendant is not liable for harm that due care would not have prevented.

blocks.name: Reynolds v. Texas & Pac. Ry. Co.
blocks.topic: negligence that increases the chance of harm
blocks.facts: Mrs. Reynolds, who weighed about 250 pounds, was hurried out of a brightly lit waiting room at night to catch her train and down unlit stairs to the platform. She fell and was badly hurt. The jury awarded $2,000. The railroad argued she might have fallen even if the stairs were lit.
blocks.held: Fenner, J.: when negligence greatly multiplies the chances of an accident and is of a kind that naturally leads to it, the mere possibility that it might have happened anyway does not break the causal connection. Courts look at "the natural and ordinary course of events," not remote speculations. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The jury may infer causation from the fact that the harm is exactly what the negligence risked.

blocks.name: Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch, Inc.
blocks.source: Canvas reading (10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder.
blocks.facts: On November 5, 1994, Brent Bacon drove to the Douglas Hereford Ranch, owned by a company controlled by his wife's grandmother and leased to Pard Cattle Co. He planned to start the furnace in a house that his wife and her friend Barbara Gentry were going to paint, and then to go deer hunting. On the way he had fired his lever-action .30-30 at a fox, cocked another round into the chamber, and lowered the hammer onto the live round. After failing to start the furnace, he got the rifle from his car and walked back toward the house carrying it on his shoulder, with a finger on the trigger and his thumb on the hammer. As he reached the wooden steps to a deck, he stumbled and fell; the rifle went off, and the bullet struck Barbara Gentry in the head. She died 69 days later. Her husband sued the ranch and cattle companies, claiming that a loose bottom step and debris around it made Bacon fall, and that the ranch was vicariously liable as Bacon's employer. (Bacon was dismissed after filing for bankruptcy.) Bacon repeatedly testified that he did not know whether he tripped on something, missed the step, or was just clumsy. The trial court granted summary judgment for the defendants.
blocks.held: Trieweiler, J.: negligence requires (1) duty, (2) breach, (3) causation, and (4) damages. Cause in fact is the but-for test, and because an intervening act was alleged, proximate cause was also in issue. Gentry offered no evidence that any condition of the steps caused Bacon to stumble. One statement ("I think it was the step") was contradicted by his own testimony that he did not know why he fell, and "a suspicion, regardless of how particularized it may be," does not defeat summary judgment. Nor was the ranch vicariously liable: Bacon's free help with the furnace did not make him its employee, and when he fell he had abandoned that task and was going hunting for himself. Affirmed.
blocks.why: But-for causation must be proved with evidence, not speculation about how an accident might have happened. Compare Reynolds (§ 17), where the jury could infer causation because the harm was exactly what the negligence risked. The case also previews respondeat superior (§ 31): no employment relationship, and no act within the scope of employment.

blocks.name: Kramer Service, Inc. v. Wilkins
blocks.facts: Wilkins, a guest at Kramer's hotel, was cut on the forehead when a piece of glass fell from a broken transom as he opened a door. The transom had been broken long enough that the hotel should have known. The wound never healed, and two years later a skin specialist found cancer at the spot. The undisputed expert testimony was that there was at most a remote possibility that the cut caused the cancer. The jury awarded damages including the cancer.
blocks.held: Griffith, J.: a mere possibility of causation does not support a verdict. Jurors have no experience with skin cancer, so they may not reject undisputed expert testimony on its cause. Wilkins may recover for the cut but not for the cancer. Affirmed on liability; reversed and remanded on damages.
blocks.why: The more-likely-than-not threshold applies to each item of harm.

blocks.name: Herskovits v. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound
blocks.facts: Group Health's doctors failed to diagnose Herskovits's lung cancer for about six months. Expert testimony showed that the delay reduced his chance of surviving five years from 39% to 25%. He died, and his estate sued under the survival statute. The trial court granted summary judgment because the estate could not show he probably would have survived (a better than 50% chance) with timely diagnosis.
blocks.held: Dore, J. (plurality): when a defendant's negligence substantially reduces a patient's chance of survival, the plaintiff need not show the patient probably would have survived; the reduction is enough to send causation to the jury, which decides what harm the increased risk caused. Damages are limited to those caused by the lost chance, not the death itself. Reversed.
blocks.why: This is the leading lost-chance case. The concurrence treated the lost chance itself as the injury, valued proportionally (14% of the full damages).

body.text: **Concurrence (Pearson, J.):** the lost chance itself is the compensable injury. Damages should be proportional: here, 14% of the full damages for death.

rows: The plaintiff must show the patient more likely than not would have survived, so above 50%
A substantial reduction in chance lets the jury find causation
Damages caused by the lost chance
Lost chance as the injury (Herskovits concurrence; now the majority of courts that allow it)
The lost chance is itself the compensable harm
Proportional: the percentage of chance lost times full damages

Each is liable for the whole (joint and several)

blocks.name: Hill v. Edmonds
blocks.facts: Bragoli left his truck parked without lights in the middle of the road on a stormy night. Edmonds, driving with Hill as a passenger, saw the truck four car lengths ahead, swerved, and hit it; she remembered nothing more. The trial court found Edmonds solely responsible and dismissed the complaint against Bragoli.
blocks.held: When separate acts of negligence combine to produce a single injury, each tortfeasor is liable for the whole, even though his act alone might not have caused it. The accident could not have happened had Bragoli not left the unlighted truck in the road. Complaint against Bragoli reinstated; new trial ordered.
blocks.why: An indivisible injury from concurrent negligence makes each defendant jointly and severally liable (§ 29).

blocks.name: Anderson v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. St. M. Ry. Co.
blocks.facts: A fire the railroad negligently started merged with a fire of unknown origin, and the combined fire burned Anderson's property. There was evidence that either fire alone would have destroyed it. The jury was instructed to find for Anderson if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial element in causing the damage, and it did.
blocks.held: Lees, Commr.: if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial factor in causing the damage, the railroad is liable even if the other fire alone would have caused the same harm. Two known negligent fires would each be liable for the whole; the result should not change because the other fire's origin is unknown. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The substantial factor test fills the gap where the but-for test would let both causes off. [[An older Wisconsin rule (Cook v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. Ste. M. Ry., 1898) excused the defendant when the other fire was of natural origin. Anderson and R2d § 432(2) reject that limit.]]

blocks.name: Summers v. Tice
blocks.facts: Summers went quail hunting with Tice and Simonson, who were each given instructions on safe shooting. A quail flew up between them and Summers, and both fired toward him at the same time with birdshot of the same size. One pellet hit his eye and another his lip. No one could tell whose gun fired which pellet. The trial court found both defendants negligent and liable.
blocks.held: Carter, J.: when two defendants are both negligent and the plaintiff cannot prove which one caused his injury, the burden shifts to each defendant to prove he did not cause it. Otherwise both are jointly and severally liable. The defendants are wrongdoers, both put the plaintiff at risk, and they are better placed to explain what happened. Affirmed.
blocks.why: R2d § 433B(3). The rule needs all the possible wrongdoers before the court and proof that all of them were negligent.

body.text: The burden shifts when (all required): (1) every defendant acted tortiously; (2) the harm was caused by one of them; (3) the plaintiff, through no fault of her own, cannot prove which; and (4) all the possible wrongdoers are before the court.

blocks.name: Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories
blocks.facts: Sindell's mother took DES, a drug to prevent miscarriage, while pregnant with her. DES caused cancer in some daughters years later, and Sindell developed cancer. About 200 companies had made DES from an identical formula, many pharmacies kept no record of which maker's pills filled a prescription, and Sindell could not identify the maker. She sued five makers. The trial court dismissed.
blocks.held: Mosk, J.: a plaintiff who cannot identify the maker of a fungible product through no fault of her own may recover if she joins makers of a substantial share of the market. Each defendant is liable for the share of the judgment matching its market share, unless it proves it could not have made the product that injured her. Summers v. Tice could not be applied directly, because the maker might not be before the court. Reversed.
blocks.why: Market share liability is a narrow exception, mostly limited to DES. [[Hymowitz v. Eli Lilly (N.Y. 1989) used a national market and did not let a defendant exculpate itself.]]

body.text: A plaintiff may recover under market share liability when (all required): (1) the defendants made a product of identical formula (fungible); (2) the product injured the plaintiff; (3) the plaintiff cannot identify the maker through no fault of her own; and (4) the plaintiff joins makers of a substantial share of the relevant market. Liability is several, in proportion to market share.

State the but-for test first. Move to substantial factor only when there are two sufficient causes, and to burden-shifting (Summers, Sindell) only when the plaintiff cannot identify which negligent actor caused the harm. Don't use substantial factor to rescue a weak but-for case.

blocks.title: Proximate Cause: Unforeseeable Plaintiffs and Consequences

blocks.text: Proximate cause, which the R3d calls scope of liability, limits liability to harms that bear a sufficient connection to the defendant's negligence. Cause in fact is about physics; proximate cause is about policy and fairness.

blocks.title: Scope of liability: R3d § 29 (the risk rule)

body.text: An actor's liability is limited to those harms that result from the risks that made the actor's conduct tortious. Ask (all required): (1) what risks made the conduct negligent; (2) was the plaintiff within the class of persons put at risk; and (3) was the harm of the type that was risked? The extent of the harm and the precise manner in which it happened need not be foreseeable.

blocks.name: Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Daniels
blocks.facts: The opinion discusses the concept in general terms, without a fact pattern the casebook relies on.
blocks.held: Every act has endless consequences, so the law must draw a practical, somewhat arbitrary line. Words like "proximate" and "natural" describe where courts stop tracing the connection between a wrongful act and an injury.
blocks.why: Proximate cause is a policy judgment about the limits of responsibility.

blocks.name: Ryan v. New York Central R.R. Co.
blocks.facts: A spark from the railroad's engine in Syracuse set fire to its own woodshed, through careless management or the engine's poor condition. The fire spread to Ryan's house, 130 feet away, and destroyed it, along with several other houses. The trial court nonsuited Ryan.
blocks.held: Hunt, J.: the railroad was liable only to the owner of the first building burned. The spread of fire to other buildings is not a necessary or usual result of a spark, and liability for every building a fire reaches would be ruinous; everyone runs some risk from neighbors and can insure. Affirmed.
blocks.why: This rule has been abandoned. Today the spread of fire is a foreseeable consequence. It shows how policy (a new industry, insurance, ruinous liability) drives proximate cause.

blocks.name: Bartolone v. Jeckovich
blocks.facts: Bartolone, a bodybuilder, suffered minor neck and back injuries in a car accident caused by Jeckovich. He then had a complete psychotic breakdown. Experts testified that he had a traumatic childhood and had used bodybuilding and a strict regimen to cope, and that when the accident disrupted his routine, his latent condition broke down. The jury awarded $500,000, but the trial court set the verdict aside as unsupported.
blocks.held: Denman, J.: a defendant takes the plaintiff as he finds him and is liable for all damages proximately caused, even if they seem out of proportion to the incident because of a pre-existing condition. The jury was entitled to believe the testimony that the accident triggered his breakdown. Reversed; verdict reinstated.
blocks.why: The eggshell plaintiff rule covers the extent of harm, including psychological harm. It is the clearest exception to foreseeability.

blocks.name: Polemis v. Furness, Withy & Co.
blocks.facts: Reported as In re Arbitration Between Polemis and Furness, Withy & Co. Furness chartered the ship Polemis, which carried petrol and benzine. While unloading at Casablanca, stevedores employed by the charterers carelessly let a plank fall into the hold. It struck something and caused a spark, which ignited petrol vapor, and the ship was destroyed. The arbitrators found that a spark could not reasonably have been anticipated, but that some damage to the ship from the falling plank could have been.
blocks.held: Once an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for all the direct consequences, even those that could not reasonably have been anticipated, so long as they are not due to an independent cause. Because some damage from dropping the plank was foreseeable, the fire was a direct result for which the charterers were liable.
blocks.why: This is the direct-consequences test, which Wagon Mound No. 1 rejected.

blocks.name: Overseas Tankship v. Morts Dock
blocks.topic: Wagon Mound No. 1: foreseeable kind of harm
blocks.facts: The Wagon Mound, moored about 600 feet from Morts Dock's wharf in Sydney Harbour, carelessly discharged a large quantity of furnace oil. The oil spread to the wharf, where Morts Dock's workers were welding. Two days later molten metal from the welding fell onto cotton waste floating on the oil, which ignited the oil, and the wharf burned. The trial court found that Overseas did not know, and could not reasonably have known, that furnace oil (flash point about 170°F) would burn when spread on water. It nonetheless found for Morts Dock under Polemis.
blocks.held: Viscount Simonds: Polemis is no longer good law. It is not consistent with justice that a negligent actor be liable for all consequences, however unforeseeable and grave, merely because they are "direct." Liability is limited to damage of the kind a reasonable person would have foreseen. Fouling of the wharf was foreseeable; fire was not. Reversed.
blocks.why: The foreseeable-type-of-harm test. Liability matches the risk that made the conduct negligent.

blocks.name: Overseas Tankship v. Miller Steamship Co.
blocks.topic: Wagon Mound No. 2: small but real risk
blocks.facts: The same fire damaged two ships owned by Miller Steamship that were being refitted at the wharf. On different evidence, the trial court found that the Wagon Mound's officers would have regarded fire as a possibility, though it would occur only in very exceptional circumstances, and it held for the defendant on the ground that the damage was not reasonably foreseeable.
blocks.held: Lord Reid: a reasonable person would not ignore a real risk, even a small one, if it could be eliminated easily and there was no valid reason for running it. Discharging oil into the harbor was unjustified, and the engineer should have known fire was possible, so the risk, though slight, made the defendant liable. Reversed; judgment for Miller.
blocks.why: This is the same accident with a different result, because foreseeability is a finding of fact and it ties back to the Hand formula (§ 11).

blocks.name: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R. Co.
blocks.facts: Mrs. Palsgraf bought a ticket to Rockaway Beach and was standing on the platform. Two men ran to catch a train that was pulling out. One guard on the train pulled and another on the platform pushed one of them aboard. He was carrying a small package wrapped in newspaper, which fell onto the rails. It contained fireworks and exploded. The shock knocked over scales at the far end of the platform, which struck Mrs. Palsgraf. The jury found for her, and the Appellate Division affirmed.
blocks.held: Cardozo, C.J.: "The risk reasonably to be perceived defines the duty to be obeyed." Negligence is not a tort in the abstract; it is a wrong only to someone within the range of apparent danger. Nothing about the package suggested danger to a person standing far away, so the guards' conduct, even if negligent toward the man or his package, was not a wrong toward Mrs. Palsgraf. Reversed; complaint dismissed.
blocks.why: The leading case on unforeseeable plaintiffs. Cardozo frames it as duty (the zone of danger), Andrews as proximate cause.

body.text: **Dissent (Andrews, J.):** everyone owes the world at large a duty to refrain from acts that unreasonably threaten others. When an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for the injuries it proximately causes, and proximate cause is a practical line drawn by "convenience, of public policy, of a rough sense of justice." Factors include a natural and continuous sequence, direct connection, foreseeability, and remoteness in time and space. Here the explosion's effect was close and direct, and he would have affirmed.

rows: Duty: is the plaintiff within the zone of foreseeable danger?
Proximate cause: is the harm too remote, as a matter of policy?
Usually the court (duty is a question of law)
Foreseeability of harm to this plaintiff

(weighed together) (1) a natural and continuous sequence; (2) a direct connection without too many intervening causes; (3) whether the cause was a substantial factor; (4) foreseeability; and (5) remoteness in time and space

blocks.name: Yun v. Ford Motor Co.
blocks.topic: plaintiff's own conduct as the sole proximate cause
blocks.facts: Chang was a passenger in a 1987 Ford van his daughter Yun was driving on the Garden State Parkway at night. The spare tire assembly fell off the back and rolled across both lanes to the guardrail. Yun pulled over on the right shoulder. Chang ran across the Parkway to retrieve the tire and was struck and killed by another car. Yun sued Ford and others, alleging a defective spare tire bracket. The trial court granted summary judgment.
blocks.held: Villanueva, J.: even assuming a defect, Chang's decision to cross a busy highway at night to retrieve a spare tire was so extraordinary and unforeseeable that it was the sole proximate cause of his death. Affirmed. [[The New Jersey Supreme Court reversed, substantially for the reasons of the Appellate Division dissent, which would let a jury decide whether his response was foreseeable (143 N.J. 162 (1996)).]]
blocks.why: A plaintiff's extraordinary response can cut off proximate cause. Many courts leave the question to the jury and handle it as comparative fault.

items: **Type of harm:** must be foreseeable (Wagon Mound No. 1).
**Extent of harm:** need not be foreseeable (eggshell plaintiff, Bartolone).
**Manner of harm:** need not be foreseeable if the type of harm was [[(Hughes v. Lord Advocate, H.L. 1963: a lamp exploded in an unforeseeable way, but the risk was burns)]].
**Plaintiff:** must be foreseeable under Cardozo (Palsgraf). Rescuers are foreseeable (§ 20).

blocks.text: **Reading:** 10/20 (hour 1), 15th ed. pp. 434–444; Module on Proximate Cause (due 10/22), pp. 449–454, 532–535; 10/22, pp. 458–462 · 13th ed. Ch. 6.C.

body.text: An intervening act (of a third person, the plaintiff, or nature) breaks the chain of proximate cause only if it is a superseding cause. It is **not** superseding when it is foreseeable, or when it is within the very risk that made the defendant's conduct negligent (Derdiarian).

**Factors, R2d § 442 (weighed together):** (a) the intervention brings about harm different in kind from that which would otherwise have resulted; (b) its operation or consequences appear extraordinary rather than normal; (c) it operates independently of any situation the actor created, or is not a normal result of that situation; (d) it is due to a third person's act or failure to act; (e) it is a third person's wrongful act toward the plaintiff; and (f) the degree of culpability of the third person's wrongful act.

items: **Usually not superseding (foreseeable):** negligent medical treatment of the injury; rescue efforts; ordinary negligence of other drivers; the victim's reasonable reactions; and suicide by someone the defendant's negligence drove insane (Fuller).

**Usually superseding:** an intentional crime or tort by a third person, unless the defendant's negligence created the very opportunity or the defendant had a duty to protect against it (R2d §§ 448–449); and an extraordinary act of nature.
**The trend:** with comparative fault and apportionment, courts more often let the jury apportion than declare the later actor the only one responsible.

blocks.name: Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting Corp.
blocks.facts: Felix, a general contractor, was installing a gas main and had an excavation on one side of a road. It set up no adequate barrier. Derdiarian, a subcontractor's employee, was working beside a kettle of 400-degree liquid enamel. Dickens, who had not taken his epilepsy medication, had a seizure while driving, lost control, and crashed into the work site. Derdiarian was thrown into the air and splashed with the burning enamel. The jury found against Felix.
blocks.held: Cooke, C.J.: an intervening act does not break the causal chain if it is a normal or foreseeable consequence of the situation the defendant's negligence created. The very reason Felix's failure to barricade was negligent was the risk of a car entering the site. That the risk materialized in an unusual way, or that the driver was also negligent, does not relieve Felix. Proximate cause was properly left to the jury. Affirmed.
blocks.why: If the intervening act is within the risk, it does not supersede. Proximate cause is usually a jury question.

blocks.name: Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge & R.R. Co.
blocks.facts: Through the railroad's negligence, a tank car full of gasoline derailed, its valve broke, and gasoline poured into the street. Duerr struck a match, igniting the vapor, and the explosion injured Watson. There was conflicting evidence whether Duerr lit the match to light his cigar or did it deliberately to cause an explosion. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.
blocks.held: Settle, J.: the jury should have decided why Duerr lit the match. If he did it inadvertently, his act was a foreseeable consequence of the spill and the railroad remains liable. If he did it maliciously, the railroad could not reasonably have anticipated it, and his act is the sole proximate cause. Reversed; new trial.
blocks.why: The traditional rule is that foreseeable negligence of a third person does not supersede, but a deliberate crime does. R2d § 448 moderates this when the defendant's negligence created the opportunity for the crime.

blocks.name: Fuller v. Preis
blocks.facts: Dr. Lewis, a surgeon, suffered head injuries in a car accident caused by Preis. He had been healthy before. Afterward he had 38 epileptic seizures, three on the day of his death, which drugs could not control. He became depressed, unsteady, and irritable, and seven months after the accident he shot himself, leaving notes saying he was sane. A neurologist testified he was in a post-seizure psychosis that put his conduct beyond his control. The jury awarded $200,000, but the Appellate Division reversed and dismissed.
blocks.held: Breitel, C.J.: suicide is not a superseding cause as a matter of law. A tortfeasor is liable for a suicide that results from an irresistible impulse caused by the injury, even if the decedent understood what he was doing. His notes declaring his sanity were not conclusive. The evidence supported the jury's finding. Reversed.
blocks.why: The defendant's tort created the mental condition, so the plaintiff's act is not a free, informed choice that cuts off liability.

blocks.name: McCoy v. American Suzuki Motor Corp.
blocks.facts: McCoy was driving on an interstate at night when the Suzuki Samurai ahead of him swerved off the road and rolled. He stopped to help and found the driver badly hurt. A state trooper asked him to set out flares. After the injured were cared for, McCoy was walking back to his car along the road when a hit-and-run driver struck him. He sued Suzuki, claiming the Samurai was defectively prone to roll over. The trial court granted summary judgment for Suzuki. The court of appeals reversed, holding that a rescuer need only show the defendant caused the danger.
blocks.held: Sanders, J.: the rescue doctrine applies in products cases. "Danger invites rescue," so a rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff, and the rescuer is not presumed to have assumed the risk unless he acted rashly. But the doctrine does not relieve the rescuer of proving proximate cause of his own injuries. Whether Suzuki's defect proximately caused McCoy's injuries was a fact question, so summary judgment was improper. Court of appeals affirmed on different grounds.
blocks.why: A rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff. To invoke the doctrine, the rescuer shows (all required): (1) the defendant's negligence (or defect) caused the peril; (2) the peril was imminent; (3) a reasonably prudent person would have concluded that the peril existed; and (4) the rescuer acted with reasonable care in carrying out the rescue.

blocks.name: Kelly v. Gwinnell
blocks.facts: Gwinnell drank at Zak's home and, according to the complaint, Zak served him until he was visibly intoxicated, then accompanied him to his car, chatted, and watched him drive off. Gwinnell's blood-alcohol level was later 0.286. He collided head-on with Kelly's car. Kelly sued Gwinnell and Zak. The trial court granted summary judgment for Zak, and the Appellate Division affirmed.
blocks.held: Wilentz, C.J.: a social host who directly serves liquor to an adult guest, knowing the guest is intoxicated and will soon drive, is liable to third parties injured by the guest's drunk driving. The law already made commercial servers and hosts serving minors liable, and the risk is foreseeable. The guest's drunk driving is not a superseding cause. Reversed. (The rule was applied prospectively.)
blocks.why: This is the minority rule. Many legislatures, including California's, have rejected it, and the dissent said the legislature should decide. [[Delaware recognizes no dram shop or social host liability (McCall v. Villa Pizza, Del. 1994).]]

body.text: **Dissent (Garibaldi, J.):** the competing social and economic interests (insurance, the burden on hosts) should be weighed by the legislature, not imposed by the court.

blocks.title: Liability for providing alcohol: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft)

body.text: **(a)** If a statute (a dram shop act) governs, the statute controls.

**(b)** Absent a statute, a commercial establishment is subject to liability for negligently providing alcohol (any one suffices): (1) to underage patrons, or (2) to visibly intoxicated patrons of any age, when the patron's intoxication factually causes later injury.

**(c)** Absent a statute, a social host (1) is subject to liability for recklessly providing alcohol to underage guests, when their intoxication factually causes later injury; but (2) is not liable for providing alcohol to guests of legal drinking age, even past the point of intoxication.
The draft rejects Kelly v. Gwinnell for adult guests, in line with most states.

blocks.name: Enright v. Eli Lilly & Co.
blocks.facts: In 1960, Enright's grandmother took DES while pregnant with Enright's mother, Patricia. DES allegedly damaged Patricia's reproductive system in utero. Enright was born prematurely, with cerebral palsy and other disabilities, allegedly as a result. She sued Eli Lilly. The trial court dismissed her claim; the Appellate Division affirmed.
blocks.held: Wachtler, C.J.: a child injured because of a tort to her mother before the child was conceived has no claim against the original tortfeasor. Liability to those who took the drug or were exposed in utero serves deterrence; extending it to later generations would create staggering, open-ended liability and could deter drug development. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Courts sometimes cut off liability for policy reasons, even where harm is foreseeable and causation is clear.

blocks.title: Duty and the Failure to Act

blocks.text: **Reading:** 10/22, 15th ed. pp. 458–462, 526–527 (note 10), 553–555, 565–570; Proximate Cause module pp. 532–535 · 13th ed. Ch. 8.A–B.

items: **Duty is a question of law** for the court. The default is a duty of reasonable care to avoid creating risks of physical harm (R3d § 7). Courts limit or modify it for reasons of principle or policy.

**Factors used to decide duty (weighed together, as in Rowland and Tarasoff):** (1) foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff; (2) the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury; (3) the closeness of the connection between the conduct and the injury; (4) the moral blame attached to the conduct; (5) the policy of preventing future harm; (6) the burden on the defendant and the consequences to the community of imposing the duty; and (7) the availability, cost, and prevalence of insurance.
**Misfeasance vs. nonfeasance.** Acting carelessly (misfeasance) creates a duty. Merely failing to help (nonfeasance) generally does not.

blocks.name: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.
blocks.topic: the end of the privity limit
blocks.facts: Buick sold a car to a retail dealer, who sold it to MacPherson. While he was driving, one of the wooden wheels collapsed because its spokes were made of defective wood, and he was thrown out and injured. Another company made the wheel, but a reasonable inspection by Buick would have revealed the defect. The jury found for MacPherson, and the Appellate Division affirmed.
blocks.held: Cardozo, J.: if a product is reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made, and the maker knows it will be used by people other than the buyer without new tests, the maker owes those users a duty of care, regardless of privity. Buick was a manufacturer of finished cars and could not escape its duty to inspect components. Affirmed.
blocks.why: MacPherson rejected Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), which required privity. A negligent manufacturer owes a duty to foreseeable users.

blocks.name: H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co.
blocks.facts: The water company contracted with the City of Rensselaer to supply water for fire hydrants, public buildings, and private customers. A fire spread from a nearby building to Moch's warehouse. The company was promptly notified but failed to supply enough water pressure at the hydrants, and the warehouse burned. Moch sued for breach of contract, common-law tort, and breach of statutory duty.
blocks.held: Cardozo, C.J.: the company owed no tort duty to individual citizens. Its failure was the withholding of a benefit (nonfeasance), not the launching of "a force or an instrument of harm" (misfeasance). Citizens were only incidental beneficiaries of the contract, and recognizing the claim would make suppliers liable to an indefinite number of people. Dismissal affirmed.
blocks.why: The test: has the defendant "launched a force or instrument of harm," or only failed to confer a benefit? Policy concerns about unlimited liability also played a role.

blocks.name: Clagett v. Dacy
blocks.facts: Dacy, an attorney, was hired by a mortgage lender to conduct a foreclosure sale. Because he did not follow proper procedures, the sale was set aside twice, and during the delay the borrower paid off the loan and redeemed the property. Clagett, the high bidder at both sales, sued Dacy for malpractice, claiming he lost a chance to buy the land and resell it at a profit. The trial court sustained Dacy's demurrer.
blocks.held: Wilner, J.: a lawyer owes no duty of care to a third party with whom he has no attorney-client relationship, unless the third party is an intended beneficiary of the representation, such as a will beneficiary. Bidders at a foreclosure sale are adverse to the lender's lawyer, who seeks the highest price while bidders seek the lowest. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Privity still limits professional malpractice duties for economic loss, subject to the third-party-beneficiary exception.

blocks.title: No duty to rescue, and its exceptions

body.text: One who has not created the risk has no duty to act to protect or rescue another, even if the rescue would be easy and safe. [[The classic example is Yania v. Bigan (Pa. 1959): no duty to rescue a man who jumped into a water-filled pit at the defendant's urging.]]

**A duty to act arises (any one suffices):** (1) a special relationship with the plaintiff, such as carrier-passenger, innkeeper-guest, possessor-invitee, custodian-ward, employer-employee, or school-student (R2d § 314A; L.S. Ayres); (2) the defendant created the peril, even innocently (R2d §§ 321–322); (3) the defendant undertook to help, then left the plaintiff worse off or induced reliance (R2d §§ 323–324); (4) a special relationship with the person who poses the danger, such as therapist-patient, parent-child, or custodian of a dangerous person (R2d §§ 315, 319; Tarasoff); (5) a statute imposes the duty; or (6) a contract imposes it.

blocks.name: L.S. Ayres & Co. v. Hicks
blocks.topic: duty to aid a business invitee
blocks.facts: Hicks, a six-year-old boy shopping with his mother at the Ayres department store, fell on an escalator and caught his fingers in the moving parts. Store employees did not stop the escalator for an unreasonable time, and his injuries were made worse. The jury found the store liable for all his injuries.
blocks.held: Shake, C.J.: a store that invites customers onto its premises and controls the instrumentality that injured one of them must use reasonable care to aid the injured invitee, even if the store did not cause the original injury and the invitee was careless. But the store is liable only for the aggravation caused by its failure to act, not for the original injury. Reversed; new trial.
blocks.why: This is the business-invitee exception. Liability is limited to harm caused by the failure to act.

blocks.name: Hegel v. Langsam
blocks.topic: no duty to supervise adult students
blocks.facts: The Hegels' 17-year-old daughter enrolled as a freshman at the University of Cincinnati and was assigned to a dormitory. The university did not monitor her comings and goings. She stopped staying in the dormitory, became involved with criminals, was seduced, and began using drugs. Her parents demanded the university return her, but officials could not. The parents sued for failure to supervise.
blocks.held: Bettman, J.: a university has no duty to regulate the private lives of its students, control their comings and goings, or supervise their associations. It is an educational institution, not a nursery, boarding school, or prison, and students are presumed mature enough to care for themselves. Judgment on the pleadings for the university.
blocks.why: There is no general custodial relationship between a college and adult students.

blocks.name: Commonwealth v. Peterson
blocks.facts: At about 7:15 a.m. on April 16, 2007, a gunman shot two students in West Ambler Johnston Hall at Virginia Tech, killing one. Police concluded it was a targeted domestic homicide, that the shooter had probably fled, and that a lockdown was unnecessary; they pursued a person of interest, a victim's boyfriend. University administrators sent a campus email about the shooting at 9:26 a.m. Around 9:40 a.m., the same gunman began shooting in Norris Hall, killing 30 more people, including Erin Peterson and Julia Pryde. Their estates sued the Commonwealth, and a jury found it negligent for failing to warn students sooner.
blocks.held: Powell, J.: assuming without deciding that a special relationship existed between the university and its students, there was no duty to warn of third-party criminal harm unless the harm was known or reasonably foreseeable. Based on what officials knew before the second shooting (a targeted killing, a shooter who had apparently fled), it was not reasonably foreseeable that students in classroom buildings would be harmed. Reversed; final judgment for the Commonwealth.
blocks.why: Even where a special relationship exists, the duty extends only to foreseeable harm. Foreseeability usually requires knowledge of an imminent probability of injury.

blocks.name: J.S. v. R.T.H.
blocks.topic: duty to protect from a spouse's abuse
blocks.facts: Two young sisters spent a great deal of time with their neighbor, R.T.H., at his horse barn. He sexually abused them over a period of time. Their parents sued him and his wife, claiming she knew or should have known of his conduct. The trial court granted summary judgment for the wife; the Appellate Division reversed.
blocks.held: Handler, J.: when a spouse has actual knowledge or special reason to know that her spouse is likely to abuse a particular person, she has a duty of reasonable care to prevent or warn of the abuse, and a breach can be a proximate cause of it. The court weighed foreseeability (the most important factor), the severity of the harm, the opportunity to prevent it, the parties' relationships, and public policy against child abuse. Affirmed; case remanded for trial.
blocks.why: The duty is based on foreseeability, the relationship, and strong public policy against child abuse.

blocks.name: Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California
blocks.topic: therapist's duty to protect third persons
blocks.facts: Prosenjit Poddar, a patient at the university's hospital, told his psychologist, Dr. Moore, that he intended to kill Tatiana Tarasoff, an identifiable young woman who had rejected him. Dr. Moore notified campus police and asked that Poddar be detained. Police held him briefly but released him when he seemed rational, and the psychiatry director ordered no further action. No one warned Tarasoff or her family. Two months later Poddar killed her. Her parents sued; the trial court sustained demurrers.
blocks.held: Tobriner, J.: when a therapist determines, or under the standards of the profession should determine, that a patient presents a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim, by warning her, notifying the police, or taking other reasonable steps. The special relationship with the patient supports the duty. Confidentiality must yield: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." The complaint stated a cause of action against the therapists (the police were immune).
blocks.why: The special relationship with a dangerous person supports a duty to an identifiable victim. [[Most states now codify and limit the duty by statute, often to a serious threat against a reasonably identifiable victim.]]

blocks.title: Other duty limits in Ch. 8 (not on the syllabus pages)

items: **Negligent infliction of emotional distress:** zone-of-danger and bystander rules (Daley v. LaCroix; Thing v. La Chusa). For the intentional tort, see § 5.
**Pure economic loss:** generally not recoverable without physical harm (State of Louisiana ex rel. Guste v. M/V Testbank).
**Prenatal harm, wrongful birth, and wrongful life** (Endresz; Procanik).
**Good Samaritan statutes** [[shield people who give emergency aid in good faith from liability for ordinary negligence.]]

body.text: On a failure-to-act fact pattern, say the no-duty rule first, then go through each exception in the rule box and say which fits. If the defendant did something (drove, served drinks, let the patient go), consider whether it is really misfeasance.

The defendant must prove that (all required): (1) the plaintiff failed to use reasonable care for her own safety; and (2) that failure was a cause in fact and a proximate cause of her harm. At common law, contributory negligence is a complete bar (Butterfield).

blocks.text: **Exceptions to the bar (any one suffices):** (1) last clear chance: the defendant had the last opportunity to avoid the harm (Davies v. Mann); (2) the defendant acted intentionally, willfully, wantonly, or recklessly; (3) the defendant violated a statute meant to protect the plaintiff from her own carelessness (e.g., child-labor laws); or (4) the plaintiff was a rescuer acting reasonably.

blocks.name: Butterfield v. Forrester
blocks.facts: Forrester, repairing his house, put a pole across part of the road, though passage was still possible. At dusk, when candles were just being lit but a rider could see 100 yards ahead, Butterfield rode out "violently," did not see the pole, crashed into it, and was thrown and injured. There was no evidence he was drunk. The jury found for Forrester.
blocks.held: Lord Ellenborough, C.J.: a plaintiff cannot recover when his own lack of ordinary care contributed to the accident. "One person being in fault will not dispense with another's using ordinary care for himself." Had Butterfield ridden with ordinary care, he would have seen the pole. Judgment for Forrester.
blocks.why: This is the origin of the all-or-nothing contributory negligence bar.

blocks.name: Davies v. Mann
