blocks.facts: Davies fettered the forefeet of his donkey and turned it onto a narrow public road to graze. Mann's wagon, driven at a "smartish pace" by a servant who was not watching, knocked it down and killed it.
blocks.held: Lord Abinger, C.B., and Parke, B.: Davies's negligence in leaving the donkey on the road does not bar recovery, because Mann could have avoided the accident with ordinary care. Otherwise a driver could run over anything lawfully or unlawfully in the road. Verdict for Davies upheld.
blocks.why: This is the origin of last clear chance, the main escape from the contributory negligence bar. [[R2d §§ 479–480 distinguish a helpless plaintiff (the defendant is liable if it knew or should have known) from an inattentive one (the defendant is liable only if it actually knew).]]

blocks.name: McIntyre v. Balentine
blocks.facts: McIntyre and Balentine collided at night on a highway. Both had been drinking, and there was evidence Balentine was speeding. The jury, instructed on contributory negligence, found them equally at fault, which barred McIntyre.
blocks.held: Drowota, J.: Tennessee abolishes contributory negligence and adopts modified comparative fault. A plaintiff may recover so long as her fault is less than the defendants' combined fault (the 49% bar), with damages reduced by her percentage. Last clear chance, remote contributory negligence, and joint and several liability are rendered obsolete. The jury might have apportioned fault differently under the new rule, so a new trial was ordered.
blocks.why: This is the 49% bar version of modified comparative fault, adopted by a court rather than a legislature. Compare Li v. Yellow Cab (Cal. 1975), which adopted pure comparative fault.

header: Plaintiff recovers when her fault is
rows: Pure comparative fault (Li; about a dozen states)
Modified, 49% bar ("not as great as"; McIntyre)
No greater than the defendants' fault

items: [[Contributory negligence remains the rule only in Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, and the District of Columbia.]]
[[Delaware: modified comparative negligence, 50% bar. The plaintiff recovers if her negligence is not greater than the defendants' combined negligence (10 Del. C. § 8132).]]

**Effects of comparative fault:** last clear chance is absorbed, implied assumption of risk is generally merged (§ 23), and the jury allocates percentages among all parties. Courts split on whether to compare the plaintiff's negligence with a defendant's intentional tort.
**Several defendants:** most modified-comparative-fault states compare the plaintiff's fault with the defendants' combined fault, not with each defendant separately.

blocks.title: Comparing fault: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment Topic 6, §§ 30–31 (approved 2022)

body.text: These sections state the rules for tort claims for economic harm, applying the general Apportionment rules. **§ 30:** a plaintiff's negligent or reckless conduct is not a basis for reducing her recovery against a defendant who intended the harm. **§ 31:** against a defendant who did not intend the harm, the plaintiff's negligence that causes her harm, and is within her scope of responsibility, reduces her recovery in proportion to her share of comparative responsibility.

Do the arithmetic on the exam. First find the plaintiff's percentage and apply the jurisdiction's threshold. Then reduce the damages. Then allocate among defendants (§ 29). State the system you are using, especially on the open-book essay.

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Assumption of Risk (due 10/29), 15th ed. pp. 765–771; 10/29 (hour 1), pp. 772–789 · 13th ed. Ch. 12.B.

rows: The plaintiff agrees in advance, usually in writing, to release the defendant from liability for negligence
The defendant owes no duty, or did not breach one, as to risks inherent in an activity (sports, spectators)
No liability: there is no negligence to compare
The plaintiff reasonably and knowingly encounters a risk the defendant negligently created
Not a defense; reasonable conduct is not fault
The plaintiff unreasonably and knowingly encounters the risk
Merged into comparative fault; reduces damages

body.text: An exculpatory clause is enforceable when (all required): (1) its language clearly and unambiguously releases the defendant from liability for its own negligence; (2) the injury falls within its scope; and (3) no exception applies.

**Exceptions (any one suffices):** (1) the defendant's conduct was intentional, reckless, or grossly negligent; (2) the bargaining power was grossly unequal, as in an adhesion contract for an essential service; or (3) the transaction affects the public interest. [[Courts often use the Tunkl v. Regents factors (Cal. 1963): a business suitable for public regulation, offering an essential service, to any member of the public, with superior bargaining power and a standardized contract.]]

blocks.name: Seigneur v. National Fitness Institute, Inc.
blocks.topic: exculpatory clause in a gym contract
blocks.facts: Gerilynne Seigneur joined NFI's gym and signed a membership agreement in which she assumed "all risk of injury" from using the facilities and released NFI from all claims, expressly including its negligence. At her initial evaluation, she hurt her right shoulder on a weight machine. She and her husband sued for negligence, both vicarious (the employee's evaluation) and direct (negligent hiring and training). The trial court granted summary judgment for NFI.
blocks.held: Salmon, J.: an exculpatory clause is valid if it clearly and specifically releases the defendant from liability for its own negligence, unless (1) the conduct was intentional, reckless, wanton, or grossly negligent; (2) the bargaining power was grossly unequal; or (3) the transaction affects the public interest. The agreement was an adhesion contract, but that alone does not show grossly unequal bargaining power: Seigneur could have gone to another gym for a non-essential service. Health clubs are not in the public-interest category. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Recreational releases are usually enforced. Releases in medical care, public utilities, and similar essential services usually are not.

body.text: The defendant must show that (all required): (1) the plaintiff actually knew of the specific risk (subjective knowledge); (2) the plaintiff appreciated its nature and magnitude; and (3) the plaintiff voluntarily chose to encounter it.

blocks.name: Rush v. Commercial Realty Co.
blocks.facts: Rush rented a house from Commercial Realty, which provided an outhouse as the only toilet for its tenants. Rush knew the floor was in bad condition. When she used it, she fell through a trap door in the floor into the pit below. The jury found for Rush, and the landlord appealed the denial of its motions for nonsuit and directed verdict.
blocks.held: Per curiam: assumption of risk requires a free and voluntary choice. Rush had no reasonable alternative to using the only toilet provided, and she was not required to leave her home and go elsewhere. Whether stepping on a floor she knew was in poor repair was contributory negligence was for the jury, but it was not assumption of risk. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Voluntariness requires a genuine choice. A choice the defendant forces on the plaintiff does not count.

blocks.name: Blackburn v. Dorta
blocks.topic: merging implied assumption of risk into comparative fault
blocks.facts: The court consolidated several cases, including car-accident cases, raising the same question: whether implied assumption of risk survived as a complete defense after Florida adopted comparative negligence in Hoffman v. Jones (1973).
blocks.held: Sundberg, J.: assumption of risk is a confused doctrine with many labels: express and implied, primary and secondary, strict ("pure") and qualified. Only implied, secondary, qualified assumption of risk has mattered as a defense, and it is indistinguishable from contributory negligence. It is therefore merged into comparative negligence and is no longer a complete bar. Express assumption of risk and the no-duty situations covered by primary assumption of risk are unaffected.
blocks.why: This is the standard way courts sort the doctrine. The labels confuse; ask whether there was a duty and whether the plaintiff acted unreasonably.

items: **Primary assumption of risk** is really a no-duty or no-breach argument. A baseball fan hit by a foul ball loses because the stadium owed no duty to screen every seat, not because of a defense [[(the "baseball rule")]].
**Knowledge is subjective.** A plaintiff who did not actually know of the specific risk did not assume it, though she may have been contributorily negligent for not knowing.

blocks.title: Firefighter's rule: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft)

body.text: An actor who innocently or negligently creates a peril that brings a professional rescuer to the scene owes that rescuer no duty when the rescuer is injured by the very peril that brought the rescuer there, and the rescuer is injured while (all required): (1) on duty; (2) acting within the scope of employment; and (3) performing emergency activities.
Compare the rescue doctrine (McCoy, § 20), which protects volunteer rescuers. The firefighter's rule rests on the idea that professional rescuers are paid and insured to face these risks.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 11/3, 15th ed. pp. 789–806 · 13th ed. Ch. 12.C.

items: **Statute of limitations:** a claim must be filed within a set time after it accrues, typically 1–3 years for personal injury. It is an affirmative defense.
**Accrual:** traditionally at the time of injury. Under the **discovery rule**, it accrues when the plaintiff discovers, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury and its cause (Teeters).
**Tolling (any one suffices):** (1) minority; (2) mental incapacity; (3) the defendant's fraudulent concealment of the claim; or (4) a continuing tort or continuous course of treatment.

**Statute of repose:** a fixed outer limit measured from the defendant's act (sale of a product, completion of construction, the medical procedure), regardless of when the injury is discovered. It can bar a claim before the injury occurs.

[[**Delaware:** personal injury actions must be filed within 2 years (10 Del. C. § 8119). Medical negligence claims must be filed within 2 years of the injury, or within 3 years if the injury was unknown and could not reasonably have been discovered within the 2 years (18 Del. C. § 6856).]]

blocks.title: Limitations and repose: R3d Misc. Prov. §§ 1–16 (T.D. 3, draft)

body.text: **When the limitations period starts (§§ 2–4):** under the **all-elements rule (§ 2)**, it starts when all elements of the claim have occurred. Under the **discovery rule (§ 3)**, it does not start until the plaintiff discovers, or with reasonable diligence should have discovered, all the factual elements of the claim against the defendant (Teeters). For **continuing torts (§ 4)**: (a) if the law requires all damages from repeated conduct to be sought in one action, it starts when it starts for any part; (b) if the injury is the cumulative, progressive result of repeated conduct, none of which alone causes an identifiable injury, it starts only after the conduct stops; and (c) for false imprisonment, it starts only after the confinement ends.

**Tolling and suspension (any one suffices):** (1) continuous representation by a lawyer on the same or a related matter (§ 6); (2) continuous medical treatment for the same or a related condition (§ 7); (3) equitable tolling, when the plaintiff was diligently pursuing her rights but an extraordinary circumstance prevented a timely suit (§ 8); (4) equitable estoppel, when the defendant's words, conduct, or silence reasonably induced the plaintiff not to sue in time (§ 9); or (5) fraudulent concealment, which suspends the period until the plaintiff discovers, or should have discovered, the fraud (§ 10). Statutory tolling rules, such as minority, are left to the statutes (§ 5).

**Statutes of repose (§§ 12–15):** a repose period runs from a specified event, such as the tortious act, the sale of a product, or the completion of a building, whether or not the plaintiff could yet sue (§§ 12–13). Common-law tolling does not suspend it (§ 14), but equitable estoppel and fraudulent concealment do (§ 15).

blocks.name: Teeters v. Currey
blocks.facts: On June 5, 1970, after delivering Mrs. Teeters's child, Dr. Currey performed a bilateral tubal ligation to prevent future pregnancies. On December 6, 1972, she learned she was pregnant again, and on March 9, 1973, she delivered a premature child with severe complications. She sued on November 15, 1973. Currey pleaded the one-year statute of limitations, and the trial court agreed.
blocks.held: Henry, J.: in a malpractice action for negligent surgery, the limitations period begins when the patient discovers, or in the exercise of reasonable care should have discovered, the injury, not on the date of the operation. It would be unfair to bar a claim before the patient could know of it. Teeters sued within a year of discovery. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: This is a judicial adoption of the discovery rule. Many legislatures responded with medical malpractice statutes of repose that cap the discovery period.

body.text: **Family and charitable immunity:** there is no spousal, parental, child, or other family immunity (§§ 1–4), and, subject to contrary statutes, no charitable immunity (§ 5).

**Parental standard of care (§ 10A):** (a) when a parent's conduct does not involve an unemancipated minor child's discipline, supervision, or care, the parent must use reasonable care; (b) when it does, the parent is liable to the child only for reckless conduct. Compare Zellmer, where Washington's parental immunity covered negligent supervision but not a stepparent.

**Government (§§ 9–10):** a state is immune unless it consents to suit or abrogates its immunity. Even when it consents, and always for local governments, immunity remains for acts or omissions that (any one suffices) (1) are specifically immunized by statute; (2) are the exercise of a judicial or legislative function; or (3) are the exercise of an administrative function involving the discretionary determination of important governmental policy.

items: **Interspousal immunity** rested on the fiction that husband and wife were one person, and on fears of collusion and disruption of family harmony. Nearly every state has abolished it (Freehe).

**Parental immunity** bars a child's negligence claim against a parent in some states. Approaches (any one may apply): (1) abolished entirely, with a reasonable-parent standard [[(Gibson v. Gibson, Cal. 1971)]]; (2) abolished except for the exercise of parental authority or discretion over the child's care [[(Goller v. White, Wis. 1963)]]; or (3) retained for ordinary negligence but not for willful, wanton, or intentional harm (Washington, as in Zellmer).

blocks.name: Freehe v. Freehe
blocks.facts: Clifford Freehe was injured by a tractor that his wife, Hazel, owned as her separate property and kept on her separate farm. He sued her for negligently maintaining the tractor and failing to warn him of its condition. The trial court granted summary judgment for Hazel on interspousal immunity.
blocks.held: Neill, J.: interspousal immunity in personal injury cases is abolished. Its rationales fail: (1) husband and wife are no longer one legal person; (2) a suit will not disrupt a harmonious marriage, since spouses at peace will not sue or will drop the suit; and (3) criminal and divorce law do not compensate for injuries. Fraud and collusion are policed by the ordinary trial process. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: This reflects the national trend. Fraud concerns are handled by the ordinary trial process and insurance law, not by a blanket bar.

blocks.name: Zellmer v. Zellmer
blocks.facts: Three-year-old Ashley McLellan lived with her mother and her stepfather, Mr. Zellmer. While he was watching her, he started a video for her and went downstairs to build a fire. About an hour later he found the sliding door to the backyard open and Ashley floating in the pool. She was resuscitated but died two days later. Her mother and biological father sued him for wrongful death. He moved for summary judgment, claiming parental immunity because he stood in loco parentis. The trial court and court of appeals agreed with him.
blocks.held: Madsen, J.: Washington keeps parental immunity for negligent parental supervision, but it does not extend to a stepparent or anyone else who is not a biological or adoptive parent, even one acting in loco parentis. A stepparent does not acquire parental rights or obligations merely by the relationship. The stepfather is held to ordinary care. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: Courts read the remaining family immunities narrowly.

blocks.name: Abernathy v. Sisters of St. Mary's
blocks.facts: Abernathy, a patient at the Sisters of St. Mary's hospital, a charitable institution, was injured when a hospital employee negligently failed to help him as he moved from his bed to the bathroom. The trial court granted the hospital summary judgment on charitable immunity.
blocks.held: Henley, C.J.: charitable immunity is abolished. A charitable institution is liable for its own negligence and for its employees' negligence within the scope of their employment. Immunity "fosters neglect and breeds irresponsibility, while liability promotes care and caution," and modern charity is big business that can insure. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: Almost every state has abolished or limited charitable immunity. [[Some states cap damages against charities or limit recovery to insurance.]]

body.text: The United States is liable for the negligent or wrongful acts of federal employees acting within the scope of their employment, in the same manner as a private person under the law of the place where the act occurred. There is no jury trial and no punitive damages.

**Exceptions (any one bars the claim):** (1) the discretionary function exception, § 2680(a); (2) most intentional torts, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment, and misrepresentation, § 2680(h), except for assault, battery, false imprisonment, and similar torts by law enforcement officers; and (3) [[injuries to service members incident to military service (Feres v. United States, 1950)]].

**Discretionary function test (all required for immunity):** (1) the conduct involves an element of judgment or choice, because no statute, regulation, or policy prescribes a specific course; and (2) the judgment is of the kind the exception was designed to shield, one grounded in social, economic, or political policy.

blocks.name: Deuser v. Vecera
blocks.facts: Deuser attended the Veiled Prophet Fair on the grounds of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial (the Gateway Arch) in St. Louis, a national park. Park rangers saw him grabbing women and urinating in public, arrested him, and turned him over to St. Louis police, who decided not to hold him. He was released in a parking lot, with no money or transportation, and later wandered onto an interstate and was struck and killed. His survivors sued the United States under the FTCA. The district court dismissed.
blocks.held: Bowman, J.: the discretionary function exception bars claims based on conduct that (1) involves an element of judgment or choice, and (2) is of the kind the exception was meant to shield, grounded in social, economic, or political policy. No mandatory policy dictated how the rangers had to handle a drunk, disorderly visitor; their choices to arrest him and turn him over to local police involved judgments about law enforcement priorities and resources. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The exception sweeps in many operational law enforcement decisions, not just high-level policy.

items: Most states have waived immunity, in whole or in part, through tort claims acts. These often keep a discretionary function exception, cap damages, and require prompt notice of claims.
The traditional line between **governmental** functions (immune: police, fire) and **proprietary** functions (liable: utilities, municipal businesses) survives in some states.
**Public duty doctrine:** a duty owed to the public at large, such as police protection, is not a duty to any individual, unless there is a special relationship (Riss; DeLong).

[[Delaware: the State Tort Claims Act (10 Del. C. § 4001) protects state officials and employees for discretionary acts done in good faith and without gross or wanton negligence. The County and Municipal Tort Claims Act (10 Del. C. § 4010 et seq.) grants immunity with listed exceptions.]]

blocks.name: Clarke v. Oregon Health Sciences University
blocks.facts: Jordaan Clarke, an infant, had surgery at the state-run Oregon Health Sciences University to repair a congenital heart defect. Through employees' negligence, he suffered prolonged oxygen deprivation and permanent brain damage, leaving him totally disabled. He sought more than $17 million. The Oregon Tort Claims Act capped damages against the state at $200,000 and made the suit against the public body the exclusive remedy, barring claims against the individual employees. The trial court entered judgment for $200,000 against OHSU and dismissed the employees; the court of appeals reversed as to the employees.
blocks.held: De Muniz, C.J.: the remedy clause of the Oregon Constitution (Art. I, § 10) guarantees "remedy by due course of law for injury done" to person or property. Eliminating the claim against the negligent employees and substituting a $200,000 claim against the state, against damages exceeding $17 million, left an "emasculated" remedy that is no substitute. As applied, the exclusive-remedy provision is unconstitutional, and the claims against the employees may proceed. Court of appeals affirmed.
blocks.why: State constitutions, not just legislatures, can limit how far immunity and damages caps reach.

blocks.name: Riss v. City of New York
blocks.topic: no duty to provide police protection
blocks.facts: For months, Linda Riss's rejected suitor, Burton Pugach, a lawyer, threatened to kill or maim her if she would not marry him. She repeatedly asked the police for protection and was refused. After she announced her engagement to another man, a thug hired by Pugach threw lye in her face, blinding her in one eye and permanently scarring her face. She sued the city for negligent failure to protect her. The complaint was dismissed.
blocks.held: Breitel, J.: absent a specific legislative mandate, a municipality is not liable for its failure to provide police protection to a member of the public, even one who was specifically threatened. Allocating limited police resources is a matter for the legislative and executive branches, and liability would expose the city to unlimited claims. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The public duty doctrine. [[Compare Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales (U.S. 2005), which found no constitutional right to enforcement of a restraining order.]] It is also a bias lens: the rule falls hardest on people, often women, who depend on the police for protection from violence.

body.text: **Dissent (Keating, J.):** the city's immunity rests on a fiction and leaves the victim of official negligence without a remedy. The fear of crushing liability was exaggerated, and ordinary negligence principles should apply when the police ignore a known, specific threat.

blocks.name: DeLong v. Erie County
blocks.facts: Amalia DeLong called 911 to report that a burglar was breaking into her home and gave her address. The call-taker wrote down the wrong address, and the dispatcher sent officers of the Village of Kenmore to an address that did not exist. Concluding the call was a prank, they left. Standard procedure required checking the tape of the call to confirm the address; no one did. Relying on the promise of help, she stayed in the house, and minutes later the burglar killed her. A jury found the county and the village liable.
blocks.held: Hancock, J.: as a rule, a government is not liable for failing to provide police protection. But by setting up an emergency number, inviting the public to rely on it, and telling DeLong help was on the way, the government assumed a special duty to her. She relied on the promise, staying home instead of fleeing or seeking help. Failing to follow standard procedures breached that duty. Affirmed.
blocks.why: A special relationship takes the case out of Riss. [[New York later framed the test (Cuffy v. City of New York, 1987) as (all required): (1) the municipality assumed, through promises or actions, an affirmative duty to act for the injured party; (2) its agents knew that inaction could lead to harm; (3) there was direct contact between its agents and the injured party; and (4) the injured party justifiably relied on the municipality's affirmative undertaking.]]

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Premises Liability (due 11/5), 15th ed. pp. 631–648 · 13th ed. Ch. 9.

blocks.title: Harm to people outside the land

items: **Artificial conditions and activities:** the possessor must use reasonable care to protect people on adjacent public ways from unreasonable risks (Salevan).

**Natural conditions:** the traditional rule is no duty, though many courts require reasonable care as to trees near highways, especially in urban areas. Taylor applied reasonable care but rejected an urban-rural distinction.

blocks.name: Taylor v. Olsen
blocks.facts: On a dark, windy January evening, Taylor's car struck a tree that had fallen across a rural highway from Olsen's adjoining timber land. After the accident, the tree was found to be decayed at its center, but nothing on its outside indicated decay. The trial court directed a verdict for Olsen.
blocks.held: Linde, J.: whether a landowner used reasonable care to protect travelers from conditions on the land is usually a jury question. But there must be evidence that a reasonable inspection would have revealed the danger, and there was none: no evidence that boring into an apparently healthy tree is a customary inspection. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Liability for natural conditions depends on what a reasonable inspection would show.

blocks.name: Salevan v. Wilmington Park, Inc.
blocks.facts: Wilmington Park operated a baseball park next to East Thirtieth Street in Wilmington. Two or three foul balls a game went over the fence onto the street, and the park took only limited precautions. While walking on the street, Salevan was hit by a foul ball. He sued for his injuries.
blocks.held: Wolcott, J.: a landowner whose property adjoins a public street must take reasonable precautions to protect travelers from activities on the land. The park knew balls regularly left the grounds during its 68-game season, so its precautions were inadequate. Judgment for Salevan for $2,500.
blocks.why: A Delaware case. The duty to people outside the land follows the ordinary negligence standard.

rows: Refrain from willful or wanton injury
Trespasser (discovered, or frequent on a limited area)
The possessor knows or should know the trespasser is there
Reasonable care in activities; warn of known, dangerous artificial conditions the trespasser is unlikely to discover (R2d §§ 334–337)
Reasonable care if the five elements are met
Enters with permission for her own purposes, including social guests
Warn of, or make safe, known dangerous conditions she is unlikely to discover. No duty to inspect
A public invitee, or a business visitor whose visit is connected to the possessor's business (R2d § 332)
Reasonable care, including reasonable inspection to discover dangers and making them safe or warning

blocks.name: Sheehan v. St. Paul & Duluth Ry. Co.
blocks.facts: Sheehan was walking along the railroad's track, at a place not open to public travel, when his foot slipped and caught in the rails. Before he could free it, a train ran over his foot. The crew did not see him until too late to stop. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad.
blocks.held: Seaman, J.: a possessor owes no duty to anticipate trespassers, who take the land as they find it. The railroad's duty of reasonable care arose only when the crew discovered Sheehan in peril, and there was no evidence they could have stopped after seeing him. Public crossings differ, because their existence gives notice that people will be there. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The duty to a trespasser starts when he is discovered.

body.text: A possessor is liable for physical harm to trespassing children caused by an artificial condition on the land when (all required): (a) the possessor knows or has reason to know that children are likely to trespass where the condition exists; (b) the possessor knows or has reason to know of the condition and realizes or should realize that it involves an unreasonable risk of death or serious bodily harm to such children; (c) the children, because of their youth, do not discover the condition or realize the risk; (d) the utility to the possessor of maintaining the condition and the burden of eliminating the danger are slight compared with the risk to children; and (e) the possessor fails to exercise reasonable care to eliminate the danger or otherwise protect the children.

blocks.name: Barmore v. Elmore
blocks.facts: Barmore and Elmore were officers of the same Masonic lodge. In August 1977, Barmore went to Elmore's home to discuss lodge business. Elmore's adult son, who had a history of mental illness, attacked Barmore with a steak knife. Barmore sued Elmore for failing to protect him from a dangerous condition on the premises. The trial court ruled Barmore a licensee and directed a verdict for Elmore.
blocks.held: Lindberg, J.: Barmore was a licensee, not an invitee, because the visit primarily benefited the lodge, not Elmore. A possessor must warn a licensee only of hidden dangers he knows of. Although the son had a history of mental illness, there was no evidence that Elmore knew or should have known he was likely to attack that night. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Classify the entrant first. A licensee gets a duty to warn only of known dangers.

blocks.name: Campbell v. Weathers
blocks.facts: Campbell was a regular customer of Weathers's cigar stand and lunch counter. One day he came in, stayed about 15 minutes without buying anything, and then went to use the toilet, which was open to the public. On the way he stepped into an open trap door and was injured. The trial court sustained Weathers's demurrer to the evidence.
blocks.held: Wedell, J.: a regular or prospective customer who enters a place of business open to the public is an invitee, even if he makes no purchase that day. A person who had no intention of becoming a customer, then or later, would not be. Whether Campbell was an invitee was for the jury. Reversed.
blocks.why: The invitation test: a person who enters where the public is invited is an invitee.

blocks.name: Whelan v. Van Natta
blocks.facts: Whelan bought some items at Van Natta's grocery and asked for a box. The grocer told him to look in the back room. While searching there, in the dark, he stepped into an unseen stairwell and fell. The trial court entered judgment for Van Natta.
blocks.held: Montgomery, J.: an invitee keeps that status only within the area of the invitation, the part of the premises where the possessor gives reason to believe his presence is desired for the purpose of the visit. Going into the back room for his own purpose (the box), with permission, made Whelan a licensee, owed only a warning of known hidden dangers. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Status can change during a single visit.

blocks.name: Rowland v. Christian
blocks.facts: Rowland, a social guest in Christian's apartment, asked to use the bathroom. The porcelain handle of a faucet cracked and broke in his hand, severing tendons and nerves. Christian had known the handle was cracked and had told the building manager, but did not warn Rowland. The trial court granted summary judgment for Christian because a social guest is a licensee who takes the premises as he finds them.
blocks.held: Peters, J.: the status of the entrant as trespasser, licensee, or invitee does not determine the possessor's duty. The test is whether the possessor acted as a reasonable person in managing the property, in view of the probability of injury to others, weighing the Rowland factors. Status may bear on what is reasonable. Christian knew of a concealed danger Rowland was about to encounter and did not warn him, which a jury could find negligent. Reversed.
blocks.why: The leading case rejecting the categories in favor of reasonable care, using the Rowland factors.

body.text: **Dissent (Burke, J.):** the categories developed over many years and give needed certainty. Changing them is for the legislature.

Departures from the general duty of reasonable care are justified only after weighing (weighed together): (1) the foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff; (2) the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury; (3) the closeness of the connection between the defendant's conduct and the injury; (4) the moral blame attached to the defendant's conduct; (5) the policy of preventing future harm; (6) the extent of the burden to the defendant and the consequences to the community of imposing a duty of care with resulting liability for breach; and (7) the availability, cost, and prevalence of insurance for the risk involved.

items: **Where states stand:** a minority follow Rowland and use reasonable care for everyone; a larger group merge licensees and invitees but keep the trespasser rule; and many, [[including Delaware]], keep the traditional categories.

[[Delaware's premises guest statute (25 Del. C. § 1501) bars a guest who enters without payment from suing the owner or occupier unless the injury was intentional or caused by willful or wanton disregard of the guest's rights.]]

**Open and obvious dangers:** traditionally no duty to invitees, but R2d § 343A imposes liability if the possessor should anticipate the harm despite the obviousness, as when the invitee is distracted.
[[**Recreational use statutes** limit duties to people using land for free recreation.]]

blocks.title: Landlords and tenants (the next sections of Ch. 9; not on the syllabus pages)

body.text: At common law a lessor is not liable for conditions on leased land, with exceptions (any one suffices) (Borders v. Roseberry): (1) undisclosed dangerous conditions known to the lessor and unknown to the lessee; (2) conditions dangerous to people outside the premises; (3) premises leased for admission of the public; (4) parts of the land retained in the lessor's control that the lessee may use; (5) the lessor's contract to repair; and (6) negligent repairs by the lessor. Pagelsdorf (Wis. 1979) replaced this with ordinary care, and Kline (D.C. Cir. 1970) required landlords to take reasonable precautions against foreseeable crime in common areas.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 11/10, 15th ed. pp. 669–681, 691–698, skim 681–691 and 698–700, and Zimmerman v. Ausland (Canvas) · 13th ed. Ch. 10.A–B.

rows: A small sum ($1) to vindicate a right
Intentional torts only; negligence requires actual harm
Past and future medical expenses, lost earnings, lost earning capacity, property damage
Future losses are reduced to present value
Pain and suffering, mental anguish, disfigurement, loss of enjoyment of life
No fixed measure; the jury's judgment, reviewed for excess. [[Many states cap these, especially in medical malpractice.]]
Punishment and deterrence for malicious, willful, or reckless conduct

items: **Single recovery rule:** all past and future damages are awarded in one lump sum. [[Some states allow periodic payments for large future losses.]]
**Present value:** future economic losses are discounted to present value, and inflation may be considered.

**Remittitur and additur:** a judge who finds a verdict excessive may order a new trial unless the plaintiff accepts a lower amount (remittitur). Additur, raising an inadequate verdict, is not allowed in federal court.
**Attorney's fees** are not recoverable under the American rule. Contingent fees come out of the award.
**Property:** the measure is diminution in market value, or the reasonable cost of repair, plus loss of use.

blocks.title: Loss of consortium: R3d Misc. Prov. §§ 48 A–48 C (approved 2022)

body.text: A family member of a person physically or emotionally harmed by a tort may recover for the resulting loss of society, meaning affection, comfort, companionship, love, support, and services (any one relationship suffices): (1) a spouse (§ 48 A, including impairment of conjugal relations); (2) a parent of an unemancipated minor child (§ 48 B); or (3) a minor child of the injured parent (§ 48 C).

blocks.name: Anderson v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.
blocks.topic: the elements of personal injury damages
blocks.facts: A defective heater made by Sears set fire to the Britain family's home. Their infant daughter, Helen, was burned over 40% of her body. She suffered extreme scarring, fingers fused together, and a permanently bent elbow, and faced many costly operations for the rest of her life. The jury awarded her $2,000,000, and Sears moved for a remittitur.
blocks.held: Cassibry, J.: to decide whether an award is excessive, the court examines each element of damages: (1) past physical and mental pain; (2) future physical and mental pain; (3) future medical expenses (here, some 27 projected operations and psychiatric care); (4) loss of earning capacity (she would likely never be self-supporting); and (5) permanent disability and disfigurement. Each element was supported, and the total was not excessive. Motion denied.
blocks.why: This is the framework for valuing a serious personal injury case, element by element.

blocks.name: Richardson v. Chapman
blocks.facts: Richardson was stopped at a red light when a semi-trailer driven by Chapman hit her car from behind. She became a quadriplegic. The trial court directed a verdict on liability against Chapman and his employer, and the jury awarded Richardson $22,358,814 (and her passenger, McGregor, $102,215). The defendants argued the award was excessive and that her expert's present-value calculations were wrong.
blocks.held: Miller, J.: an award is excessive if it falls outside the range of fair and reasonable compensation, results from passion or prejudice, or shocks the conscience. The jury's award for future medical costs was $1.5 million above the higher of the two figures offered at trial, which unitemized future costs could not explain, so $1 million was remitted. The rest, including large non-economic damages, was within the jury's discretion. Affirmed as modified.
blocks.why: Future economic damages must rest on evidence. Non-economic damages get more deference.

body.text: Benefits the plaintiff receives from a source independent of the defendant do not reduce the damages the defendant must pay. Collateral sources include (any one suffices): (1) the plaintiff's own insurance, such as health, disability, or life insurance; (2) employment benefits, such as sick pay or pensions; (3) gratuitous services or payments from family, friends, or charity; and (4) government benefits.

**Reasons:** the defendant should not benefit from the plaintiff's foresight or others' generosity, and many collateral sources are reimbursed through subrogation. [[Many states have modified the rule by statute, especially in medical malpractice.]]

blocks.name: Montgomery Ward & Co. v. Anderson
blocks.facts: Anderson fell in Montgomery Ward's Little Rock store and incurred about $25,000 in hospital bills. Her lawyer negotiated a 50% discount with the hospital. Ward moved to limit her proof to what she actually had to pay and to introduce the discount. The trial court held the discount was a collateral source and allowed evidence of the full bill.
blocks.held: Newbern, J.: gratuitous or discounted medical services are a collateral source and cannot be used to reduce the damages owed by a tortfeasor. The wrongdoer should not benefit from the plaintiff's good fortune, even if she recovers more than her out-of-pocket loss. The rule yields only when collateral-source evidence is relevant for another purpose (such as rebutting a claim of financial need or impeaching testimony). Affirmed.
blocks.why: [[Courts split on whether the "billed" or the "paid" amount is recoverable when insurers negotiate discounts.]]

body.text: The plaintiff cannot recover for harm she could have avoided with reasonable effort or expense after the injury, such as by getting reasonable medical treatment or following medical advice. The defendant must prove (all required): (1) a reasonable course of action was available to the plaintiff; (2) the plaintiff unreasonably failed to take it; and (3) it would have reduced the harm, and by how much.

blocks.name: Zimmerman v. Ausland
blocks.source: Canvas reading (11/10), from the opinion text in the course folder.
blocks.facts: Zimmerman, a substitute teacher, was injured in a car accident. Ausland admitted liability, so only damages were tried. She had a torn semilunar cartilage in her right knee, with swelling and pain after walking, and could no longer join in physical-education games or play volleyball and tennis. Her doctor testified the injury was permanent and would gradually get worse, and that she would "very probably" need surgery to remove the cartilage, after which recovery would be "fairly good." He had prescribed no treatment and said surgery is "not always" required. The defense doctor, who doubted the diagnosis, testified that if she had the tear, routine surgery would let her recover completely. Neither doctor said surgery was called for when he examined her, and no one testified about the operation's risks. The jury was instructed on permanent injury and life-expectancy tables and awarded $7,500. Ausland argued that because routine surgery could cure the injury, and she had a duty to mitigate, it could not be treated as permanent.
blocks.held: Tongue, J.: a plaintiff cannot recover for a permanent injury whose permanence she could have avoided by submitting to treatment, including surgery, that a reasonable person would accept in the same circumstances. The defendant bears the burden of proving an unreasonable failure to mitigate, and the question is ordinarily for the jury. The factors include (1) the risk involved in the operation; (2) its probability of success; and (3) the money or effort required; some courts add the pain involved. Here there was no evidence of the surgery's risk, no evidence that any doctor advised surgery, and no requested instruction on mitigation, so the court could not hold as a matter of law that she had to have surgery. The permanency issue was properly submitted. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Avoidable consequences reduces damages, not liability, and courts are "cautious about insisting that due care requires submission to an operation." It concerns the plaintiff's conduct after the injury; comparative fault (§ 22) concerns her conduct before it.

blocks.title: Bias lens: valuing lives and earnings

items: Lost earning capacity is often projected from statistical tables. [[Tables broken out by race and sex have predicted lower earnings and shorter work lives for women and people of color, which lowers their awards for the same injury (McMillan v. City of New York, E.D.N.Y. 2008, rejecting race-based life expectancy figures). Cal. Civ. Code § 3361 (2019) bars reducing these damages based on race, ethnicity, or gender.]]
Non-economic damages make up a larger share of the recovery for children, retirees, and people outside the paid workforce, so caps on non-economic damages fall hardest on them.

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Punitive Damages (due 11/12), 15th ed. pp. 700–717 · 13th ed. Ch. 10.C.

body.text: The plaintiff must show (all required): (1) a tort that supports compensatory damages (most states require actual damages); and (2) aggravated conduct: malice, fraud, oppression, or willful, wanton, or reckless disregard of others' rights. Many states require clear and convincing evidence. Evidence of the defendant's wealth is admissible.

**Vicarious punitive damages, R2d § 909 (any one suffices):** the principal is liable for punitive damages because of an agent's act if (a) the principal authorized the doing and the manner of the act; (b) the agent was unfit and the principal was reckless in employing or retaining him; (c) the agent was employed in a managerial capacity and was acting in the scope of employment (Fisher, § 3); or (d) the principal or a managerial agent ratified or approved the act.

blocks.title: Due process limits: BMW v. Gore (1996); State Farm v. Campbell (2003)

body.text: A court reviewing an award considers three guideposts (weighed together): (1) the degree of reprehensibility of the defendant's misconduct; (2) the disparity between the actual or potential harm and the punitive award (the ratio); and (3) the difference between the punitive award and civil penalties authorized or imposed in comparable cases.

**Reprehensibility factors (weighed together):** (1) whether the harm was physical rather than economic; (2) whether the conduct showed indifference to or reckless disregard of others' health or safety; (3) whether the target was financially vulnerable; (4) whether the conduct was repeated rather than isolated; and (5) whether the harm resulted from intentional malice, trickery, or deceit rather than accident.

blocks.name: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell
blocks.facts: Campbell, passing six vans on a two-lane highway, caused a crash that killed Ospital and permanently disabled Slusher. State Farm, his insurer, refused offers to settle for the $50,000 policy limits ($25,000 each), assured Campbell his assets were safe, and took the case to trial. The jury returned $185,849 against him, and State Farm at first refused to cover the excess, telling him to put a "For Sale" sign on his house. Campbell then sued State Farm for bad faith, fraud, and IIED. To show a nationwide scheme to cap payouts, he introduced evidence of State Farm's practices across the country over 20 years. The Utah jury awarded $1 million in compensatory damages (reduced from $2.6 million) and $145 million in punitive damages.
blocks.held: Kennedy, J.: the award violated due process under the Gore guideposts. (1) Reprehensibility: State Farm's conduct merited some punishment, but a state may not punish lawful out-of-state conduct or dissimilar conduct unrelated to the plaintiff's harm. (2) Ratio: few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio will satisfy due process, and where compensatory damages are substantial, a 1:1 ratio may be the limit; 145:1 is far beyond it. (3) Comparable penalties: the most relevant civil sanction was a $10,000 fine for fraud. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: This sets the constitutional limit: the single-digit ratio, punishment only for conduct toward this plaintiff, and reprehensibility as the most important guidepost. [[Philip Morris USA v. Williams (2007) bars punishing for harm to nonparties.]]

blocks.name: Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker
blocks.facts: In 1989 the Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, spilling millions of gallons of crude oil. Its captain, a relapsed alcoholic whom Exxon knew was drinking again, had left the bridge just before the grounding, though he was the only officer licensed to navigate that passage. Exxon paid over $1 billion to settle government environmental claims. Commercial fishermen and Native Alaskans sued for economic losses. The jury awarded $5 billion in punitive damages, which the Ninth Circuit reduced to $2.5 billion. Compensatory damages were about $507.5 million.
blocks.held: Souter, J.: as a matter of federal maritime common law, not constitutional due process, punitive damages for reckless conduct (without intentional or malicious wrongdoing or a profit motive) are limited to a 1:1 ratio with compensatory damages. The chief problem with punitive damages is unpredictability, and studies showed a median ratio below 1:1. Vacated and remanded, effectively reducing the award to about $507.5 million.
blocks.why: The 1:1 ratio is a federal common-law rule for maritime cases. It is not a constitutional limit on the states.

blocks.name: Cheatham v. Pohle
blocks.facts: Four years after their divorce, Michael Pohle distributed at least 60 copies of nude photos of his ex-wife, Doris Cheatham, and photos of the two of them having sex, around the small Indiana community where both lived and worked. She sued for invasion of privacy and IIED, and the jury awarded $100,000 in compensatory and $100,000 in punitive damages. Indiana's statute gave the plaintiff only 25% of a punitive award and sent 75% to the state's Violent Crime Victims Compensation Fund. Cheatham challenged the statute as a taking.
blocks.held: Boehm, J.: the statute does not violate the federal or Indiana Takings Clause. Punitive damages are quasi-criminal, serve public purposes, and compensate no one, so a plaintiff has no vested property right in them. The legislature could abolish punitive damages entirely, so it may limit the plaintiff's share. Judgment for the state on the challenge.
blocks.why: Punitive damages are quasi-criminal. [[Several states use split-recovery statutes or cap punitive awards.]]

blocks.title: Joint and Several Liability, Satisfaction, Release, and Settlement

blocks.text: **Reading:** 11/12 (hour 1), 15th ed. pp. 463–476; Module on Joint and Several Liability (due 11/17), pp. 476–484, 489–492 · 13th ed. Ch. 7.A–B.

blocks.title: When joint and several liability applies

body.text: Each defendant is liable for the plaintiff's entire damages, and the plaintiff may collect from any one or more of them (but not more than once), when (any one suffices): (1) the defendants acted in concert, by agreement or by knowingly giving substantial assistance or encouragement (R2d § 876; Bierczynski); (2) independent tortfeasors caused a single, indivisible injury (Hill v. Edmonds, § 18); (3) one defendant is vicariously liable for another (§ 31); or (4) the defendants breached a common duty.

**Divisible injuries** are apportioned: each defendant pays only for the harm it caused, and the plaintiff must prove the division (Bruckman, § 30). When the harm cannot reasonably be divided, many courts shift the burden of apportionment to the defendants.

blocks.name: Bierczynski v. Rogers
blocks.facts: Race and Bierczynski were drag racing side by side on a public highway. Coming over a hill, they saw the Rogerses' car approaching. Race tried to swing back into his lane, lost control, and hit the Rogerses' car at about 70 mph. Bierczynski's car never touched it. The trial court held both racers jointly liable.
blocks.held: Herrmann, J.: participants in a motor vehicle race on a public highway are acting in concert, and each is liable for harm caused by any of them, because each participated in and encouraged the wrongful conduct. Otherwise the victim might be left with only an insolvent defendant, and the driver who happened to collide would bear the whole loss. Affirmed.
blocks.why: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Concert of action makes every participant jointly and severally liable, even one who did not touch the plaintiff.

blocks.title: Concerted negligence: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft)

body.text: **Agreements to act negligently:** actors are subject to liability for harm from concerted action when (all required): (1) they agree to engage in conduct that is negligent or reckless; (2) each engages in the agreed conduct; (3) at least one actor's agreed-to conduct factually causes physical, emotional, or dignitary harm to another; and (4) the harm is within the scope of liability of the agreed-to conduct. Their liability is joint and several unless a statute changes the rule.

**Aiding and abetting negligence:** an actor is liable when (all required): (a) another commits a negligence tort causing physical, emotional, or dignitary harm to a third person; (b) the actor had actual knowledge that the other might engage in negligent or reckless conduct posing a risk to others; and (c) the actor substantially assisted or encouraged the other's conduct, and thereby increased the risk.
A drag race (Bierczynski) fits both: an agreement to race recklessly, and mutual encouragement.

blocks.name: Coney v. J.L.G. Industries, Inc.
blocks.facts: Jasper was killed while operating a hydraulic aerial work platform made by J.L.G. Coney, as administrator of his estate, sued J.L.G. in products liability and negligence. J.L.G. argued that Jasper's employer was partly at fault and that, since Illinois had adopted pure comparative negligence, joint and several liability was abolished and its liability should be reduced by the employer's share. The question was certified to the Illinois Supreme Court.
blocks.held: Moran, J.: adopting comparative negligence does not require abolishing joint and several liability. Comparative negligence reduces the plaintiff's recovery by her own share of fault; it says nothing about relations among defendants. The injury remains indivisible, and the policy that the tortfeasor, not the injured plaintiff, should bear the risk of an insolvent co-defendant still applies. Affirmed and remanded.
blocks.why: The traditional view: the risk of a defendant who cannot pay falls on the other defendants, not the plaintiff.

blocks.name: Bartlett v. New Mexico Welding Supply, Inc.
blocks.facts: Bartlett was injured in an accident involving a New Mexico Welding vehicle and a third, unidentified car. The jury found Bartlett not negligent, New Mexico Welding 30% responsible, and the unknown driver 70%. Bartlett argued joint and several liability required New Mexico Welding to pay all his damages. The trial court ordered a new trial, and New Mexico Welding took an interlocutory appeal.
blocks.held: Wood, J.: in a pure comparative fault system, joint and several liability among concurrent tortfeasors is abolished. Fault-based apportionment should apply among defendants as it does between plaintiff and defendant, so each defendant pays only its own percentage. New Mexico Welding owed 30%. Reversed.
blocks.why: The several-liability view: fault-based apportionment should run in all directions, and the plaintiff bears the risk of an unknown or insolvent defendant.

rows: P collects $100,000 from D1. D1 seeks $40,000 contribution from D2 (worthless)
P collects $60,000 from D1 and bears D2's $40,000 share
Hybrid: joint and several for economic damages only
D1 pays all economic damages and 60% of non-economic damages
The uncollectible share is reallocated among the solvent parties, including a plaintiff at fault, by their percentages

items: **One satisfaction:** a plaintiff may obtain judgments against several tortfeasors but may collect full compensation only once. Full payment by one discharges the rest (Bundt).

**Release:** at common law, releasing one joint tortfeasor released all. Today a release discharges only the person released unless it says otherwise (Cox; Uniform Contribution Among Tortfeasors Act). A covenant not to sue never discharged others.

**Credit for a settlement** against the non-settling defendants' liability (any one approach): (1) pro tanto, a dollar-for-dollar reduction; (2) pro rata, a reduction by the settling defendant's per-capita share; or (3) proportionate share, a reduction by the settling defendant's percentage of fault [[(McDermott v. AmClyde, U.S. 1994, in admiralty)]].

blocks.name: Bundt v. Embro
blocks.facts: Two cars collided, and passengers sued the owners and drivers of both cars. The passengers had also sued the State of New York in the Court of Claims, for the same accident, and recovered judgments that the state paid. When the defendants learned of this, they moved to amend their answers to plead satisfaction and discharge.
blocks.held: Groat, J.: there is one wrong and one recovery. When a plaintiff receives full satisfaction from one joint tortfeasor, the others are discharged, and it does not matter that the payer was the state, which could only be sued in a different court. Motion granted.
blocks.why: There is one injury and one recovery.

blocks.name: Cox v. Pearl Investment Co.
blocks.facts: Cox was injured on property owned by Pearl Investment and leased to Goodwill Industries. She settled with Goodwill for $2,500, signing an instrument that expressly reserved her right to sue anyone else who might be liable. When she sued Pearl, Pearl moved for summary judgment under the common-law rule that releasing one joint tortfeasor releases all. The trial court granted it.
blocks.held: Hodges, J.: an instrument that expressly reserves rights against other tortfeasors does not release them. (1) Contract law gives effect to the parties' intent, and Cox plainly did not intend to release Pearl; (2) there is no risk of double recovery, because Pearl gets credit for the $2,500; and (3) the nonsettling tortfeasor is helped, not hurt, by that credit. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: The harsh common-law rule that releasing one released all gives way to the parties' intent.

blocks.name: Elbaor v. Smith
blocks.facts: Smith sued three doctors, Elbaor, Syrquin, and Stephens, for malpractice. Syrquin and Stephens entered a "Mary Carter" agreement: they guaranteed Smith $425,010 if she did not recover that much from Elbaor, and she would repay them from any recovery from Elbaor above that amount. They stayed in the case, and at trial their lawyers helped Smith against Elbaor. The jury found Elbaor 88% responsible and awarded $1,872,848 against him.
blocks.held: Gonzalez, J.: Mary Carter agreements are void as against public policy in Texas. They do not promote settlement, since they virtually guarantee a trial against the non-settling defendant, and they distort the trial by aligning supposed adversaries while the jury may not understand the true alignment. Reversed and remanded for a new trial.
blocks.why: A Mary Carter agreement has (all required) (1) a settling defendant who stays in the case; (2) whose liability is reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's recovery from the non-settling defendants; and (3) whose agreement is often kept secret. Most states allow them with disclosure; Texas and a few others ban them.

body.text: **Dissent (Doggett, J.):** the trial court disclosed the agreements to the jury and protected the adversarial process; so long as genuinely adverse parties remain, the search for truth is not impaired.

blocks.text: **Reading:** 11/17 (hour 1), 15th ed. pp. 492–498 · 13th ed. Ch. 7.C–D.

body.text: A tortfeasor who pays more than its share of a common liability may recover the excess from other tortfeasors. It requires (all required): (1) common liability, so that the other tortfeasor was also liable to the plaintiff (Dreslin); (2) payment of more than the payer's fair share; and (3) no discharge of the other tortfeasor, as by a good-faith settlement (Slocum).

**Shares (one approach applies):** (1) pro rata, equal shares per tortfeasor, under the older Uniform Contribution Among Tortfeasors Act [[(Delaware's version is 10 Del. C. § 6301 et seq.)]]; or (2) comparative, in proportion to fault, in most comparative-fault states.

blocks.name: Knell v. Feltman
blocks.facts: Langland, riding as a passenger in her friend Knell's car, was injured when it collided with Feltman's taxi. Because Knell was her friend, she sued only Feltman. Feltman filed a third-party complaint against Knell for contribution. The jury found both negligent.
blocks.held: Miller, J.: when an injury results from the concurrent negligence of two people who did not intend it, one who pays the judgment may obtain contribution from the other, even though the plaintiff did not obtain a joint judgment against both. Letting the plaintiff choose who pays the whole would be unjust and could invite collusion. Feltman could recover half. Affirmed.
blocks.why: The common law barred contribution [[(Merryweather v. Nixan, 1799)]]. Courts and statutes now allow it among negligent tortfeasors.

blocks.name: Yellow Cab Co. of D.C., Inc. v. Dreslin
blocks.facts: Mrs. Dreslin was injured in a collision between a Yellow Cab and a car driven by her husband. Both drivers were negligent. She sued Yellow Cab, which cross-claimed against Mr. Dreslin for contribution toward whatever it paid her.
blocks.held: Proctor, J.: under interspousal immunity, the husband was not liable to his wife, so there was no common liability and no right of contribution. Allowing contribution would let the wife's recovery be shifted back to her husband indirectly, undercutting the immunity's purpose of preserving domestic peace. Affirmed.
blocks.why: No liability to the plaintiff means no contribution. With immunities mostly abolished (§ 25), this matters less today.

blocks.name: Slocum v. Donahue
blocks.facts: Donahue was backing his Ford out of his driveway when, he said, the engine raced and the car kept accelerating though he pressed the brake. It crossed the street, hit the curb, went airborne, and hit a fence, killing the Slocums' 18-month-old son. Donahue pleaded guilty to motor vehicle homicide; there was a vodka bottle under his seat. His expert blamed a defective floor mat. The Slocums sued Donahue, who brought in Ford for contribution and indemnity. Before trial, the Slocums settled with Ford for $150,000. The trial court dismissed Donahue's claims against Ford.
blocks.held: Under the Massachusetts contribution statute, a release given in good faith to one tortfeasor discharges it from liability for contribution to others. Donahue showed no collusion or bad faith: the amount was reasonable given the strong case against him, and the Slocums' use of experts Ford had retained was not collusive. Indemnity was unavailable because Donahue was not free of fault. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Settlement bars encourage early settlement. Non-settling defendants get credit for the settlement, and they can challenge only its good faith.

body.text: Indemnity shifts the entire loss from one tortfeasor to another. It is available when (any one suffices): (1) a contract provides for it; (2) the payer was only vicariously liable for the other's tort, as an employer for an employee (§ 31); (3) the payer's fault was passive or secondary compared with the other's active or primary fault, under the traditional rule; or (4) a retailer who passed on a defective product seeks indemnity from the manufacturer. Many comparative-fault states replace the active-passive rule with comparative contribution.

blocks.title: Settlement, indemnity, and contribution: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment Topic 6, §§ 34–36 (approved 2022)

body.text: These sections state the rules for tort claims for economic harm, applying the general Apportionment rules.

**Settlement (§ 34):** a nonsettling defendant gets a credit against the judgment equal to the settling person's percentage share of comparative responsibility (the proportionate-share approach), and neither the settling nor the nonsettling person may seek contribution from the other.

**Indemnity (§ 35):** a person who discharges another's liability may recover the amount paid plus reasonable legal expenses if (any one suffices): (1) the indemnitor agreed by contract to indemnify; or (2) the indemnitee was liable only vicariously for the indemnitor's tort.

**Contribution (§ 36):** a person who paid more than its share of comparative responsibility, and so discharged another's liability, may recover the excess from that person, except after a settlement, as above, or where indemnity is available instead.

blocks.name: Bruckman v. Pena
blocks.facts: On July 21, 1964, Pena was hurt in a collision caused by Bruckman, who was driving a truck owned by Armored. On June 11, 1965, Pena's injuries were aggravated in a second, unrelated accident. The jury was told to apportion his damages between the defendants and the later tortfeasor, but that "if you find the evidence does not permit such an apportionment, then the defendants are liable for the entire disability." It awarded $50,000.
blocks.held: Dwyer, J.: the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the damages the defendant's negligence caused. It was error to make the first tortfeasor liable for injuries from a later, independent accident just because apportionment is difficult. (A tortfeasor who aggravates a pre-existing condition is liable for the whole, but the reverse does not follow, since the first tortfeasor did not cause the later injury.) Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: Successive, independent injuries are apportioned. The first tortfeasor is liable for later aggravation only if it is a foreseeable result of the first injury, such as negligent medical treatment.

items: **Plaintiff's fault.** Apply the comparative fault threshold, then reduce the damages (§ 22).
**Liability to the plaintiff.** Joint and several, several, or hybrid? Divisible or indivisible harm?
**Settlements.** Is a settling defendant discharged? What credit do the others get?
**Contribution and indemnity among defendants.** Common liability? Pro rata or comparative shares? Grounds for full indemnity?

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Vicarious Liability (due 11/19), 15th ed. pp. 843–853; 11/19 (hour 1), pp. 853–856, skim 866–868 · 13th ed. Ch. 13.

body.text: An employer is liable for an employee's tort when (all required): (1) the tortfeasor is an employee (a servant), meaning the employer controls or has the right to control the physical conduct of the work; and (2) the tort was committed within the scope of employment.

**Scope of employment, Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228 (all required):** (a) the conduct is of the kind the employee is employed to perform; (b) it occurs substantially within the authorized time and space limits; (c) it is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the employer; and (d) if force is intentionally used, its use is not unexpectable by the employer.

items: **Rationales:** the enterprise should bear the costs it creates as a cost of doing business; the employer can spread the loss and is best placed to prevent it; and the employer usually has the money.
**The employee remains liable.** The employer who pays may seek indemnity from the employee (§ 30), though it rarely does.
**Going and coming rule:** commuting is generally outside the scope of employment. Exceptions include special errands, travel required by the job, and risks created at work (Bussard).

**Frolic and detour:** a minor deviation from the employer's business (detour) stays within the scope. A substantial departure for the employee's own purposes (frolic) does not, until the employee returns to the employer's business (O'Shea).

**Intentional torts** are within the scope if done to further the employer's business or if they are a foreseeable, characteristic risk of the enterprise [[(Ira S. Bushey & Sons v. United States, 2d Cir. 1968: a drunken sailor opened a drydock's valves)]]. Compare Western Union v. Hill (§ 3).

blocks.name: Bussard v. Minimed, Inc.
blocks.topic: going and coming: a risk created at work
blocks.facts: Minimed had its offices sprayed with pesticide overnight. The next morning an employee, Hernandez, became ill from the fumes and left work early, declining to see the company doctor. Driving home, she rear-ended Bussard's car.
blocks.held: The going-and-coming rule does not apply when the employee's commute is affected by a risk arising from the job. The test is foreseeability in the respondeat superior sense: whether the conduct is so startling or unusual that it would be unfair to charge it to the business. Her impairment from workplace fumes was foreseeable. Summary judgment for Minimed was reversed.
blocks.why: Foreseeability here asks whether the risk is typical of the enterprise, not the negligence version of foreseeability.

blocks.name: O'Shea v. Welch
blocks.facts: Welch, an Osco Drug store manager, was driving his own car during work hours to Osco's district office to deliver Kansas City Chiefs tickets to other managers, a task done for the company. On a whim, he decided to pull into a service station to get an estimate on his car, turned left across traffic, and hit O'Shea's car. The district court granted summary judgment to Osco on vicarious liability.
blocks.held: McKay, J.: under Kansas law, as predicted, conduct reasonably incidental to the employment and foreseeable to the employer is within its scope. Under the "slight deviation" rule, a detour remains within the scope of employment; a frolic does not. A reasonable jury could find that a brief stop for a car estimate while on a work errand was a slight deviation. Reversed and remanded.
blocks.why: The question is one of degree, so modern courts usually leave frolic and detour to the jury.

blocks.title: Employee or independent contractor: Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2)

body.text: Whether a worker is a servant or an independent contractor is decided by the employer's right to control the details of the work. **Factors (weighed together):** (a) the extent of control which, by the agreement, the master may exercise over the details of the work; (b) whether or not the one employed is engaged in a distinct occupation or business; (c) the kind of occupation, and whether it is usually done under direction or by a specialist without supervision; (d) the skill required; (e) whether the employer or the worker supplies the instrumentalities, tools, and place of work; (f) the length of time for which the person is employed; (g) the method of payment, whether by the time or by the job; (h) whether or not the work is part of the regular business of the employer; (i) whether or not the parties believe they are creating a master-servant relationship; and (j) whether the principal is or is not in business.

blocks.name: Murrell v. Goertz
blocks.facts: Goertz delivered the Oklahoma Publishing Company's newspaper. He got into an argument with a customer, Murrell, and struck her. She sued Goertz and the publisher for assault and battery. Goertz had been hired by an independent distributor that contracted with the publisher; the publisher set general guidelines for delivery but did not supervise how carriers did their work. The trial court granted summary judgment for the publisher.
blocks.held: Reynolds, J.: an independent contractor is one who performs a service for another free from the other's control over the details of the work, except as to the result. The publisher had no direct relationship with Goertz and did not control his manner of delivery; general guidelines about results are not control. It is not vicariously liable. Affirmed.
blocks.why: No vicarious liability for an independent contractor's torts, unless an exception applies.

blocks.text: **Exceptions: the hiring party is liable for an independent contractor's negligence when (any one suffices):** (1) the duty is nondelegable, as with duties imposed by statute or regulation for public safety (Maloney), duties of a possessor to invitees, and duties of a landlord to tenants; (2) the work is inherently dangerous (R2d §§ 416, 427); (3) the hirer was itself negligent in selecting, instructing, or supervising the contractor (direct liability, not vicarious); or (4) the contractor appeared to be the hirer's employee and the plaintiff relied on that appearance (apparent agency, as with hospital emergency rooms).

blocks.name: Maloney v. Rath
blocks.facts: Rath's car hit Maloney's when its brakes failed. Three months earlier, Rath had had the brakes overhauled by a mechanic, Evanchick, whose negligent work caused the failure. Rath had no reason to know of the defect. The trial court entered judgment for Rath, because an owner is not liable for an independent contractor's negligence.
blocks.held: Traynor, J.: the statutory duty to maintain a car's brakes in good working order is nondelegable. An owner who hires an independent contractor to perform it is liable for the contractor's negligence, though the owner may seek indemnity from the contractor. This is not strict liability for brake failure; it refuses to let the owner shift responsibility to someone who may not be able to pay. Reversed.
blocks.why: Traynor, J.: a nondelegable duty puts the loss on the person who benefits from the activity and can insure against it.

blocks.title: Joint enterprise, automobile owners, and imputed contributory negligence

body.text: Each member of a joint enterprise is vicariously liable for the others' negligence in furthering it. A joint enterprise requires (all required): (1) an express or implied agreement among the members; (2) a common purpose to be carried out by the group; (3) a community of pecuniary interest in that purpose; and (4) an equal right to a voice in the direction of the enterprise, giving an equal right of control.

blocks.name: Popejoy v. Steinle
blocks.topic: no joint enterprise in family errands
blocks.facts: Mrs. Steinle was driving her daughter to buy a calf, which the daughter was to raise as a pet, when she collided with Popejoy's car. The Steinles owned a ranch, but the evidence was that the calf was not for the ranch business. Mrs. Steinle died in the accident. Popejoy, whose injuries first seemed minor, did not file a claim against her estate in time, and later sued Mr. Steinle's estate (he had since died) on the theory that he was vicariously liable as a member of a joint enterprise with his wife. The trial court granted summary judgment.
blocks.held: Golden, J.: a joint enterprise requires (1) an agreement; (2) a common purpose; (3) a community of pecuniary interest; and (4) an equal right of control. The pecuniary-interest element means the enterprise must be commercial and the act must further it. Buying a pet for their daughter was personal, so there was no joint enterprise, and a spouse is not vicariously liable for personal errands. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Joint enterprise is mostly a business doctrine.

items: **Family purpose doctrine:** the head of a household who provides a car for family members' use is liable for their negligent driving (Malchose, applying a totality-of-the-circumstances test). [[About a dozen states follow it.]]
**Owner-consent statutes** make a car's owner liable for anyone driving with permission, often up to a cap.
**Negligent entrustment** is the owner's own negligence in lending a car to an incompetent, inexperienced, or intoxicated driver. It is direct, not vicarious, liability.

**Imputed contributory negligence (the "both ways" rule):** a driver's negligence is imputed to a plaintiff only if the plaintiff would be vicariously liable as a defendant for the driver's conduct (Smalich).
**Parents** are not vicariously liable for their children's torts at common law. [[Statutes in most states impose limited liability for willful or malicious acts.]]

blocks.name: Malchose v. Kalfell
blocks.facts: Eric Kalfell, an adult college student living away from home, struck a car driven by Kelly Malchose. She sued Eric for negligence and his parents, Lance and Lisa Kalfell, under the family purpose (family car) doctrine and for negligent entrustment. The parents were the titled owners, Eric listed their ranch as his address, they claimed him as a dependent, and they supported him at college; but Eric had used the car as loan collateral and had moved away. The trial court found Eric negligent and the parents liable under the family car doctrine.
blocks.held: Neumann, J.: the family car doctrine makes a head of household who furnishes a car for a family member's use, pleasure, or business liable for that member's negligent driving. Title is not required, and whether the doctrine applies depends on the totality of the circumstances. The parents' title, financial support, and dependency claim supported the finding, which was not clearly erroneous. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Ownership of record is not required. What matters is who furnished and controlled the car for family use.

blocks.name: Smalich v. Westfall
blocks.facts: Smalich owned a car and was riding in it as a passenger while Westfall drove it with her permission. It collided with a car driven by Blank, and Smalich was killed. Her estate sued both drivers. The jury found for the estate against Blank and found that Westfall's negligence also caused the crash. The trial court entered judgment n.o.v. for Blank, imputing Westfall's negligence to Smalich as the owner.
blocks.held: Eagen, J.: a third person's negligence is imputed to a plaintiff only if their relationship would make the plaintiff vicariously liable as a defendant for that person's negligence. In car cases, only a master-servant relationship or joint enterprise justifies imputation. An owner-passenger ordinarily does not retain control over the details of driving, and the jury found no such control here. Reversed.
blocks.why: The "both ways" test ties imputed contributory negligence to vicarious liability.

body.text: **Concurrence (Roberts, J.):** imputed contributory negligence should be abolished entirely: a passenger cannot safely control a moving car even if he owns it.

blocks.title: Strict Liability: Animals and Abnormally Dangerous Activities

rows: Strict liability for damage caused by livestock that trespass, except in "fencing-out" states, where the landowner must fence them out
Wild animals (wild by nature, such as bears or snakes)
Strict liability for harm resulting from the animal's dangerous propensities, even if the keeper used the utmost care (R2d § 507)
Domestic animals with known dangerous propensities

Strict liability once the keeper knows, or has reason to know, of the animal's abnormally dangerous tendency (scienter, the "one-bite rule"; R2d § 509). [[Many states impose strict liability for dog bites by statute.]]

blocks.name: Sandy v. Bushey
blocks.facts: Sandy turned his horses out to pasture in a neighbor's field, where Bushey's horse was also pastured. Bushey knew his horse had vicious tendencies. While Sandy was in the pasture feeding his mare, Bushey's horse attacked and kicked him, seriously injuring him. Bushey pleaded Sandy's contributory negligence.
blocks.held: Sturgis, J.: the keeper of a domestic animal known to be vicious is strictly liable as an insurer; the plaintiff need prove only the keeping, the vicious propensity, and the keeper's knowledge (scienter). Because negligence is not the basis of liability, ordinary contributory negligence is no defense. Only a plaintiff who voluntarily and knowingly puts himself in harm's way, or provokes the animal, is barred. Defendant's motion overruled; judgment for Sandy.
blocks.why: Contributory negligence does not bar strict liability, but knowingly encountering the danger does (R2d § 515).

blocks.name: Rylands v. Fletcher
blocks.topic: the origin of strict liability for dangerous land uses
blocks.facts: Rylands, a mill owner, had a reservoir built on his land. The contractors did not seal abandoned mine shafts beneath it, and when the reservoir filled, the water broke through and flooded Fletcher's coal mine nearby. Rylands himself was not negligent. (The case was Fletcher v. Rylands below; the names reversed on appeal.)
blocks.held: Blackburn, J. (Exchequer Chamber): a person who brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for the damage its escape naturally causes. Lord Cairns (House of Lords) limited this to a "non-natural use" of the land. Judgment for the mine owner.
