blocks.why: This is the source of strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities. Non-natural use came to mean an unusual use for the place, not merely something artificial.

body.text: One who carries on an abnormally dangerous activity is strictly liable for harm to the person, land, or chattels of another resulting from it, even if he exercised the utmost care (§ 519). The harm must be of the kind whose possibility makes the activity abnormally dangerous (Foster).

**Factors, § 520 (weighed together):** (a) existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land, or chattels of others; (b) likelihood that the harm that results from it will be great; (c) inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care; (d) extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage; (e) inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on; and (f) extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.

**R3d § 20 (all required):** (1) the activity creates a foreseeable and highly significant risk of physical harm even when reasonable care is exercised by all actors; and (2) the activity is not one of common usage.

items: **Typical examples:** blasting (Spano, § 1), storing or using explosives, fumigation, crop dusting in some states, and certain toxic waste and hazardous chemical operations.
**Not usually:** firearms use (Miller), driving, ordinary utilities, and transporting chemicals by rail (Indiana Harbor Belt).

**Policy:** strict liability makes the actor consider the activity level and location, not just the care taken, because negligence law cannot reach the decision to do the activity at all (Posner in Indiana Harbor Belt).

blocks.name: Miller v. Civil Constructors, Inc.
blocks.facts: Law enforcement officers were holding firearms practice at a gravel pit owned by Civil Constructors. Miller, on nearby property, was struck by a stray bullet that ricocheted out of the pit. He sued the pit's owners, including two counts of strict liability. The trial court dismissed the strict liability counts.
blocks.held: Bowman, J.: discharging firearms is not an ultrahazardous activity. Under the R2d § 520 factors, (1) reasonable care can make it safe, (2) guns are in common use, and (3) firearms practice at a gravel pit is appropriate to the place and has social value, especially for training police. Negligence, not strict liability, governs. Affirmed.
blocks.why: Factor (c), whether reasonable care can eliminate the risk, often decides the case.

blocks.name: Indiana Harbor Belt R.R. Co. v. American Cyanamid Co.
blocks.facts: American Cyanamid, a chemical manufacturer, loaded 20,000 gallons of liquid acrylonitrile, a flammable and toxic chemical, into a leased rail tank car bound for New Jersey. At Indiana Harbor Belt's switching yard in suburban Chicago, about 5,000 gallons leaked from a faulty lid or valve. Nearby homes were evacuated, and the railroad spent about $981,000 on cleanup, which state authorities required. It sued the shipper. The district court held the shipper strictly liable.
blocks.held: Posner, J.: shipping acrylonitrile by rail is not abnormally dangerous. Strict liability is for activities whose risks cannot be eliminated by due care, so that the only way to reduce them is to change the activity's level or location. This spill resulted from carelessness, which negligence law can deter. Rerouting hazardous shipments around Chicago's rail hub is impractical, and the shipper did not control the car in transit. The relevant activity is transporting the chemical, not the chemical itself. Reversed and remanded for trial on negligence.
blocks.why: Strict liability is for risks that care cannot prevent. Ask who controls the activity and whether a change in activity level or location is the real solution.

blocks.name: Foster v. Preston Mill Co.
blocks.facts: Foster raised mink on a ranch about two and a quarter miles from where Preston Mill was blasting to build a logging road. Mink are very nervous animals. The blasts frightened the mother mink during whelping season, and they killed their kittens. Foster told the company, which kept blasting. The trial court awarded Foster $1,953.68 on strict liability.
blocks.held: Hamley, J.: strict liability for an ultrahazardous activity covers only harm that results from the risk that makes the activity ultrahazardous, such as debris and concussion. The mink's reaction to noise and vibration came from their exceedingly nervous disposition, not from the normal risks of blasting. Reversed.
blocks.why: The scope limit for strict liability works like proximate cause. Note also the abnormally sensitive activity of the plaintiff.

blocks.name: Golden v. Amory
blocks.facts: Amory and others owned a hydroelectric plant with a dike along a river. During a hurricane, the river flooded to unprecedented heights, and water overflowed and damaged the Goldens' land. The Goldens sued on strict liability (Rylands) and negligence.
blocks.held: Lummus, J.: the strict liability rule for the escape of stored water does not apply when the escape results from an act of God the owner had no reason to anticipate. The flood was beyond anyone's anticipation, and negligence was not shown. Exceptions overruled; judgment for the defendants.
blocks.why: An unforeseeable force of nature is a defense to strict liability. A foreseeable storm is not.

items: **Defenses to strict liability:** assumption of risk (knowing, voluntary exposure) and the plaintiff's abnormally sensitive activity are defenses. Ordinary contributory negligence is not (Sandy), but most comparative-fault states now compare it.
**Plead negligence too.** If the activity fails the § 520 factors, the plaintiff still has a negligence claim.
**Products liability** is the other major strict liability field (13th ed. Ch. 15), but it is not on the syllabus.

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Private Nuisance (due 12/3), reading materials on Canvas. This section uses the 13th ed. Ch. 16 instead.

body.text: The defendant is liable when (all required): (1) its conduct is a legal cause of (2) a substantial invasion of the plaintiff's interest in the private use and enjoyment of land, and (3) the invasion is either (a) intentional and unreasonable, or (b) unintentional and otherwise actionable under the rules for negligent or reckless conduct or for abnormally dangerous conditions or activities.

items: **Plaintiff:** a person with a possessory or property interest in the land, such as an owner or a tenant. A buyer of the land cannot sue the seller in nuisance (Philadelphia Electric).
**Substantial:** a definite offensiveness, annoyance, or inconvenience to a normal person in the community, not a hypersensitive one.

**Intentional (R2d § 825):** the defendant acts for the purpose of causing the invasion, or knows it is resulting or substantially certain to result. Continuing after notice of the harm makes an invasion intentional (Morgan).

**Nuisance and trespass:** trespass protects exclusive possession against physical entry; nuisance protects use and enjoyment against noise, odors, smoke, vibration, light, and the like. The same conduct can be both.

body.text: An intentional invasion is unreasonable if (any one suffices): (a) the gravity of the harm outweighs the utility of the actor's conduct; or (b) the harm caused by the conduct is serious, and the financial burden of compensating for this and similar harm to others would not make the continuation of the conduct not feasible.

**Gravity of the harm, § 827 (weighed together):** (a) the extent of the harm involved; (b) the character of the harm involved; (c) the social value that the law attaches to the type of use or enjoyment invaded; (d) the suitability of the particular use or enjoyment invaded to the character of the locality; and (e) the burden on the person harmed of avoiding the harm.

**Utility of the conduct, § 828 (weighed together):** (a) the social value that the law attaches to the primary purpose of the conduct; (b) the suitability of the conduct to the character of the locality; and (c) the impracticability of preventing or avoiding the invasion.

blocks.name: Morgan v. High Penn Oil Co.
blocks.facts: Morgan owned a nine-acre tract with his home, a restaurant, and a trailer park. High Penn built an oil refinery on adjoining land about 1,000 feet from his house. Several days a week the refinery emitted nauseating gases and odors that made people on Morgan's land sick and interfered with their use of it. High Penn kept operating after notice and demand to abate. It argued that its plant was modern and carefully run, so without negligence it could not be liable.
blocks.held: Ervin, J.: a person who intentionally creates or maintains a private nuisance is liable for the resulting injury, regardless of the care or skill used to avoid it. The refinery was a nuisance in fact because of its location and operation, and continuing after notice made the invasion intentional. Negligence is not an element. The court found error on another point and ordered a new trial.
blocks.why: Intentional nuisance does not depend on negligence. Due care is not a defense.

blocks.name: Carpenter v. Double R Cattle Co.
blocks.facts: Homeowners sued Double R, whose feedlot had expanded to about 9,000 cattle, complaining of manure, odors, flies, and river pollution. The trial court refused instructions based on R2d § 826(b), which allows a nuisance finding when the harm is serious and the defendant could pay damages and still operate, even if the activity's utility outweighs the harm. The jury, told to weigh utility against harm, found for Double R. The court of appeals reversed.
blocks.held: Bakes, J.: Idaho declines to adopt § 826(b). A nuisance is not found where the utility of the activity outweighs the gravity of the harm. People in a developing state must accept some interference for the sake of important industries like cattle feeding. The trial court's instructions were correct. Court of appeals reversed; jury verdict reinstated.
blocks.why: Courts are split on § 826(b), which separates whether the defendant must pay from whether the conduct must stop.

body.text: **Dissent (Bistline, J.):** § 826(b) would require the feedlot to pay for the serious harm it causes without shutting it down; refusing even damages leaves the neighbors without any remedy for a real wrong.

blocks.name: Philadelphia Electric Co. v. Hercules, Inc.
blocks.topic: no nuisance claim by a buyer against a seller
blocks.facts: Pennsylvania Industrial Chemical operated a hydrocarbon resin plant on a site in Chester, Pennsylvania, on the Delaware River. It sold the site to Gould, which later sold it to Philadelphia Electric (PECO). Hercules acquired Pennsylvania Industrial and assumed its liabilities. Resins and chemicals from the old operations were found seeping into the river, and the state required PECO to clean up, at a cost of about $400,000. PECO sued Hercules in private and public nuisance. The jury found for PECO.
blocks.held: Higginbotham, J.: a buyer of land cannot sue the seller in private nuisance. The duty not to maintain a nuisance runs to neighboring owners and occupiers, not to a later buyer of the same land, whose remedies lie in the sale contract under caveat emptor. PECO also could not sue for public nuisance, because it suffered no injury different in kind from the public's (cleanup costs it was ordered to bear are not special injury). Reversed.
blocks.why: Private nuisance protects neighbors. Public nuisance requires special injury (§ 34).

items: **Coming to the nuisance:** a plaintiff who moves next to an existing nuisance is not barred, but the priority of the defendant's use is a factor in reasonableness and remedy (Spur, § 34).
[[**Right-to-farm statutes** in most states protect established agricultural operations from nuisance suits by later neighbors.]]

**Bias lens:** [[polluting land uses have long been sited near low-income communities and communities of color, the subject of the environmental justice movement. The § 827(d) factor, suitability to "the character of the locality," can entrench that pattern if the locality's character is the product of past siting decisions.]]

blocks.text: **Reading:** Module on Public Nuisance (due 12/3), reading materials on Canvas. This section uses the 13th ed. Ch. 16 instead.

body.text: A public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the general public. **Circumstances that may make it unreasonable (any one suffices):** (a) the conduct involves a significant interference with the public health, the public safety, the public peace, the public comfort, or the public convenience; (b) the conduct is proscribed by a statute, ordinance, or administrative regulation; or (c) the conduct is of a continuing nature or has produced a permanent or long-lasting effect, and the actor knows or has reason to know that it has a significant effect upon the public right.
**Who may sue, § 821C:** a public official, or a private person who suffered harm of a kind different from that suffered by the general public (special injury). A private plaintiff need not own land.

items: **Examples:** blocking a public road or waterway, polluting a public water supply, operating an illegal business, and keeping a dangerous condition on a public way.
**Special injury:** personal injury, property damage, or a distinct business loss usually qualifies. Greater inconvenience of the same kind usually does not.

[[**Modern mass litigation:** states and cities have used public nuisance against makers of lead paint, opioids, and fossil fuels, with mixed results. Several state high courts (e.g., Oklahoma, 2021) have refused to extend it to the sale of lawful products.]]

blocks.name: Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co.
blocks.topic: permanent damages instead of an injunction
blocks.facts: Atlantic Cement built a $45 million cement plant near Albany that employed more than 300 people. Neighbors sued for injunctions and damages, alleging dirt, smoke, and vibration from the plant damaged their property. The trial court found a nuisance but refused an injunction, awarding temporary damages to the time of trial and leaving the neighbors to bring successive suits for later damages.
blocks.held: Bergan, J.: New York's rule was that a nuisance causing substantial damage must be enjoined, even if the defendant's cost of abating far exceeds the harm. But closing the plant would be drastic, and controlling air pollution is a matter for government, not private litigation. The court ordered an injunction that would be vacated once the plant paid permanent damages for the present and future harm to the plaintiffs' land, in effect granting the plant a servitude. Reversed and remanded to set permanent damages.
blocks.why: The defendant can, in effect, buy a servitude to pollute. The dissent (Jasen, J.) said this licenses a continuing wrong and removes the incentive to reduce pollution.

body.text: **Dissent (Jasen, J.):** the majority licenses a continuing wrong; once permanent damages are paid, the incentive to reduce pollution disappears, and the neighbors are forced to accept a servitude for a private party's benefit, a kind of inverse condemnation without public use.

blocks.name: Spur Industries, Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.
blocks.facts: Spur ran a large cattle feedlot west of Phoenix in an area long devoted to farming. Del Webb bought cheaper farmland nearby and developed Sun City, a retirement community. As it grew, it came within 500 feet of the feedlot, and flies and odor drifted over the homes, discouraging buyers. Webb sued to enjoin the feedlot as a public nuisance. An Arizona statute defined a public nuisance to include a place in a populous area that breeds disease-carrying flies. The trial court enjoined the feedlot but gave Spur no compensation.
blocks.held: Cameron, V.C.J.: (1) the feedlot, lawful when established, had become a public nuisance to the residents of Sun City, who were entitled to relief, so the injunction was proper even though Webb itself "came to the nuisance" and would have been barred if it alone were injured; (2) but because Webb, for profit, brought the people to the nuisance, it must indemnify Spur for a reasonable amount of the cost of moving or shutting down. Affirmed as to the injunction; remanded to fix the indemnity.
blocks.why: The court protected the residents, who had a right to relief, while making the developer who created the conflict pay. This is the "fourth rule" in the table below.

rows: Damages only: the defendant may continue and pay
No nuisance: the plaintiff must tolerate the harm or buy the defendant out
Injunction conditioned on the plaintiff compensating the defendant

body.text: [[The four rules are from Calabresi & Melamed, Property Rules, Liability Rules, and Inalienability (Harv. L. Rev. 1972).]] On an essay, argue for the remedy that fits the facts: the relative harms, who came first, the number of people affected, and whether a court can supervise the remedy.

items: **Duty.** Is there a general duty of reasonable care (affirmative conduct)? If the claim is failure to act, does an exception apply (§ 21)? Is the plaintiff foreseeable (Palsgraf)? Premises: what is the entrant's status (§ 26)?
**Standard of care.** Reasonable person, adjusted for children, disability, emergency, or a professional (§§ 12–13). Is there a statute supporting negligence per se (§ 14)?
**Breach.** Apply the Hand formula or the risk-utility factors to the specific precaution not taken (§ 11). Custom (Trimarco). Proof: notice, mode of operation, res ipsa (§§ 15–16).
**Cause in fact.** But-for; substantial factor for multiple sufficient causes; Summers or Sindell for unidentified defendants; lost chance (§§ 17–18).
**Proximate cause.** Foreseeable type of harm (Wagon Mound); eggshell plaintiff; intervening causes within the risk (Derdiarian), rescuers, medical treatment; superseding crimes (§§ 19–20).
**Damages.** Compensatory elements, collateral source, mitigation; punitive damages if reckless or malicious (§§ 27–28).
**Defenses.** Comparative fault (do the math), assumption of risk (which kind?), statute of limitations (discovery rule), immunities (§§ 22–25).
**Allocation.** Vicarious liability (scope, independent contractors, nondelegable duties); joint and several or several; contribution and indemnity (§§ 29–31).

items: Treating intent as a desire to harm. Intent is purpose or knowledge of the consequence, and motive does not matter.
Forgetting that assault needs awareness and battery does not.
Applying transferred intent to IIED or conversion.
Allowing deadly force to protect property.
Calling a statute violation negligence per se without checking class of persons, type of harm, and excuse.
Skipping cause in fact and jumping to proximate cause.
Treating every intervening crime as superseding. Ask whether it was within the risk.
Ignoring the jurisdiction's comparative fault threshold, or doing no arithmetic.
Calling a failure to rescue negligence without first finding a duty to act.
Assuming an employer is liable for an independent contractor without checking the exceptions.

blocks.title: Working the three parts of the final

items: **Closed-book short essay (30 minutes):** state the rule with its labeled elements, apply each element to the facts, and conclude. Use case names only when they help.
**Closed-book multiple choice (30 questions, 60 minutes):** about two minutes each. Identify the issue before reading the choices, and watch for the element the facts leave out.

**Open-book essay (90 minutes):** spend the first 15 minutes on an issue list built from the roadmaps above. Use this outline's tables to check elements, not to look up rules for the first time. Argue both sides on reasonableness, proximate cause, and policy, then pick the better answer.
